title: Anthropic previews Claude Duet personal AI agent for subscribers
summary: Anthropic said Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for paying subscribers. Here's what it can do.
story: Anthropic has joined the race to develop AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of humans with Claude Duet, a new app it previewed this week.
The agent competes with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, rival developers' agents that are already popular with consumers.
Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for Claude U.S. Pro and Max subscribers, according to Anthropic.
What can Claude Duet do?
Claude Duet works as a "proactive agent" for human customers, taking autonomous actions to complete tasks assigned to it.

"It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said, noting that it was designed for professionals and small business owners "with more on their plates than they can track."
Anthropic said Claude Duet's utility lies in its superior judgment, describing it as smart enough to know what to prioritize and which tasks require a user's attention.

Each morning, Claude Duet sends its user a daily brief outlining the day's most important items. For the agent to have context, it must be connected to a person's apps, like their email accounts and calendars. Some security professionals have raised concerns about new AI agents' access to such information, warning users to limit how much they share.
"Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work," Anthropic said.
What about security issues?
Anthropic highlighted built-in security measures that it says make the app safe to use, noting that the agent never directly sees a person's passwords or sign-in tokens.

Claude Duet can also handle administrative tasks like scheduling meetings and creating financial or sales forecasts. It can build web apps, too, Anthropic said. It can draft job postings or make purchases on a business owner's behalf.
Anthropic researchers who have tested the app have used it to manage their to-do lists, build apps, schedule interviews and more.
How do you sign up?
Anthropic said people can sign up on the waitlist at its Claude Duet product page.
Invitations are issued in waves, and the product is only available in the U.S. during its research preview, the company said.
"We're adding people gradually, and you'll get an email when it's your turn," the company said.

title: What to know about ACA open enrollment this year
summary: As open enrollment for Affordable Care Act health insurance kicks off, consumers face rising premiums, additional identity checks, and fewer brokers.
story: Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.
Shoppers need to plan accordingly.
Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts start earlier, and some states are already allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.

A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.

But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.
Have your ID ready

One of the biggest changes will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents via requirements aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.

The new rules, outlined in a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services FAQ, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.

For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.

Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed "high-risk" must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as "high-risk" first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.

Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because "someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer."

The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.
The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned "that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing" and may just give up and not get insured.

Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian's help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver's license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.

"Some people may have trouble not because they're not real, but because they don't have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names," said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
She said the changes might "be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles."
There may be fewer brokers

CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.

CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of "significant compliance concerns" in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out "hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers" this year.

Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients' coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.
"Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense," he said. However, in the short term, "I don't know if they care about the chaos it will cause."

That's because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he's unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.

He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.
"They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long," Fine said.

Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.

"Just because you're a new agent doesn't mean you are fraudulent," said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. "All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won't be able to work."

It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown's Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. "If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early."
Costs will continue to be an issue

This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.
But most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will still receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.
The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.
This helps offset premium increases.

"For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same," said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst for HealthInsurance.org. "That's not to say it's great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that."
But there are other factors at work, too.

Last year's average premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers' fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs, inflation, and labor shortages.
For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.

Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.

"The biggest issue we will face is affordability," said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. "There definitely will come a breaking point for people."

Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.

"If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity," Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.

That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.

Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.

title: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner over alleged leaks
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official told CBS News.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, several sources confirmed to CBS News late Wednesday.

A Pentagon official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was accused of misconduct for allegedly leaking classified information related to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.
Sylvia failed three polygraph tests about sharing classified information with the press, the official said, adding that the case has been referred to the Department of Justice.
Two other Pentagon sources confirmed to CBS News that the firing was related to the polygraph tests, but said those accusations are not true.

Hegseth has made rooting out leakers at the Pentagon a priority, with sources telling CBS News last month that high-ranking military officials were subject to polygraph tests. Three staffers from his office were escorted out last year amid a leak investigation, but the Pentagon never released the results of any investigation.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell did not name Sylvia by name in a statement on social media, but said that "following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information."

"To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action," Parnell continued. "This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action. Classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it. Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
Sylvia's firing comes as President Trump weighs resuming strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, and was coordinating the Iran battle plan. Sylvia is the second general during Hegseth's tenure to be removed from what is known as a "J5" post, which is the lead on how the Iran war affects long-term planning. Sylvia's predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire in October 2025.
No replacement for Sylvia has been named.
The firing was reported earlier by The Atlantic.
After initially issuing a statement extending "the deepest gratitude" for Slyvia's 32 years of service, a spokesperson for the Joint Staff retracted the statement and issued a new one.

"Upon further review, we determined that the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances," the spokesperson said. "Out of respect for the servicemember and the ongoing personnel process we will not comment further."

Sylvia is a former commander of the 101st Airborne Division with multiple deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq, earned a Bronze Star for Valor. He was a Purple Heart recipient after being wounded in battle in that gunfight with the Taliban, and he had a storied combat career that spanned 32 years.

title: El-Sayed's faith, family under scrutiny in campaign. Here's what we know.
summary: If elected, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed would become the first Muslim U.S. senator in American history.
story: Few U.S. Senate races have captured the public's attention like the battle in Michigan between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. It pits a 63-year-old former FBI agent and former congressman who has strong backing from President Trump against a charismatic doctor and political newcomer who, if elected, would become the first Muslim U.S. senator in American history.

Trump and Rogers have made El-Sayed's identity the focus of their stump speeches. The president has called him "a jihadist" and suggested El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate" — derisive rhetoric denounced by critics as Islamophobic. At a recent rally in Grand Rapids, El-Sayed shot back at the president: "I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November."
Recent polls show El-Sayed with a slight edge on Rogers; a new poll out Wednesday from CBS Detroit and other Michigan TV stations shows him ahead by 7 percentage points.

As Election Day nears, reports about El-Sayed's faith and background have ricocheted around the internet. Several outlets, including the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, have discussed questions surrounding El-Sayed and his family's possible "ties" to the Muslim Brotherhood. The Democratic candidate emphatically told Fox News: "I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."

His campaign told CBS News they consider the topic a "bad faith attack" on his religion and family, meant to distract voters. He is "a dad and a doctor. He has spent his entire career working to keep Michiganders healthy and safe," a spokeswoman said. The campaign did not respond to detailed questions.
"I'm Abdul El-Sayed, man of faith," he said in one campaign ad. "That's a good thing."
An examination of El-Sayed's past writings and new documents obtained by CBS News provides a window into his pre-campaign worldview, and sheds light on the controversy. Here's what we know:
The candidate's mother

El-Sayed was born and raised in southeast Michigan. His Egyptian immigrant parents separated when he was a toddler. Following the divorce, El-Sayed's mother, Fatten Elkomy, moved away to Missouri and worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA) as a nurse. The FBI raided her offices in Columbia, Missouri, on Oct. 13, 2004, searching for documents and financial records linking the group to overseas terrorist organizations. She described being interviewed by the FBI to her local newspaper.

The IARA, which raised $20 million and did humanitarian work with children in Africa and Asia,  was shut down by the Treasury Department and Justice Department that same year, for violating sanctions and providing aid to al Qaeda and other terrorist groups. An expert witness in the case told The New York Times last week that the nonprofit was so small, with only 14 employees, that workers likely knew what was going on at the charity. Among the nearly 1,000 exhibits produced at the trial, 13 were letters Elkomy sent, documenting financial transactions between 1999 and 2001, the newspaper reported.
Elkomy was not accused of any wrongdoing.

El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, is a University of Chicago professor who posted on social media years ago that their mother had been involved with the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt. The social media posts were first reported by the Washington Free Beacon. In the 14-year-old posts, she wrote in part: "Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early '70s when she was in college."
"My family has long been MB [Muslim Brotherhood], but I have always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively," she posted on June 24, 2012.
El-Sayed told NBC News that he wasn't raised by his mother and that her ties to the Muslim Brotherhood were hearsay. "Are you serious?" El-Sayed said when pressed. "I have no ties. We have no ties."

El-Sayed described his mother as "smart, warm and charismatic" in his 2020 book "Healing Politics: A Doctor's Journey into the Heart of our Political Epidemic." His campaign said he is estranged from his mother. But there appears to have been some contact between them. The New York Post reported that his mother attended El-Sayed's medical school graduation in 2014. And in a 2021 column for his Substack, obtained by CBS News, he wrote he was "off to Columbia, MO to visit my mother for the [Thanksgiving] holiday."
The candidate's father

Mohamed El-Sayed, 74, an automotive engineer and former professor at Alexandria University, left Alexandria, Egypt, in his 20s when the government of Anwar Sadat was cracking down on militant students and professors who rebelled after the Egyptian leader made peace with Israel in the late 1970s. Abdul El-Sayed's book says his father's "political agitation against Egypt's increasingly brutal military dictatorship coupled with his proximity to young minds, made him a threat to the regime. He had to leave. There were few options."

El-Sayed's father fled to America where he pursued a PhD in mechanical engineering at Wayne State University in Detroit. The politician's book said his father was drawn to Detroit because "his name, the color of his skin and how he prayed shouldn't matter. … America was also the home of democracy, that thing he had so wanted for Egypt."
The candidate's father-in-law

Abdul El-Sayed met his wife at the University of Michigan, where both were prominent members of the Muslim Students' Association. Her father, Tayeb Jukaku, has held leading positions with Muslim community groups. Jukaku is a kidney doctor and a past president and current board member of CAIR Michigan, according to federal tax filings of the group. Jukaku also served on the founders' committee of the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA), according to their website.

Both organizations have been the subject of controversy. Supporters of CAIR, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, say it is a well-established civil rights organization focused on empowering American Muslims through legal advocacy, education and civic engagement. "Our consistent moral stance is the reason that extremist voices on all sides target our civil rights group with conspiracy theories, bigotry and even threats of violence," a CAIR spokesman said in a statement to CBS News.

Both groups were named as unindicted coconspirators in the 2007 Holy Land Foundation federal terrorism trial which found that U.S. nonprofits had funneled more than $12 million to Hamas. Neither ISNA nor CAIR was charged with any crime. Lara Burns, a retired FBI agent and the lead investigator in the Holy Land Foundation case, told CBS News that "the Muslim Brotherhood operated covertly through nonprofits" that it set up in the U.S. in the 1960s.

"The funding that flowed through the Holy Land Foundation was designed to support Hamas, primarily its social infrastructure  that it used to radicalize the population to believe violence was the only solution," she told CBS News. "They claimed to provide all sorts of aid to the needy and they did, but as with all things Hamas, nothing is provided without a price."
The Trump administration designated several overseas chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as foreign terrorist organizations in January of this year, including those in Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon.
Jukaku has donated more than $300,000 in support of his son-in-law's Senate bid, according to public records.
Muslim Students' Association

While a student at University of Michigan between 2003 and 2007, El-Sayed served as a board member and later "Brothers' Outreach Chair" for the Muslim Students' Association. The group was originally founded by Muslim students at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1963. The group spread to campuses across the country, and by the early 2000s, the largest chapter was at the University of Michigan.

The student association defined its mission around student support, religious accommodation, interfaith dialogue, and leadership development. Lorenzo Vidino, the director of George Washington University's Program on Extremism, said the group encompasses activists from various backgrounds. He says members and sympathizers of the Muslim Brotherhood played a crucial role in its founding in the 1960s. "While MSA was not a 'pure' Brotherhood organization, links to it were strong," he said.
MSA did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday.
The petition

After the Arab Spring, El-Sayed was one of 46 Egyptian-Americans who signed on to a petition to Egypt's new democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, who was a senior leader of the Muslim Brotherhood. The letter called on Morsi to crack down on allies of the country's prior authoritarian leader.
It read in part: "We, the leaders of the Egyptian community, support the revolutionary decisions taken by the president, and call on him to purge the media and the police as soon as possible…"

Some signatories have been contributors to El-Sayed's campaigns, including Amr Abbas, a cardiologist and member of Michigan's Egyptian-American community, who donated $5,000 to El-Sayed's gubernatorial primary bid in 2018.
Rogers voted in the Senate to maintain $250 million in annual aid to Egypt after Morsi came to power in June 2012.
The Substack

El-Sayed maintained a Substack column from February 2021 to at least December 2022, shared in emails with 55,000 subscribers. The columns range widely in topic and tone. CBS News viewed 233 posts. Regarding the Middle East, he wrote: "When President Biden claims 'unwavering' support for Israel, he is indeed, offering unwavering support to this status quo, which rests on the dehumanization of the Palestinian people who get neither rights or land."

"Claiming to support a two-state solution while supporting a regime that is actively destroying it isn't supporting a two-state solution," El-Sayed wrote in a column following the outbreak of violence in Israel and Gaza in 2021. "It's perpetuating a two-tiered society — freedom and democracy for Israelis, occupation and apartheid for Palestinians."
In an earlier column, El-Sayed criticized the "unquestioning support for Israel" in the U.S.

"We're told that it's because Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East," he wrote. "Yet, like Saudi Arabia, Israel's government is under the control of a small cadre of extremists — and the country has perpetrated shocking violations of human rights and international law against the Palestinians, whose land it has occupied for the better part of a century."
He added: "Perhaps there are so few democracies in the region because our country has so consistently backed dictators in the region."
In a column titled "Gaza," posted on May 20, 2021, El-Sayed was also critical of Hamas, writing: "Hamas is wrong. And its violent co-option of non-violent protest is part of the problem."
The endorsements
El-Sayed's Senate candidacy has drawn a wide range of endorsements, including from unions and grassroots groups, among them the United Auto Workers, the Teamsters and the Sierra Club.

The Democratic candidate also has received the endorsement of CAIR Action. Its super PAC, the Unity & Justice Fund, donated $115,000 to a committee supporting El-Sayed's campaign. And El-Sayed has public backing from Americans for Justice in Palestine, the political giving apparatus of American Muslims for Palestine (AMP).

Joyce and Stanley Boim, whose 17-year-old son was killed in a 1996 Hamas terrorist attack, sued AMP in Chicago federal court alleging that the organization helped fund the terror that led to their son's death. The Boims had earlier won a jury verdict against the Islamic Association for Palestine (IAP), an advocacy group started by Muslim students in 1981. They were awarded $156 million, but IAP shut down before those damages could be paid. The Boims allege AMP is the "alter-ego" of IAP. AMP calls the claim "guilt by association" and is fighting the suit.
El-Sayed's campaign didn't respond to questions about the groups' support.

title: Alaska gov. orders probe into Peltola over 2nd Dan Sullivan on ballot
summary: A report alleged that people aligned with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola denied the allegations.
story: Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy on Wednesday ordered an investigation into Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign after a New York Times report that people aligned with the campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as her main opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Dunleavy said in a post on social media that there had already been a probe by the Alaska Division of Elections, so he was ordering the Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

"Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy wrote. "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections."
Peltola's campaign and the Democrats' Senate campaign arm have strongly denied any hand in getting the duplicate Sullivan on the ballot.
At a campaign stop in Soldotna, Alaska, Peltola called the report a "distraction," according to Alaska Public Media.
"Nobody's waking up worried about ballot composition," she said. "Not even me. I'm worried about my bills. I'm worried about affordability in health care."

President Trump weighed in on Wednesday, telling reporters, "I think (Peltola and the other Sullivan) should be prosecuted." In an earlier social media post, he said the Democrat "shouldn't be allowed to run" and that the party had "crated fake candidates."

"I don't think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD," the president wrote in one of several Truth Social posts about the issue. "The Democrats cheated!"

Voters in Alaska's closely watched Senate contest are choosing between four candidates who survived a nonpartisan primary earlier this year. Those include Peltola and Sullivan, along with a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The ballot — which allows voters to rank the candidates rather than just selecting one — identifies the sitting senator as a Republican and an incumbent, while Danial J. Sullivan Jr. has no party affiliation listed.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that a Democratic operative who worked with Peltola's campaign and national Democrats helped encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run, citing text messages and interviews. The newspaper reported that it appeared to be part of a wider effort to draw more candidates into the race.

The second Sullivan has vexed Republicans for months, with the incumbent senator calling his same-name challenger a "sham candidate" who was trying to trick voters. Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those allegations and insisted he is genuinely interested in running for Senate.

State officials initially sought to keep him off the ballot, finding that he was trying to confuse voters and arguing his was not a "good-faith candidacy." The Alaska Supreme Court rejected that decision and ruled that the other Sullivan can appear on the ballot.

Last week, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the election from being certified if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion" about the dueling Sullivans, in what Attorney General Todd Blanche described as an effort to "put guardrails in place." Asked what he thought about the suit, Mr. Trump told reporters: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'Do it.'"
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Dan Sullivan's campaign, said in a statement in reaction to the Times' reporting that "Alaskans deserve the truth."
"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Adams said.
Democrats have denied any role in Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy. A Peltola campaign spokesperson said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

"Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," the campaign spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for the the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, or DSCC, also said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."

The spokesperson argued Republicans "have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns." The organization pointed to a man serving a 20-year prison sentence in New York who ran for Alaska's House seat in 2024, and an Arizona man who ran in this year's Alaska Senate primary.

summary: Opposition to the rapid emergence of data centers in states such as Ohio and Arizona has ginned up activism and unified voters. A range of public health issues have played into the resistance.
story: Page, Arizona — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health.
"I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers."
"There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said.

Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction.

The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building.

Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes.

It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds.
"Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio.
"That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending."

The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI, with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists.

Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies.

Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside.

Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing.

Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands.

"We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now."

A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts.
"Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition.
It cuts across politics
Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth.
Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.

Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned.

Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Mr. Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won.

Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Mr. Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support.
"This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in."
In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards.

The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Mr. Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new construction in their district.
The House seat they're vying for is considered competitive, and the contest could be pivotal in determining which party gains House control after the Nov. 3 midterms.
In Arizona, 57% of registered voters oppose construction of more large data centers, according to an August opt-in online poll of 1,040 registered voters by Noble Predictive Insights.
More than costs
Photos from across the nation featuring politicians at groundbreaking ceremonies for data centers held only a year or two ago are now campaign fodder.

That has become a big problem for some elected leaders in Ohio, where more than a dozen local referendums or initiatives related to construction of the facilities will appear on ballots — the most of any state.

The issue has forced its way to the forefront of the state's marquee U.S. Senate race. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is hoping to return to Congress with pointed attacks against Republican Sen. Jon Husted over the matter.

Roughly $2.5 billion in state and local tax breaks over the last decade have prompted Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech companies to erect dozens of data centers across Ohio. That boom has spurred protests across the state, organized by local residents who are worried about the health, environmental, and financial impact of the structures.
Brown has pinned the blame on Husted directly with ads airing widely across Ohio that call him "the face of data centers."
"They're devouring our farmland, sucking up our water, and using our energy," Brown says in one recent video.
A memo circulated by the National Republican Senatorial Committee in August and obtained by Politico described Brown's critiques as a big problem for Husted.
"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck," warns the Aug. 18 memo, which was shared with artificial intelligence companies.

Husted has rebuffed these critiques by framing the construction of data centers as a local issue. More recently, he has said he wants to make sure that the companies building data centers pay for infrastructure costs, including energy.
In a statement, Husted spokesperson Tom Evans reiterated that point, saying the senator believes "data centers should remain a local decision."

It's not just costs that voters care about. An early-October opt-in survey of 1,650 Ohio adults by Ohio Northern University and SurveyUSA found that 55% were opposed to data center construction. About two-thirds had a negative opinion of data centers' impact on their community's environment, and about half said the same about their impact on quality of living.
Opponents of data centers cite noise, air, and water pollution as a concern, according to a Gallup poll. Americans are more opposed to data centers in their area than nuclear power plants.

The air pollution comes from gas turbines and diesel generators that have been linked to cardiovascular problems, asthma, and other health risks. Cooling system chemicals, heavy metals, and construction runoff can enter the water supply or rivers.

"When they are fired up and powered by diesel, they emit a lot of air pollution like nitrogen oxide, and this pollutant can travel around the community and to those downwind," said Shaolei Ren, an electrical and computer engineering professor at the University of California-Riverside.

In Page, residents in July voted out the mayor amid backlash over the Council's approval of the land sale for the data center. Opponents of data centers say it's a warning to candidates in the midterm elections who back new construction.

Some residents in this picturesque town of about 7,000 people remain worried that the health effects could plague them if the project goes forward. Jan Boehme lives in a neighborhood close to the proposed site. From her front lawn with its "No Data Center" sign, she said she is concerned that a data center could become her new neighbor — and cause harms such as hearing loss.
"We're against it," she said. "In this area, there are a lot of houses, and I'm concerned about all the noise."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Judge rejects DOJ's push to force California to set aside ballots
summary: A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration's bid to require California election officials to separate out mail ballots received from roughly 20,000 people it claims are not U.S. citizens.
story: Washington — A federal judge on Wednesday rejected the Trump administration's bid to require California election officials to separate out mail ballots received from roughly 20,000 people it claims are not U.S. citizens.

The decision from U.S. District Judge David Carter is the latest setback for the Trump administration in its efforts to exert more federal control over election administration just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when voters will decide which party controls the House and Senate.

Carter said that the Justice Department's request for California to segregate and exclude more than 20,000 ballots violates "longstanding constitutional principles" giving states the authority to administer their own elections.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," the judge wrote in a 26-page decision. "In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too."
If he granted the Trump administration the relief it sought, either political party could "create chaos for their own political purpose to disrupt the election process," Carter wrote.
"Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve," he said.

Carter echoed concerns raised by lawyers for California and Los Angeles County about the accuracy of the list of people that the Justice Department said are not U.S. citizens, writing that its protocol for verifying citizenship "raises significant concerns."
The judge called the Trump administration's methodology for creating the list "vague" and said he "cannot conclude that plaintiffs' process is credible."
Carter also warned that requiring California election officials to set aside mail ballots received from those alleged noncitizens would likely lead to disenfranchisement.

"Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection," he said. "Individuals who have met the requirements of California's voter registration laws must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors."
The Justice Department plans to appeal Carter's decision and will seek an emergency order from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution," Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said in a statement.

During a hearing a day earlier, Carter appeared skeptical of the government's arguments that thousands of ballots should be set aside and not counted while election workers verify they were cast by U.S. citizens.
"I think there's always been an encouragement of people's right to vote, we the people, because when we exercise our right to vote, we exercise equality," Carter said.

The judge pressed the Justice Department as to why, rather than risk disenfranchising lawful voters, prosecutors can't instead pursue indictments after the election of those they believe voted illegally. He noted the Justice Department can rely on the envelopes from returned ballots, which have identifying information, to show a noncitizen voted in violation of federal and state law.
"The remedy as a good prosecutor is to make sure these people are prosecuted," he told Justice Department lawyers.

Carter said the Justice Department's request to separate out ballots from people the government believes are noncitizens until their citizenship can be verified would be a "monumental change" to election procedures while voting is taking place.

The decision from Carter, appointed by former President Bill Clinton, came after the Justice Department went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit on Friday and asked that court to require California election workers to set apart ballots from voters on a government list of 20,000 people it claims are noncitizens.

But the appeals court ruled 2-1 on Monday to dismiss the appeal, finding that the Trump administration failed to give the district judge "adequate opportunity" to consider whether to grant temporary relief.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit against California, its secretary of state Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk Dean Logan earlier this month after it sent them letters claiming that roughly 20,000 suspected noncitizens were registered to vote and had received mail ballots. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California.

The government gave the elections officials 48 hours to review its list of people it said are ineligible to vote and asked California to ensure ballots received from them are not tabulated until their citizenship can be confirmed.

Shortly after California officials raised concerns with the accuracy of the list and the Justice Department's demand, the government sued and asked the court to issue a temporary order requiring state election workers to sequester ballots from the suspected noncitizen voters.

The Justice Department has argued that California's refusal to segregate the ballots risks diluting Americans' votes. Additionally, because California is potentially commingling lawful ballots with those cast by alleged noncitizens, the state is thwarting Congress's efforts to protect election integrity, Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said during a hearing.
Federal and California law prohibit noncitizens from voting.
"There's an interest in the American public having trust and confidence in their elections," Essayli said.
He stressed that the Trump administration is not asking to void or cancel any ballots.
But California officials have denounced the Justice Department's lawsuit as a "reckless political stunt" designed to cast doubt on its election results.

Anne Bellows, a deputy attorney general for California, told the court during the hearing that the relief sought by the Trump administration — an order prohibiting California from tabulating ballots from the voters it identified as "likely" noncitizens — would be "incredibly disruptive" for election officials and a "recipe for disenfranchisement."

Lawyers for the state also said the Trump administration has not been transparent about how or when it received California's publicly available voter registration list, raising concerns the government used outdated information to come up with its list of the 20,000 alleged noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The Trump administration said that it "enhances" that voter data using a third-party service.

Lawyers for Los Angeles County, meanwhile, warned that it would be "impossible" for election workers there to segregate ballots returned by alleged noncitizens by the end of the election period, since they would have to review ballot envelopes by hand to identify those received from voters on the Trump administration's list.

And in court filings, Los Angeles County argued the Justice Department's data is "unreliable." Of the 20,000 records on the government's list, only just over 7,000 had addresses in Los Angeles County, lawyers said.

Additionally, a review of a sample of 200 records from the list found that more than half corresponded to voter registrations that were canceled or inactive, so no ballot was mailed. For the sample of 200 voters who reported their birthplace, just over 38% indicated they were born in the U.S., Los Angeles County officials said.

But an official with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said in a declaration filed with the district court that the agency conducted its own review of immigration records for the 200 people in the county's sample and determined none were born in the U.S.

The official, Nicolas Bartell, separately acknowledged that as part of an "ongoing" analysis of voter data, USCIS identified roughly 189 records "with minor data discrepancies" that were on the list of 20,000 registered voters sent to California.

Voting in California has been underway since early October, when mail ballots were sent out to registered voters. In Los Angeles County, more than 550,000 ballots have already been processed, lawyers for Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk, said. More than 3.5 million mail ballots have been returned statewide.

President Trump has for months claimed that Democratic-led states had voters on their rolls who are not U.S. citizens, though instances of noncitizen voting are rare. The president's claims are part of a broader effort by his administration to assert more control over federal elections.

Beyond the effort in California, federal prosecutors in Washington state asked election officials there to set aside ballots received from more than 400 people they allege are not U.S. citizens and warned legal action could follow. The Trump administration has also filed a lawsuit against Alaska election officials seeking to block certification of its Senate results if the incumbent, GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, loses.

title: Charges filed against activists who posed as Minnesota voters
summary: Activists who call themselves the Citizen Justice League said they were testing Minnesota's 53-year-old voter voucher law. Videos from the August primary showed them claiming to be registered voters.
story: Hennepin County prosecutors on Wednesday charged James O'Keefe, 42, and Cam Higby, 26, with felony unlawful voting and identity theft over videos they filmed during Minnesota's Aug. 11 primary, according to a news release from the Hennepin County Attorney's Office.

The office said both men visited multiple precincts in Hennepin County and misrepresented their identities by giving election judges the names of registered voters in the precinct, without those voters' knowledge or permission. The office said they posted the videos to social media to try to undermine confidence in Minnesota's voting systems.

The charges say the two visited three polling places in all. They did not vote or sign a voter oath, but they did apply for a ballot, according to the charges. The names they gave belonged to real voters with real addresses, the charges say.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to elections "will be held accountable." "You cannot go into a polling place and misidentify yourself and use other people's identities to our election judges as you apply for a ballot, whether or not you intend to vote," she said.

Moriarty said the system for identifying and responding to misconduct "functioned well during the primary," and that her office is prepared for the general election. She said the charges aren't meant to "send a message," but to make clear that what the two did is unlawful.
Secretary of State Steve Simon said in the release that any attempt to disrupt or deceive election workers "will not be tolerated."

The release cites a Minnesota law that bars intentionally misrepresenting a person's identity when applying for a ballot, depositing a ballot in a ballot box or attempting to vote by machine. It did not say when O'Keefe and Higby are due in court.
"I never voted, I never signed an affidavit, and I never violated a law," Higby said in a statement to WCCO.

The charges stem from videos seen more than 7 million times as of mid-August, in which activists who call themselves the Citizen Justice League posed as Minnesota voters. They described themselves as independent journalists trying to expose loopholes in Minnesota's election security. The group said they were testing Minnesota's 53-year-old voter voucher law.
The video begins with undercover activists, donning what they called Muslim costumes, using fake accents and claiming to be Minnesota voters vouching for the others.

Minnesota's voucher law is intended to help people who just moved to the state vote. It allows a registered voter to vouch that someone lives where they say they do. The law does not allow people to impersonate real Minnesota voters.

The video shows James O'Keefe, the ousted founder of Project Veritas and now of O'Keefe Media Group, falsely identifying himself to election officials as William Pomeranz. CBS News Minnesota spoke to the real William Pomeranz, who, on Election Day, kept getting odd messages.
"I actually had a student contact me that had showed me what was online about my identity being misrepresented. So, that was pretty much a shock. I found out on Friday," Pomeranz said.
"Kudos to the poll workers. They reported it afterwards, and frankly, I got to vote that evening without a problem. So, you know, the voting process, in my mind, worked," Pomeranz said.
"It's illegal in the state of Minnesota to impersonate another voter, and this is apparently what O'Keefe did," David Schultz, a constitutional law professor at Hamline University, said in August.
In August, Schultz, Pomeranz and Simon said the video shows the system worked.
"As I read the law, you can't impersonate another registered voter, and that's exactly what they appear to have filmed themselves doing," Simon said at the time.

In 2024, Project Veritas and O'Keefe said in statements that they were not aware of any evidence of election fraud at an Erie, Pennsylvania, post office, after a postmaster's defamation lawsuit over their 2020 videos was settled, the Associated Press reported.

title: "Your vote is your voice": A look at why voting matters
summary: Why is it important to vote even if the president isn't on the ballot? House and Senate control, governor's mansions, ballot questions and more that will be determined by the 2026 midterm elections.
story: Brody Saner, a college student in Kansas says he believes it's his duty to vote."If there's something you're not happy with, go out and vote. Do your part to change it."

Early voting is underway throughout the country in the 2026 midterm elections and Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. All 435 seats in the House are on the ballot, and voters in 35 states will be electing senators, 36 states will be voting in governor's races and there are more than 150 ballot measures across 40 states. The people and policies elected will shape the future of the Iran War, AI regulation and so much more.

However, midterm elections tend to draw millions fewer voters than presidential, despite being "arguably more opportune moments for voters to get what they want," according to Professor Donald Green, a Columbia University political scientist who has spent three decades studying voting, "because relatively small shifts in the overall vote can lead to dramatic shifts in policy."
Here's what's at stake and why the experts say showing up matters:
Why is voting important in general?
"Your vote is your voice," said Kansas voter Tracy Preisser when asked why she thinks it's important to vote. And it's true. Voting decides who writes the rules communities live under.

At the national level, which party controls the House and the Senate is at stake. And whether the Democrats or the Republicans win will determine whether Congress acts as a check or an enabler on presidential power for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Locally, candidates down the ballot vote play a part in deciding taxes, the price of a doctor's visit, school funding, or who sits on the bench in a local court.

But a CBS News/YouGov poll conducted found that most voters don't believe that either party has a plan to make people better off. The majority of voters believed that they wouldn't be better off financially regardless of which party wins the electorate.

This sentiment is leading some voters to consider sitting this election out. "I just don't trust anybody at this point enough to vote for them, Republican [or] Democrat," says Kansas farmer Mandy Sieren. "I think they're all crooked."

To that, Green would argue that "although they might be dissatisfied with both parties, typically it comes down to the candidates themselves, and [voters] have to make an informed choice one way or the other," he said.
Why does your vote in midterm elections matter?

By some metrics, midterm elections are when a person's vote can matter the most, because less people participate in them. In the 2022 midterms, 46% of eligible voters cast ballots, compared to 65% in the 2024 presidential elections. The smaller the electorate, the more weight each ballot carries.

And the margins can be razor-thin. In  Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert race in the 2022 midterm election, she held onto her Colorado seat by 546 votes. In 2024, Democrat Adam Gray won California's 13th Congressional District by just 187 votes. And in  2020, Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks won her Iowa House race by just six votes. This round of elections is expected to have some equally contentious races.
But Green says voting isn't only about an individual's ballot. What matters, he said, is who shows up as a group.

"It may be surprising to them how attentive politicians are… to which groups vote at high rates and which groups don't," says Green. He says that this is the reason that candidates tend to pay more attention to older voters, who are most likely to vote, and issues important to young and poor people, who vote less frequently, "are often devalued."
How could votes in the 2026 midterm elections impact our country?

Midterm elections are when voters most often change the course in Washington, and are a check on the president's power halfway through a term. The president's party has lost seats in 37 of the past 41 midterm elections
And this time around, control of both chambers of Congress is in play, and the margins couldn't be slimmer.

In the house, Republicans currently hold a narrow majority. Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to win control. In the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber. Whoever controls Congress will decide whether more funding for the Iran War is approved or if AI regulation is proposed, amongst countless other pieces of potential legislation.

Meanwhile, more than 30 states are electing governors, with competitive races from Georgia to Ohio. Governors have immense power over the fate of the data center buildout, because of their power to approve moratoriums, decide on tax breaks, and appoint utility commissioners. And there are 41 ballot initiatives on data centers across 13 states.
In New York City, voting is personal for poll worker Sandra Strother. She says her uncle was killed trying to vote in Alabama in the 1950s because he was an African American.
"That's my great motivator" she says for why she makes time not just to vote herself, but to ensure others can too.

title: SPLC alleges DOJ is treating witness as a member of prosecution team
summary: The group's lawyers are asking a judge to let them subpoena a former SPLC informant who has been voluntarily providing material to the government.
story: Washington — Lawyers for the Southern Poverty Law Center are asking a judge to allow them to subpoena a former informant who has provided material to the Justice Department, saying that investigators are treating the witness like he is "part of the prosecutorial team itself."

Defense attorneys for the civil rights nonprofit accused the government on Wednesday of obtaining troves of documents, recordings and intelligence briefings using peculiar PowerPoint presentations from the source, known as "F-9," without a subpoena or search warrant.

Investigators typically obtain information from witnesses using subpoenas or search warrants so they can authenticate the material at trial and ensure that all relevant documents are produced. One former federal prosecutor told CBS News that obtaining evidence without taking either step, while not unheard of, was unusual — particularly with a witness like the one in this case.
In their motion to the court, they asked the judge to order the former informant to preserve all of his original documents and allow the group's lawyers to subpoena the witness themselves.

"To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a witness in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them," SPLC's attorneys wrote.
"F-9 admitted that he has a 'house full of documents,' some of which he has referenced plans to 'shred.'"

The Southern Poverty Law Center has been indicted on 11 counts of wire fraud, bank fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors alleged it defrauded its donors and duped its banks by creating shell accounts to funnel money to insiders who belonged to the same hate groups it pledged to dismantle. The SPLC has pleaded not guilty.

The government later also charged the group's former executive Heidi Beirich with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to submit false statements to a federally insured bank. She has also pleaded not guilty.

In the indictment, the government alleged that Beirich had a romantic relationship with F-9. Prosecutors described F-9 as an SPLC informant who infiltrated the Neo-Nazi group National Alliance and even once broke into its headquarters to steal documents.
According to the defense team's court filing, F-9 was staring down a potential tax prosecution for failing to pay income tax for 30 years when he began cooperating with the Justice Department.

He spoke with investigators in March 2022 when the case was still being investigated for the first time. It was subsequently closed without charges being filed. He resumed his talks with DOJ again in 2025 when the case was revived, the group's lawyers said.
"Just since November 2025, F-9 has met with the government more than
20 times — including at least four in-person meetings. He has exchanged approximately 1,800 text messages with the lead agents from the FBI and IRS," the group's lawyers wrote.

"F-9 regularly sends the government's lead FBI agent reports on how his search for evidence against the SPLC is going. He is not a lawyer, but he gave four 'Intelligence Briefings' to the government, accompanied by 162 pages of PowerPoint slides that analyze what charges the government should bring against the SPLC, describe what evidence he believes supports the charges, identify possible witnesses, and suggest new investigative directions," the filing said.
Some of those PowerPoint slides, meanwhile, have been unintelligible.
One example included in the filing, for instance, depicts a flow chart featuring mathematical notations, with SPLC's attorneys noting: "It is entirely unclear what some of the information means."

The lawyers added that F-9 "has provided a vast number of documents and recordings, but has done so in a selective fashion, including sending clips made from secret recordings when he possesses the full recording, seemingly sending only what supports his view of the SPLC."

"At the center of this baseless investigation is an informant with every incentive to tell the government what it wants to hear. He faced possible criminal exposure, blamed the SPLC for his financial problems, and told the government a one-sided and incomplete story to score his own broad immunity which the prosecution was willing to provide," SPLC's attorneys Abbe Lowell and Addy Schmitt said in a joint statement.

"Our motion also lays out how this immunized individual is not merely a witness, but someone who is so deeply embedded in the prosecution team that he tells them what to charge and provides only the information he wants them to see."
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

title: Lawyers question case against ex-FBI officials over Hunter Biden probe
summary: Defense attorneys for two former FBI counterintelligence officials accused of lying to Congress raised doubts about the strength of the evidence and the motives behind the charges.
story: A criminal case charging two former FBI counterintelligence officials with lying to Congress that was directed by Director Kash Patel could be in jeopardy, after defense attorneys raised doubts about the strength of the evidence and the motives behind the charges.

In a two-day hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., lawyers for Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides grilled FBI agent Bryan Witt about the details of the investigation, including its origins and what evidence the FBI had to assert that the pair willfully lied to the House Judiciary Committee about their role in the bureau's various Hunter Biden investigations.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said he wants to review the charging document and go line by line through each of the alleged false statements to see if there is probable cause that a crime was committed.
That review process is expected to take place on Thursday.

On the stand, Witt acknowledged that FBI agents did not interview certain key witnesses — including Floris herself or any congressional staff with direct knowledge about their testimony before the House Judiciary Committee.
Witt told defense attorneys on Tuesday that he feels confident in the veracity of the allegations against Benavides and Floris.

The defense lawyers also raised pointed questions intended to cast doubt on whether their clients actually made false statements, fleshing out the context of each question and noting how some of them lacked the specificity that would normally be needed in order for the government to prevail at trial in a false statements case.

When Floris, who did not work on criminal cases, was asked whether she was involved in the Hunter Biden "investigation," for example, the questioner did not specify which investigation — even though Witt acknowledged there were multiple different criminal and counterintelligence investigations involving Hunter Biden.
"Which investigation is she responding to?" Floris' attorney Margaret Donovan asked.
Witt said it was "probably" the FBI's criminal investigation out of the Baltimore field office.
"For her to give a false statement, you need to have an understanding of what the question is that she was responding to," Donovan replied.

Although Floris and Benavides were not part of the investigative team in Baltimore, the government alleges that they spoke with the team before they provided a defensive briefing on possible Russian disinformation to Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson.
The criminal case against Floris and Benavides has been highly unusual since it first came to light last week.

Prosecutors charged the pair in a criminal complaint, a charging document that is customarily only used in felony cases that pose exigent public safety or national security threats, rather than securing a grand jury indictment.

After midnight on the eve of the court hearing's first day Tuesday, prosecutors sought to add new charges of obstructing Congress with an unsigned and unsworn superseding complaint — a maneuver the magistrate judge said was improper and unheard of.
The magistrate struck the superseding complaint from the record, saying it lacked proper judicial review.  But he allowed the hearing on the original complaint to proceed.
Defense lawyers, meanwhile, identified discrepancies between the two versions of the complaint, such as whether a key congressional staffer was an eyewitness when Floris and Benavides testified.
As it turned out, the staffer — House Judiciary Committee Republican Counsel Steve Castor — was not present for the testimony nor had he reviewed the transcript, Witt later admitted.

He also acknowledged that agents were not permitted to interview any other congressional staffers for the case, an issue that defense attorneys said raises concerns about whether the alleged false statements were material to the congressional investigation.
"Did you approach any Democrats for their view on materiality?" Donovan asked.
"Absolutely not," Witt said, adding that agents were instructed to submit written questions only.
"Do you understand there is a general counsel for the Democrats?" Donovan asked.
"No one explained to me the partisanship nature" of the committee, Witt said.

Prosecutors told the judge on Tuesday that the FBI was limited in its interactions with the committee because of the Constitution's Speech and Debate clause, which insulates the legislative branch's deliberative process from the executive branch.

In a stunning admission, Witt acknowledged that Patel told his supervisor in the Kansas City field office to open the investigation, just one day after President Trump gave a televised speech where he directed the Justice Department to look at an alleged cover-up by intelligence officials related to efforts by China to interfere in the 2020 election.

The White House released a trove of classified records in conjunction with the speech, some of which showed that Floris had played a role in recalling a classified report prepared by an analyst in the Albany field office alleging that China produced fraudulent drivers licenses to manufacture mail-in votes amid concerns about the source's credibility.
Witt testified that he was initially directed to investigate the former FBI officials to see if they suppressed evidence about China.

But the investigation, which Witt told defense lawyers he feared might be viewed as "political," later shifted after agents began reviewing transcripts of testimony that Benavides and Floris provided to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023.

The involvement of Patel, whom defense attorney Margaret Donovan said had effectively "injected himself as a witness and almost a case agent" into the investigation, marked the latest in a string of oddities.

Witt on Wednesday testified that both Patel and the deputy director of the FBI were "closely monitoring our progress" on the case, and that he and his coworkers would "routinely" provide updates to FBI headquarters.
In at least two instances, he said Patel participated with the case team on video conferences and FBI deputy directors also visited the Kansas City field office in person.

Prosecutors later told the magistrate judge that the testimony about the origins of the case was not relevant to a probable cause finding, saying those kinds of issues could be raised at a later time.
"This has gone a little bit far astray from the limited purpose of this hearing," prosecutor Cory Jacobs said, adding that he feared it was "hard to unring that bell."

title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil, lands in U.S. after election loss
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential election, left the country with his family and State Department official told CBS News they would receive U.S. visas.
story: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family left the country on Tuesday after he lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend, and landed in Miami Wednesday morning.
Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News that Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.

Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, departed Brazil for the U.S. days after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election. En route to the U.S., Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters first arrived in Argentina and then took a private plane to Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to Argentinian officials and flight tracking data.
In a letter to the Brazilian people posted on X, Bolsonaro called the election results illegitimate and accused the government of targeting him for persecution.

"Facing the political weaponization of Justice in Brazil, I decided to move with my family to the United States, where we are safe. I personally thank President Trump and the American government for welcoming us," he said in the letter, translated from the Portuguese. He added, "I want to make it clear: I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil."
Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."
Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."
Mr. Trump told reporters early Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., though he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
"It would be OK with me," Mr. Trump said.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.
"This is what the Bolsonaro family is like: Brazil is their second nation, the U.S. is the first," Lula said Tuesday, according to Reuters.

Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
