title: Apple's first foldable phone broke within hours, some owners say
summary: "I didn't even make it through setup," one consumer said after his new iPhone Duo cracked shortly after he bought it.
story: Apple's first foldable iPhone went on sale on Oct. 23, and some new owners report that their devices are already broken.

Within days of the new iPhone Duo hitting stores, photos and videos of cracked screens began popping up online. Consumers said the device's inner screen broke down the middle near the hinge where the phone folds, leaving a line across the display.
The Duo, whose price starts at nearly $2,000 and tops $3,000 for higher-end models, represents Apple's biggest bet in years and the first major product rollout under new Apple CEO John Ternus.
"Loud pop"

Jesse Dalton, who lives near Frisco, Texas, bought the Duo the day it came out. He told CBS News he had just put a case on the phone and went to open the device when it "just got super tight about halfway up the hinge."

"Just pushed past it, assuming it was just stuck on the case or something for some reason, and the whole thing just snapped. I just heard a loud pop, and the screen just cracked right in the middle," Dalton said.
"I didn't even make it through setup," he added.
Dalton said he paid about $800 for the 512-gigabyte model after an AT&T trade-in promotion, bringing the full retail price to around $2,200.
A local Apple Store had a replacement on hand, he noted. "So they had one, and they were able to swap it out immediately. So I was in and out like 30 minutes."
But Dalton voiced concern about the phone's durability.
"Every time I open it, I kind of have a little pause where I'm waiting to see if it catches that same way," he said.
Justin Smith bought a Duo as a graduation gift for his wife, Roneshia. She said it cracked the following morning, less than 24 hours after purchase.
"We both woke up, and like most people, I grabbed my phone off the nightstand. I went to open it up like a book, and I realized I just could not get it open. It was a lot of resistance," she said.

"When I finally was able to get it opened, that's when we heard the crack noise, like an egg cracking. We just totally just started laughing basically because we were, like, no way, it's been less than 24 hours," Roneshia added.

After taking her device to an Apple Store, she said the staff said they were unable to fix it and that the only option was a replacement. But because the phone is backordered, she's unsure when she'll receive a new Duo. "I'm kind of stuck in this limbo."
What Apple says
Apple told CBS News it is aware that some Duo owners are reporting problems with the phone.

"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," the company said in a statement. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

Lance Ulanoff, editor at large at technology news website TechRadar, said the Duo's folding screen consists of multiple layers, including an OLED panel, glass, a plastic covering and a mechanical hinge. The ultra-thin glass could be the most fragile part, he said.
Apple's quick acknowledgment of an issue with the device is also unusual, Ulanoff noted.
"I honestly was shocked that Apple responded and acknowledged that they had seen a small number of these things. That's not typical of Apple to do that," he said.

Ulanoff, who said he had been using a Duo for a week and a half, hasn't had trouble with his own device. "I think that this right now looks like a blip. We'll keep an eye on it if it becomes more than that."
Ulanoff said owners with a damaged Duo should go to Apple, and he recommends making an appointment at an Apple Store rather than walking in.
"I would be making a beeline right back to Apple," he said.
The reports came as Apple prepared for another product event in Los Angeles this week, where the company is expected to unveil a touchscreen laptop.

title: Jury selection begins in Meta, Snap social media addiction case
summary: The plaintiffs allege that features on the companies' social media platforms, like endless scrolling, kept them hooked and harmed their mental health.
story: Jury selection begins today in Los Angeles for a trial against Meta and Snap brought by two plaintiffs who claim the companies' platforms were designed to be addictive — the latest in a wave of cases focusing on social media's impact on young people's mental health.
The plaintiffs sued in 2023, alleging that endless scrolling, Snapstreaks and other features on social media platforms kept them hooked and harmed their mental health.

The first, a 16-year-old from Illinois identified in court documents as S.J., started using Snapchat as a young child and alleges the app's features led to compulsive use and contributed to depression, reduced sleep, anxiety, an eating disorder, suicidal ideation and self-harm. The other plaintiff, K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, said her use of Meta's platforms and Snapchat from a young age also contributed to mental health issues and self-harm.

"Defendants defectively designed the platforms to specifically appeal to and addict minors and young adults, who were particularly unable to appreciate the risks posed by the platforms, and particularly susceptible to harms from those products," the plaintiffs' lawyers argued in the complaint, filed in a Los Angeles trial court.
TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube were part of the original lawsuit, but settled ahead of the trial. Meta also settled with S.J., the Illinois plaintiff.
A spokesperson for Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said the company disagrees with allegations brought by K.D.B.

"A young person's mental health is shaped by many factors, as the evidence in this trial will show," the spokesperson said in an email. "The plaintiff used TikTok far more than Instagram or Facebook, and her personal circumstances were a substantial factor in her struggles."
A spokesperson for Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, also disputed the claims and defended the company's actions.

"We have built safeguards into the platform, introduced safety tools and educational resources, and we believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs' experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed," they said in a statement.
The companies are expected to argue that other factors, not their platforms, were responsible for the plaintiffs' mental health issues.
Plaintiffs are seeking an unspecified amount in compensatory and punitive damages.

"This will be the first case against Snapchat and the first time the public has a chance to see some of their documents," Mark Lanier, the founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in an email.

Instagram head Adam Mosseri, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel are all expected to take the stand during the trial, which the plaintiffs' lawyers say will likely run until mid-December. Opening statements are scheduled to begin in early November, with Judge Carolyn Kuhl presiding.
Earlier this week, Meta and Snap requested that the cases be split into two separate trials — a matter Judge Kuhl has yet to rule on, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The case was selected as one of several bellwether cases for a trove of similar claims brought against social media players in recent years. It could intensify scrutiny of social media platforms at a time when many are already wary of the technology's impact on young people. Nearly half of teens said they're online almost constantly, according to a 2024 Pew Research Center survey of U.S. teens ages 13 to 17.

In a separate landmark case earlier this year, Meta and YouTube were ordered to pay $6 million after a jury found they were liable for creating products that led to harmful and addictive behavior by young users.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: DoorDash gobbles up Instacart in $17 billion deal
summary: DoorDash's purchase of Instacart for $65 per share will unite two of the country's largest grocery and food-delivery companies.
story: DoorDash said Thursday that it will buy Instacart for $17 billion, uniting one of the nation's top grocery delivery services with a major food delivery company.
DoorDash, which will pay $65 per share for Instacart, said the acquisition will benefit communities by enabling more supermarkets to use Instacart's platform to run their websites.

"Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said in a statement. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
Consumers will benefit by having more stores to choose from, speedier delivery options and access to savings when they shop locally, DoorDash also said in announcing the acquisition.
"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," DoorDash said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada.

DoorDash was founded a year later in San Francisco as a restaurant-delivery business and expanded into grocery delivery in 2020 amid a pandemic-induced surge in demand. The San Francisco-based company later teamed with the supermarket chain Kroger in 2022 and with Costco last month.
The deal will beef up DoorDash's grocery delivery services, making it a more potent competitor to Amazon and Walmart.

DoorDash's most recent earnings report, released on Wednesday, shows its revenue grew 34% from a year ago. Its total number of orders rose 28%, a sign the company is continuing to grow in the highly competitive delivery business. By the end of 2024, DoorDash held nearly 61% of the food delivery market share, topping Uber Eats and Grubhub, which held around 26% and 6%, respectively, according to Consumer Edge.
Survival of the biggest

The acquisition is the latest sign of consolidation in the delivery services industry, which is increasingly dominated by larger players. As competition intensifies, companies like Instacart have struggled to maintain their market share. Instacart now commands 18% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms, down from 26% five years ago, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company.

DoorDash's acquisition of Instacart  also comes as more people migrate from in-person stores toward apps to order their weekly groceries. Nearly 150 million Americans grocery shopped online as of 2025, according to Capital One.
As online shopping becomes more prevalent, some companies are experimenting with personalized pricing, which involves using AI and consumer data to charge shoppers different prices for the same item.

The advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative has slammed the practice as unfair and predatory. In a months-long investigation last year, the group found that identical grocery items on Instacart could differ in price by as much as 23% from one customer to the next.

Federal regulators are now scrutinizing such practices. The Federal Trade Commission on Thursday said it has opened a probe into DoorDash and Instacart, along with seven other companies across retail and transportation, to examine how they set prices.

DoorDash, which has a market value of $73 billion, said the companies will operate as separate entities until the merger is finalized, which is expected in late 2027 or early 2028. After the deal closes, DoorDash said it plans to maintain Instacart's brand, technology and app.

title: Alaska gov. orders probe into Peltola over 2nd Dan Sullivan on ballot
summary: A report alleged that people aligned with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola denied the allegations.
story: Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy on Wednesday ordered an investigation into Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign after a New York Times report that people aligned with the campaign helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as her main opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

Dunleavy said in a post on social media that there had already been a probe by the Alaska Division of Elections, so he was ordering the Department of Public Safety to "investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted."

"Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support," Dunleavy wrote. "Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections."
Peltola's campaign and the Democrats' Senate campaign arm have strongly denied any hand in getting the duplicate Sullivan on the ballot.
At a campaign stop in Soldotna, Alaska, Peltola called the report a "distraction," according to Alaska Public Media.
"Nobody's waking up worried about ballot composition," she said. "Not even me. I'm worried about my bills. I'm worried about affordability in health care."

President Trump weighed in on Wednesday, telling reporters, "I think (Peltola and the other Sullivan) should be prosecuted." In an earlier social media post, he said the Democrat "shouldn't be allowed to run" and that the party had "crated fake candidates."

"I don't think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD," the president wrote in one of several Truth Social posts about the issue. "The Democrats cheated!"

Voters in Alaska's closely watched Senate contest are choosing between four candidates who survived a nonpartisan primary earlier this year. Those include Peltola and Sullivan, along with a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The ballot — which allows voters to rank the candidates rather than just selecting one — identifies the sitting senator as a Republican and an incumbent, while Danial J. Sullivan Jr. has no party affiliation listed.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that a Democratic operative who worked with Peltola's campaign and national Democrats helped encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run, citing text messages and interviews. The newspaper reported that it appeared to be part of a wider effort to draw more candidates into the race.

The second Sullivan has vexed Republicans for months, with the incumbent senator calling his same-name challenger a "sham candidate" who was trying to trick voters. Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those allegations and insisted he is genuinely interested in running for Senate.

State officials initially sought to keep him off the ballot, finding that he was trying to confuse voters and arguing his was not a "good-faith candidacy." The Alaska Supreme Court rejected that decision and ruled that the other Sullivan can appear on the ballot.

Last week, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the election from being certified if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses due to "voter confusion" about the dueling Sullivans, in what Attorney General Todd Blanche described as an effort to "put guardrails in place." Asked what he thought about the suit, Mr. Trump told reporters: "Well, I'm the one that said, 'Do it.'"
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Dan Sullivan's campaign, said in a statement in reaction to the Times' reporting that "Alaskans deserve the truth."
"Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along," Adams said.
Democrats have denied any role in Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy. A Peltola campaign spokesperson said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

"Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," the campaign spokesperson said.
A spokesperson for the the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, or DSCC, also said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."

The spokesperson argued Republicans "have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns." The organization pointed to a man serving a 20-year prison sentence in New York who ran for Alaska's House seat in 2024, and an Arizona man who ran in this year's Alaska Senate primary.

title: Brewers defeat Rays in 5 games to win first World Series in franchise history
summary: The win at Tropicana Field in Tampa gave the Brewers their first World Series title since their founding as an expansion franchise 57 years ago.
story: The Milwaukee Brewers are finally World Series champions after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night, taking the series 4-1.

Wednesday's 4-1 win at Tropicana Field in Tampa gave the Brewers their first title since their founding as an expansion franchise 57 years ago. It was just their second trip to the World Series, with the first appearance coming in 1982, when they fell to the St. Louis Cardinals in seven games.

Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of two-hit ball and rookie Cooper Pratt got two more hits and two RBIs to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.

"It's the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city's waited a long, long time for this," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. "We're so happy to bring it home to them. I can't wait to get back there and celebrate."
Misiorowski left the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee's dugout for the last three games.
The 22-year-old Pratt set a Series rookie record with six straight hits before a sacrifice fly in the sixth inning. Jackson Chourio set a five-game Series record with 11 hits.
"This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn't even feel real," said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June. "This is surreal. It only took four months!"

The Rays, also an expansion team, though from 1998, were seeking their first World Series championship as well, but the odds were stacked against the American League champions after falling behind 3-0 in the best-of-seven series. They were able to scratch out just one win with a dramatic come-from-behind 4-3 victory in the 12th inning of Game Four on Tuesday to avoid getting swept, but the Brewers finished the job the next night.

Pat Murphy's team displayed the resilience of the 67-year-old manager, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.
With their flame-throwing, 24-year-old two-time All-Star on the mound, the Brewers rebounded from Game 4.
"I don't even have words," Misiorowski said. "It's amazing, just watching my guys celebrate. And the city — I know they're going crazy in Milwaukee. It's awesome."

Pitching on four days' rest for only the fifth time in 34 starts this season, including the playoffs, the Miz had his longest outing since throwing 6 1/3 innings against the Cubs on Sept. 8. Leg cramps also forced him out of two outings earlier in the season.

Misiorowski, who broke the World Series velocity record with a 103.5 mph fastball on the first pitch of the Series last Friday, opened with 12 straight four-seamers between 100.9-103 mph. He topped at 103 twice among his 86 pitches, 58 strikes.

Misiorowski didn't record a strikeout in the first three innings for the first time in his brief career and finished with two, matching his career low. He was fired up after Yandy Diaz missed a cutter to end the fifth. The Miz pumped his fist twice and punched the air walking off the mound.
The NL Cy Young Award favorite allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter in a 3-2 victory in the series opener. He was 2-0 with a 0.84 ERA in the Series.
JoJo Romero got two outs, Abner Uribe recorded two more and closer Trevor Megill pitched the last two innings, allowing an RBI double to Chandler Simpson with two outs in the ninth.
Megill retired Richie Palacios on a grounder to second to end it, threw his arms in the air and was mobbed by teammates near the mound while Brewers fans celebrated in the stands.

Pratt, who was 4 for 5 with a tiebreaking solo homer in the 12th inning in Game 4, gave the Brewers a 1-0 lead off Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in the second. Pratt singled for his sixth straight hit in the series in the fifth and scored on David Hamilton's single off Kevin Kelly.
William Contreras hit an RBI double off Garrett Cleavinger in the sixth and Pratt added a sac fly to extend Milwaukee's lead to 4-0.

The teams combined to hit just four homers in the series, three for Milwaukee. The Brewers scored a major league-low 32.1% of their runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Brewers led the majors with 103 wins in the regular season and went 11-2 in the postseason, including seven comeback wins and a sweep of the mighty Dodgers in the NLCS.

Milwaukee's only other MLB championship was won in 1957 by the Braves, who moved to Atlanta for the 1966 season.  Brewers fans have been waiting for this moment since 1970 — the franchise began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee a year later.

Murphy's team finished what Harvey Kuenn's star-studded crew couldn't accomplish 44 years ago as the AL champions. Harvey's Wallbangers had five Hall of Famers: Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers. But Fingers missed the postseason with a forearm injury. They also had Hall of Famer Bob Uecker in the broadcast booth.

The Rays dropped to 0-3 in the World Series after defeats in 2008 and 2020. The only other clubs to lose in their first three Series appearances were the Brooklyn Dodgers (0-7) and Detroit Tigers (0-4), according to the Elias Sports Bureau.

The Brewers won the World Series at a time when owners are pushing for a salary cap from the players' association because they maintain small-market teams can't regularly succeed. A management lockout is likely to start Dec. 2 and could threaten the 2027 season.
This was the first Series since 1991 between teams in the bottom half of payrolls. The Brewers ranked 19th as of Aug. 31 and Rays were 25th.

title: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains high
summary: The U.S. central bank left borrowing costs unchanged this month after hiking rates in September for the first time in three years.
story: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday after hiking borrowing costs in September to clamp down on inflation.
The central bank left the federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4%, keeping it unchanged after raising rates last month for the first time in three years.
In a statement, the Fed said economic activity is growing at a "strong pace" while acknowledging that inflation remains elevated.
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal," Fed officials said.
Wall Street had forecast that the Fed would stand pat on rates. Investor reaction was muted, with the three major indexes remaining essentially flat after the Fed's announcement.

The Fed's benchmark rate is its main weapon for stabilizing consumer prices, which have crept up in recent months. The latest rate decision comes less than a week before Americans head to the polls for the midterm elections, where affordability issues will be top of mind for voters. President Trump has long urged the Fed to ease borrowing costs.
Stubborn inflation

During a press conference after the rate decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said economic indicators are moving in the right direction, citing robust consumer spending, a low unemployment rate and healthy overall economic growth.

He also said credit conditions — the terms lenders set for borrowing — have tightened for businesses and households since the Fed's September rate hike, a sign the economy is heading toward a "more durable period" of growth and price stability.
At the same time, he said inflation remains "too high" and acknowledged that the Fed hasn't yet succeeded in bringing inflation under control.

"On the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive, and yet Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the committee's objective for close to six years," he told reporters. "It's our responsibility to get inflation down."
Two dissents

Ten members of the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rates, voted to hold the benchmark rate steady. Two FOMC members — Fed Board Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank President Beth Hammack — voted to raise it by 0.25 percentage points.
"We just came out of a heck of a family fight, a serious, sober discussion," Warsh said Wednesday. "I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment."

Investors and Wall Street analysts widely expected the Fed to remain on hold in October, but many economists think policymakers will raise rates at their last meeting of the year in December and again in 2027.

"The two hawkish dissents, the wording of the policy statement, and prior comments from officials all suggest the central bank will hike rates in December," Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist for forecasting firm Oxford Economics, said in an email following the Fed's decision.

Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at investment advisory firm Pantheon Macroeconomics, said financial markets are pricing in an additional 0.75 percentage points of tightening over the next year as the Fed tries to douse inflation.
Warsh stays tight-lipped
Warsh demurred when asked if Fed officials would raise rates at their Dec. 8-9 meeting, citing his stated reluctance to telegraph his policy views.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now," he told a reporter.

The Iran war has kept global energy costs elevated, making it harder to bring down prices in the U.S. Last month, the closely watched Consumer Price Index rose at a 3.7% annual rate; core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.6% from a year ago. Both measures were above economists' expectations.
Solid economic growth and steady consumer spending are also exerting upward pressure on prices, complicating the task of taming inflation, according to economists.
What does this mean for your money?

The federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — influences the cost of borrowing across the U.S. economy. A rate hike can spur higher borrowing costs for bank loans, credit cards and auto loans, while boosting returns for savings accounts.

The Fed's pause in rate hikes could provide borrowers with some breathing room, Bankrate home lending expert Linda Bell said, citing potential relief for home equity rates. Still, consumers may be in for higher borrowing costs down the road. Matt Schulz, a chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, said it's possible some loan rates could continue to climb heading into the holiday shopping season.

"Even though the Fed is leaving rates alone this month, it might raise rates again at its last meeting of the year in December," Schulz said in an email ahead of the Fed's decision. "That is far from guaranteed, but it is something that Americans should be aware of. It means that the debt they run up during the holidays could get a little more expensive to pay off before the year ends, through no fault of their own."
A surprise change
While the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged was widely expected, Warsh elicited surprise by announcing changes to the central bank's meeting schedule.

Policymakers will continue to meet eight times throughout the year. But starting in 2027, one of those meetings will be reserved for discussion and strategizing on monetary policy, Warsh said. At that meeting, the Fed will not vote on interest rates or issue a policy statement.
By 2028, Warsh said he expects two meetings to be dedicated to policy discussion and six to issuing rate decisions.

The change aligns with Warsh's broader vision for the Fed. He has been vocal in arguing for more limited communication from Fed officials, known as forward guidance, to preserve their flexibility in setting policy.

"Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals," he said. "But it's equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point."

title: Whistleblower says DEA let fentanyl pills hit the streets
summary: DEA Special Agent David Howell tells CBS News the agency tasked with enforcing federal drug laws has allowed millions of fentanyl pills to hit the streets.
story: As New Mexico officials sounded alarms this month about a growing fentanyl crisis, a veteran Drug Enforcement Administration agent has alleged the agency has contributed to the problem by allowing the deadly pills to reach the streets.

"For three years, I've told my DEA managers that we're allowing dangerous amounts of fentanyl to hit the street, and we're doing nothing to stop it, and they didn't listen to me," DEA Special Agent David Howell told CBS News in his first television interview.

Howell, who is still an active agent, claims the agency tasked with enforcing federal drug laws has allowed millions of fentanyl pills to "walk" — a tactic in which investigators allow drug traffickers to distribute their product and then follow the trail to build bigger cases.
But because fentanyl is so lethal, Howell said the tactic has done more harm than good.
"We at the DEA have let drugs hit the street, yes. The difference was we were told not to with fentanyl," he said.

In 2023, Howell was part of a team tracking a suspect in Albuquerque from the air. Images obtained by CBS News from congressional investigators on the House Oversight Committee showed a person driving a white SUV picking up a child.
"We knew we weren't going to let the drugs … hit the streets or go to the house when we knew the kid was in the car," Howell said.
Agents in a black truck stopped the SUV, secured the child and detained the suspect.
"We took his drugs. We took his gun. It was in a little compartment underneath the seat that the child was sitting on," Howell said.
Howell said agents found between 6,000 and 7,000 fentanyl pills in the vehicle.
But he says they faced backlash for taking the fentanyl pills off the streets.

"We thought the U.S. Attorney's Office [for the District of New Mexico] would be pleased," Howell said. "Instead, they brought us into their office and chastised us. They were perfectly willing to allow that fentanyl to go to the house with the kid."
Howell's whistleblower complaint was first reported last June by The Associated Press and Albuquerque Journal.
New Mexico state Attorney General Raúl Torrez has sued the federal government over the practice of letting fentanyl walk.
"There's no escaping the conclusion that New Mexico moving in the wrong direction seems to be directly connected to this practice of walking fentanyl in this community," Torrez said.
Officials in the wider Albuquerque area have declared a state of emergency because of the rising number of fentanyl overdose calls they are receiving.

The DEA and the DOJ declined CBS News' request for an interview, but the DOJ provided a statement saying: "When this whistleblower came forward, DEA Administrator Cole immediately requested an independent investigation by DOJ IG. That investigation remains ongoing, and we cannot comment on the status of ongoing investigations." The DEA has also said, "If improvements are identified, DEA will implement them."
"Our city is being destroyed by this drug," Howell said. "That's why we're sitting here, and that's what I'm here to tell the people."

title: Ship sunk by infamous Nazi sub in 1944 found off coast of Maine
summary: The U-boat that landed two Nazi spies on the Maine coast sank the 400-foot steamship SS Cornwallis four days later.
story: A German submarine slipped through frigid New England waters and covertly dropped off two Nazi spies in Maine on Nov. 29, 1944. Their assignment was to gather intelligence in the United States at the height of World War II.

Just four days later, the same U-boat spotted a merchant ship in the area and fired a torpedo that struck its cargo hold. The vessel, a 400-foot Canadian steamship called SS Cornwallis, sank in just 10 minutes. Only five of the 48 people on board survived.

Now, more than 80 years later, the wreckage of the Cornwallis has been found. The ship was finally located in July nearly 400 feet below the ocean's surface, the Nomad Exploration Team announced this week.

The New Hampshire-based team said it had to contend with cold water, strong currents and remote locations to reach the massive vessel. Finally, side scan sonar revealed the wreck, and later dives confirmed the vessel's identity, the team said.

"For the team, finding the wreck was the culmination of years of persistence," said dive team member Danny Allan. "For the families and communities connected to the ship, it brings renewed attention to a largely forgotten tragedy."
The Cornwallis' final voyage

Launched in 1921, the Cornwallis was a 5,458-ton steam merchant ship built in Vancouver, British Columbia. Originally called the Canadian Transporter, the ship was later renamed Cornwallis after transferring to Canadian National Steamships.

On Sept. 11, 1942, while anchored in Barbados, a German sub fired torpedoes at the Cornwallis, severely damaging the vessel. However, the ship only partially sank in shallow waters and was later repaired and put back in service.

In November 1944, the ship left Barbados packed with a cargo of sugar and molasses, bound for St. John, New Brunswick. According to nautical historian Eric Wiberg, the Cornwallis was equipped with a 4-inch gun, a 12-pound gun and machine guns on the bridge. None of the weapons were ever fired.

On Dec. 3, as the ship moved along the Maine coastline, it was spotted by the German submarine U-1230, commanded by Hans Hilbig. The U-boat fired a torpedo that struck near the Cornwallis' bow and the vessel plunged below the surface in less than 10 minutes.

Only six of the 48 people aboard were able to reach life rafts, and one died of hypothermia. The five survivors were ultimately picked up by fishing boats, then transferred to a U.S. Navy ship that took them to Rockland, Maine.
"Underwater time capsule"

The demise of the Cornwallis gained notoriety when it was revealed what the U-boat had done just a few days before. On Nov. 29, 1944, the same submarine landed two German agents, Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh, near Hancock, Maine, to spy on the U.S. According to a 2018 Main Line Today article, Colepaugh was an American who traveled to Germany in 1944 to train in espionage. After being dropped off by the sub, the two agents ultimately made their way from Maine to New York City without being detected.

After the Cornwallis was sunk off Maine, American authorities launched an investigation to determine whether the same submarine had landed enemy agents on U.S. soil. The FBI later learned that residents had seen strangers roaming through Hancock, Maine, around the time of the sinking of the merchant ship.

Ultimately, the agents' mission came to a crashing halt in New York City. Colepaugh confessed to a friend, who contacted the FBI, and Gimpel was arrested just days later. Both men were sentenced to death by a military court, but their sentences were later commuted to life in prison.
While U-1230 survived the war until it was scuttled in 1945, the location of the Cornwallis long remained a mystery – until now.

"Lying at nearly 400 feet, the Cornwallis is no longer the ship that sailed north with sugar and molasses," the Nomad Exploration Team wrote. "She is an underwater time capsule from one of the most unusual episodes of the war along the Maine coast."

title: First map of U.S. Mason-Dixon Line going up for auction
summary: The first map of the Mason-Dixon Line dividing U.S. Northern free states from Southern states that had slavery decades before the Civil War is going up for auction.
story: It's perhaps the most consequential map in American history. And it could be yours.
The hand-drawn chart of the Mason-Dixon Line that eventually divided the free from the slave states is going up for auction.
Remounted on backing made of Japanese rice paper, the document will go on sale Thursday in a livestreamed event.

"It's not that often that you can really get this close to something that is so historically important," said Lauren Brunk, vice president of Brunk Auctions in Asheville, North Carolina. "And it was awe-inspiring, really."
Brunk estimates it could fetch anywhere from $800,000 to $1.2 million for the anonymous seller.
"Drawn between 1767 and 1768 by Charles Mason ... and Jeremiah Dixon ... the Mason-Dixon Line is the symbolic boundary between Northern and Southern states," Brunk says on its website.

The survey by Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon was originally meant to settle a border dispute between the then-colonies of Maryland and Pennsylvania. But when it was used in the 1820 Missouri Compromise to establish the limits of human bondage in the still adolescent United States, it became synonymous with the fundamental divisions that exploded into Civil War four decades later.
"The Mason-Dixon Line that most Americans know is this dividing line between the Northern free states and the Southern slaveholding states," Brunk said. "But the line was not drawn for that reason."
A popular theory is that the term "Dixie" comes from Dixon, though the true origin is disputed.

Soon after it was drawn, the linen-backed strip of paper -- 76 inches long and 6.5 inches tall -- was given to the family of attorney Benjamin Chew, who represented the descendants of Pennsylvania founder William Penn. The map remained in the family's hands until 1982, when late publisher Malcolm S. Forbes outbid the Library of Congress and bought it for $360,000, Brunk said.
At the time, it was said to have been the highest price ever paid at auction for an American map.
The map changed hands again in 2002.
A vertical section showing the Delaware-Maryland border is housed at Princeton University.
Brunk reached out to officials at the Library of Congress to see if they wanted to bid on it again.
"I wanted them to be aware that this was coming back to the market," she said. "And they said, at this point, budgets being what they are, they were just not in a position to buy it."
But if some patriot out there wants to purchase it on the library's behalf, Brunk said, "they'd be happy to have it."

title: Data center health worries animate midterm campaigns
summary: Opposition to the rapid emergence of data centers in states such as Ohio and Arizona has ginned up activism and unified voters. A range of public health issues have played into the resistance.
story: Page, Arizona — Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor — a proposed $10 billion mega data center — could imperil his health.
"I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers."
"There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said.

Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid desert studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction.

The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building.

Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes.

It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds.
"Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio.
"That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending."

The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power AI, with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists.

Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies.

Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California-Riverside.

Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing.

Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands.

"We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now."

A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market — Virginia — found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts.
"Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition.
It cuts across politics
Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth.
Two in 3 Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.

Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned.

Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Mr. Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won.

Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Mr. Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support.
"This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in."
In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards.

The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Mr. Trump. He says they are key to keeping up with China. Democratic opponent Amish Shah wants a pause on new construction in their district.
The House seat they're vying for is considered competitive, and the contest could be pivotal in determining which party gains House control after the Nov. 3 midterms.
In Arizona, 57% of registered voters oppose construction of more large data centers, according to an August opt-in online poll of 1,040 registered voters by Noble Predictive Insights.
More than costs
Photos from across the nation featuring politicians at groundbreaking ceremonies for data centers held only a year or two ago are now campaign fodder.

That has become a big problem for some elected leaders in Ohio, where more than a dozen local referendums or initiatives related to construction of the facilities will appear on ballots — the most of any state.

The issue has forced its way to the forefront of the state's marquee U.S. Senate race. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is hoping to return to Congress with pointed attacks against Republican Sen. Jon Husted over the matter.

Roughly $2.5 billion in state and local tax breaks over the last decade have prompted Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech companies to erect dozens of data centers across Ohio. That boom has spurred protests across the state, organized by local residents who are worried about the health, environmental, and financial impact of the structures.
Brown has pinned the blame on Husted directly with ads airing widely across Ohio that call him "the face of data centers."
"They're devouring our farmland, sucking up our water, and using our energy," Brown says in one recent video.
A memo circulated by the National Republican Senatorial Committee in August and obtained by Politico described Brown's critiques as a big problem for Husted.
"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck," warns the Aug. 18 memo, which was shared with artificial intelligence companies.

Husted has rebuffed these critiques by framing the construction of data centers as a local issue. More recently, he has said he wants to make sure that the companies building data centers pay for infrastructure costs, including energy.
In a statement, Husted spokesperson Tom Evans reiterated that point, saying the senator believes "data centers should remain a local decision."

It's not just costs that voters care about. An early-October opt-in survey of 1,650 Ohio adults by Ohio Northern University and SurveyUSA found that 55% were opposed to data center construction. About two-thirds had a negative opinion of data centers' impact on their community's environment, and about half said the same about their impact on quality of living.
Opponents of data centers cite noise, air, and water pollution as a concern, according to a Gallup poll. Americans are more opposed to data centers in their area than nuclear power plants.

The air pollution comes from gas turbines and diesel generators that have been linked to cardiovascular problems, asthma, and other health risks. Cooling system chemicals, heavy metals, and construction runoff can enter the water supply or rivers.

"When they are fired up and powered by diesel, they emit a lot of air pollution like nitrogen oxide, and this pollutant can travel around the community and to those downwind," said Shaolei Ren, an electrical and computer engineering professor at the University of California-Riverside.

In Page, residents in July voted out the mayor amid backlash over the Council's approval of the land sale for the data center. Opponents of data centers say it's a warning to candidates in the midterm elections who back new construction.

Some residents in this picturesque town of about 7,000 people remain worried that the health effects could plague them if the project goes forward. Jan Boehme lives in a neighborhood close to the proposed site. From her front lawn with its "No Data Center" sign, she said she is concerned that a data center could become her new neighbor — and cause harms such as hearing loss.
"We're against it," she said. "In this area, there are a lot of houses, and I'm concerned about all the noise."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: RFK Jr. to ease access to unapproved peptides, draft policy states
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps Wednesday that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.
story: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took steps this week that could open up access to certain unapproved peptide drugs that are being promoted for wellness.

In a draft policy filed Wednesday, Kennedy said he had determined that compounding pharmacies could prepare six specific peptides — BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax, TB-500 — even though they do not have approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
"By allowing limited compounding of the substances addressed in this guidance under appropriate safeguards, the policy provides patients with a more controlled alternative," Kennedy wrote.
Compounding pharmacies mix ingredients to prepare customized medications for individual patients.
Although they are not FDA approved, the six peptides in Kennedy's new policy are often still marketed with health claims.

The Department of Health and Human Services "did not intend to take action" against licensed pharmacies or physicians that compound "a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product," Kennedy's policy said.

Peptides are small proteins that can have powerful effects. There are several, such as insulin, that are FDA approved as being safe and effective. GLP-1 medications used for weight loss and to treat diabetes also contain FDA approved peptides.

In July, an FDA advisory panel voted to recommend allowing the six unapproved peptides to be used in compounding, although that decision did not constitute FDA approval. That vote, however, went against the recommendations of the FDA's own scientists, who said there isn't enough evidence of safety and effectiveness for each of the six peptides to make such a determination.
Kennedy cited that panel's recommendation in his decision, saying he had determined the policy "advances patient choice and freedom while appropriately protecting patient safety."

In a statement provided to CBS News, an HHS spokesperson said that pharmacies will have to do quality testing and safety reporting, and that should help patients know what is in these peptide drugs that are currently being sold by unregulated sources.

"The policy does not grant FDA approval or establish clinical safety and effectiveness," the HHS spokesperson said. "It requires patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality testing, and safety reporting to hold compounders accountable and give patients an alternative to unregulated sellers."
The draft policy requires an FDA-registered ingredient maker, a lab certificate for the raw ingredients, and reports of serious side effects.

In a CBS News investigation published last week, a laboratory test was conducted on an experimental peptide weight-loss drug known as retatrutide that was purchased from a bodega in Brooklyn, New York.
The lab test, however, found that the sample of retatrutide purchased from the bodega did not contain a peptide at all.

A CBS News investigation last summer found that dozens of clinics across the country, staffed by licensed physicians and nurse practitioners, have been openly advertising retatrutide even though it has not been reviewed by the FDA and remains in clinical trials by drug giant Eli Lilly.

Kennedy's draft policy will be open to public comment beginning Friday through Nov. 13. The policy will remain in place until the FDA finalizes a rule regarding compounded peptides. However, at this point, the FDA has not proposed one.

title: CEO says plan is to file for bankruptcy after ending luxury never-ending cruise
summary: More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs.
story: More than 200 passengers, mostly Americans, are stranded in Cambodia after the operator of a luxury U.S. cruise ship that was on a continuous around-the-world voyage ran out of money due to skyrocketing fuel costs.
Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based operator of the MV Odyssey, said the war with Iran quadrupled fuel costs and forced it to suspend operations on Tuesday.

CEO Mikael Petterson told CBS News in a phone interview Wednesday that Villa Vie Residences was paying an average of $700 a ton for fuel before the war broke out in late February. Since then, it has been paying anywhere from $2,000 to $3,000 per ton.
The Odyssey uses between 700 and 800 tons per month in fuel, Petterson disclosed.
"When you divide it over 300 people on board, it's just backbreaking," Petterson told CBS News. "And this has been going on for nine months. We've tried to do everything we can do."
In a statement, Villa Vie Residences said the per cabin fuel costs rose from an average of $1,800 per month before the war to between $6,000 and $8,000.
The company was unwilling to pass those rising costs on to its passengers, Petterson said.

The Odyssey launched in October 2024 for a continuous around-the-world journey. At the time, passengers could become residents of the ship by purchasing a permanent cabin for several hundred thousand dollars. Some sold their homes to do so. At the time, they were given a 15-year minimum guarantee of residency aboard the Odyssey.

The Odyssey attempted to counter the spiking fuel prices by slowing down its itinerary and spending five or six days in each port "hoping that things would come to a close in the Middle East," Petterson said, but it wasn't enough.
"For us, when our monthly expenses go up from $400,000 to $2 million, where are we going to get the $1.6 million?" Petterson asked.
The Villa Vie Residences CEO said that the ship ran out of money as it searched for a financial partner, and the plan is now to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
"We've borrowed money, we've stretched our payrolls as far as we can, and we're at a point where it's just at a breaking point where we need capitalization," Petterson said.
Passenger Benjamin Schatz thought the MV Odyssey would be his forever home.
"Honestly, right now, I'm in denial and in shock, and I'm heartbroken," Schatz, a retiree, told CBS News.

CBS News met Schatz in April 2025 for a story featuring Villa Vie Residences. At that point, he had been living on the ship for about one year. On Wednesday, he was given just hours to pack up his life and leave.
Said Schatz: "There are people now who are homeless and who have very little money and don't know what they're going to do."

title: Experts react to new findings on CTE in former NFL players
summary: A new study from Boston University looks at the rate of the brain disease CTE in former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023.
story: A new study from Boston University estimating that nearly 75% of NFL players who died over a 15-year period had signs of CTE in their brains is raising concern, and experts say it demonstrates the need to collect more data on the condition.

CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is a degenerative brain disease found in people who have suffered repeated blows to the head. It can only be definitively diagnosed after death. It has also been found in the brains of other athletes, first responders and military members, but is rarely seen in the general population.

The Boston University research builds on data published in The British Medical Journal in August. That data estimated that anywhere from 25% to 98% of ex-NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE. The broad estimate reflected uncertainty about how representative brain donors studied were of the overall NFL population, since brain donors are more likely to have symptoms believed to be related to CTE.

The Boston researchers looked for signs of the condition in brains donated by 387 players who died between 2008 and 2023 — a subset of the 2,362 former NFL players who died during that period. Ninety-four percent of the donors had some form of CTE. The researchers estimated that former NFL players with cognitive symptoms were 5 times more likely to have their brains donated to science than others, and estimated from there that 74.5% of players had some form of CTE. The research is published in JAMA Network Open.

CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook cautioned that that figure may be an overestimate. He noted that the research looked at how many former players had signs of CTE in their brain — not how many showed actual symptoms of CTE.

Dr. Kristen Dams-O'Connor, director of the Brain Injury Research Center at Mount Sinai, said the results of the paper "cannot and should not be interpreted as being representative of current living athletes." She pointed out that of those whose brains were studied, "many ... ended their careers long ago." In recent years, the NFL has implemented rule changes that are designed to reduce concussions on the field, and introduced more protective equipment, including Guardian Caps.
"This should translate to lower CTE risk in recent generations of players, compared to those who played decades ago," Dams-O'Connor said.
The NFL told CBS News in a statement that it "continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts."

Dams-O'Connor said that while Boston University used "strong methods" to adjust for selection bias in the data, there are still other gaps, such as accounting for the approximately 20,000 NFL players who could have died during the study's 15-year timeframe but did not. She also said the results could not be applied to the "vast majority of people who played youth football" or other non-professional contact sports.

"It's a helpful study in trying to look at the bigger picture, recognizing that those who donate their brain are more likely to have cognitive symptoms, and often are more likely to have had changes," said Dr. Jeremy Tanner, assistant professor of neurology at The Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's and Neurological Diseases at the UT San Antonio Health Science Center. "Even taking that selection bias into account, when you look more broadly, it's at a minimum 20 to 25%, which is eye-opening and really shows the need to both advance the research."
Searching for CTE in its "silent phase"
Dr. Jay Alberts, director of the Cleveland Clinic Concussion Center, said the data shows the need to look for early warning signs of CTE.

"We often think about neurological disease, including CTE, as having a silent phase. These things are changing, and we can't detect them," Alberts said. "But I don't think it's silent, per se. I think what we need to do is listen more carefully and use better measurements to understand what those changes are."

Those measurements could include studying a person's "instrumental activities of daily living," or IADLs, Alberts said. That includes skills like driving a car or balancing a checkbook, where a person must use both cognitive function and motor function simultaneously. In patients with Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease, IADLs start to change between five and seven years before a diagnosis is made. He said CTE may be similar.
"Those types of activities are really insights into brain function, and I would argue those are things that would help us to listen more effectively," he said.
Finding other signs of CTE

Understanding how a person's brain function may change during the early stages of CTE could make it easier to diagnose, Alberts said. That could also lead to interventions that might "slow it or even potentially reverse it."

Alberts and Tanner also highlighted research focused on determining if there are biomarker changes that could be connected to CTE. Ongoing studies, including one that has a study site at UT Health San Antonio, follow current or former players throughout their life to see if there are any abnormal changes to the body or brain over the years. Alberts called for even more long-term research, and Tanner said that such studies can benefit more than just former NFL players.

"This has really been a rapid area of scientific advancement over the last 10 to 20 years, and has led to breakthroughs in the new therapies for Alzheimer's disease, and hopefully (will) for many other neurodegenerative diseases like CTE, Lewy body disease, and others in the years to come," Tanner said.

"Hopefully we can develop tools and biomarkers to detect these brain changes during life, which will enable us to study these diseases during life, and in the best case, learn ways to better prevent or treat these diseases."

title: SPLC alleges DOJ is treating witness as a member of prosecution team
summary: The group's lawyers are asking a judge to let them subpoena a former SPLC informant who has been voluntarily providing material to the government.
story: Washington — Lawyers for the Southern Poverty Law Center are asking a judge to allow them to subpoena a former informant who has provided material to the Justice Department, saying that investigators are treating the witness like he is "part of the prosecutorial team itself."

Defense attorneys for the civil rights nonprofit accused the government on Wednesday of obtaining troves of documents, recordings and intelligence briefings using peculiar PowerPoint presentations from the source, known as "F-9," without a subpoena or search warrant.

Investigators typically obtain information from witnesses using subpoenas or search warrants so they can authenticate the material at trial and ensure that all relevant documents are produced. One former federal prosecutor told CBS News that obtaining evidence without taking either step, while not unheard of, was unusual — particularly with a witness like the one in this case.
In their motion to the court, they asked the judge to order the former informant to preserve all of his original documents and allow the group's lawyers to subpoena the witness themselves.

"To be clear, F-9 should have been merely a witness in this case. But the government has treated him like part of the prosecutorial team itself, choosing to allow F-9 to decide which of the documents, recordings, and photographs in his possession he will produce, and how and when he will produce them," SPLC's attorneys wrote.
"F-9 admitted that he has a 'house full of documents,' some of which he has referenced plans to 'shred.'"

The Southern Poverty Law Center has been indicted on 11 counts of wire fraud, bank fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors alleged it defrauded its donors and duped its banks by creating shell accounts to funnel money to insiders who belonged to the same hate groups it pledged to dismantle. The SPLC has pleaded not guilty.

The government later also charged the group's former executive Heidi Beirich with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to submit false statements to a federally insured bank. She has also pleaded not guilty.

In the indictment, the government alleged that Beirich had a romantic relationship with F-9. Prosecutors described F-9 as an SPLC informant who infiltrated the Neo-Nazi group National Alliance and even once broke into its headquarters to steal documents.
According to the defense team's court filing, F-9 was staring down a potential tax prosecution for failing to pay income tax for 30 years when he began cooperating with the Justice Department.

He spoke with investigators in March 2022 when the case was still being investigated for the first time. It was subsequently closed without charges being filed. He resumed his talks with DOJ again in 2025 when the case was revived, the group's lawyers said.
"Just since November 2025, F-9 has met with the government more than
20 times — including at least four in-person meetings. He has exchanged approximately 1,800 text messages with the lead agents from the FBI and IRS," the group's lawyers wrote.

"F-9 regularly sends the government's lead FBI agent reports on how his search for evidence against the SPLC is going. He is not a lawyer, but he gave four 'Intelligence Briefings' to the government, accompanied by 162 pages of PowerPoint slides that analyze what charges the government should bring against the SPLC, describe what evidence he believes supports the charges, identify possible witnesses, and suggest new investigative directions," the filing said.
Some of those PowerPoint slides, meanwhile, have been unintelligible.
One example included in the filing, for instance, depicts a flow chart featuring mathematical notations, with SPLC's attorneys noting: "It is entirely unclear what some of the information means."

The lawyers added that F-9 "has provided a vast number of documents and recordings, but has done so in a selective fashion, including sending clips made from secret recordings when he possesses the full recording, seemingly sending only what supports his view of the SPLC."

"At the center of this baseless investigation is an informant with every incentive to tell the government what it wants to hear. He faced possible criminal exposure, blamed the SPLC for his financial problems, and told the government a one-sided and incomplete story to score his own broad immunity which the prosecution was willing to provide," SPLC's attorneys Abbe Lowell and Addy Schmitt said in a joint statement.

"Our motion also lays out how this immunized individual is not merely a witness, but someone who is so deeply embedded in the prosecution team that he tells them what to charge and provides only the information he wants them to see."
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

title: Caregivers face soaring costs, taking a toll on income and jobs
summary: Caregivers spend an average of $11,500 per year looking after an aging parent, relative or friend, up roughly 60% since 2021, according to AARP.
story: Wendy Mayo knows firsthand how expensive and time-consuming caring for an aging parent can be. The 44-year-old Connecticut resident and her two siblings help look after their mother, who has Alzheimer's disease and requires around-the-clock supervision.
The siblings split the cost of care, which includes employing a professional caregiver, paying their mother's rent, and spending to adapt the home to accommodate her condition.

"We pay her rent and bought stuff to prevent bedsores, plus bed alarms because she was getting out of bed and wandering around," Mayo told CBS News. "So we also invested in cameras to watch her, and all those things add up when you're a caregiver."
Mayo estimates she spends $15,000 annually caring for her mom, while the siblings spend a combined $45,000.

Caregivers for aging relatives and other loved ones have seen their out-of-pocket costs skyrocket over the past five years, according to a new study from AARP. On average, caregivers today spend more than $11,500 per year looking after people who need support, up roughly 60% from 2021, the group found.
For households that earn less than $40,000 a year, caregiving costs consume more than three-quarters of their annual income, on average, according to AARP.
The hardships can also be significant for members of the "sandwich generation" — middle-aged adults who are raising children while also caring for aging parents.
AARP based its findings on a survey of more than 2,500 people who provided care for an adult relative or friend in June and July.
The toll on caregivers

Family caregivers' financial commitment to caring for a loved one can affect their own economic security, AARP noted. For her part, Mayo said she never hesitated to offer care for her mom, but acknowledged it wasn't a cost she had budgeted for.
"It's a role you're thrust into. It's not like retirement, which we plan for," she told CBS News, noting that supporting her mother has forced her to pull back on saving for her own retirement.

Housing and other household costs — which often include food, rent, mortgage payments and property taxes — are the largest expense for caregivers, according to AARP. The group estimates that people spend an average of nearly $4,800 a year on those expenses.

Healthcare costs are the second-largest financial burden for caregivers, including insurance premiums, copayments and payments to hospitals. Other major costs include nursing homes, medical equipment and supplies, and prescription and over-the-counter drugs.
Megan O'Reilly, AARP's vice president of government affairs for health and family, told CBS News that such costs can drain caregivers financially and make it hard for them to retire.
"The financial outputs they provide for their loved one have implications for their own retirement security," she said.
Impact on jobs

Along with the financial toll that often accompanies looking after a loved one, caregivers may also experience an impact on their jobs or income. Nearly two-thirds of working caregivers surveyed by AARP said that those added responsibilities had affected their work lives.

Sometimes the added costs required them to work additional hours, while the time commitment in offering care sometimes forced them to reduce their work schedules or even quit altogether, affecting their earnings.
"They have to make decisions about staying in the workforce or leaving, and increasing or reducing their hours to meet caregiving needs," O'Reilly said.
She also highlighted how many additional unpaid hours caregivers can spend assisting patients.

"There is the financial component, but there's also the time that caregivers spend navigating the healthcare system for loved ones," O'Reilly said. "They are spending time finding providers, making appointments, and providing transportation to and from those appointments."
