title: Apple's first foldable phone broke within hours, some owners say
summary: "I didn't even make it through setup," one consumer said after his new iPhone Duo cracked shortly after he bought it.
story: Apple's first foldable iPhone went on sale on Oct. 23, and some new owners report that their devices are already broken.

Within days of the new iPhone Duo hitting stores, photos and videos of cracked screens began popping up online. Consumers said the device's inner screen broke down the middle near the hinge where the phone folds, leaving a line across the display.
The Duo, whose price starts at nearly $2,000 and tops $3,000 for higher-end models, represents Apple's biggest bet in years and the first major product rollout under new Apple CEO John Ternus.
"Loud pop"

Jesse Dalton, who lives near Frisco, Texas, bought the Duo the day it came out. He told CBS News he had just put a case on the phone and went to open the device when it "just got super tight about halfway up the hinge."

"Just pushed past it, assuming it was just stuck on the case or something for some reason, and the whole thing just snapped. I just heard a loud pop, and the screen just cracked right in the middle," Dalton said.
"I didn't even make it through setup," he added.
Dalton said he paid about $800 for the 512-gigabyte model after an AT&T trade-in promotion, bringing the full retail price to around $2,200.
A local Apple Store had a replacement on hand, he noted. "So they had one, and they were able to swap it out immediately. So I was in and out like 30 minutes."
But Dalton voiced concern about the phone's durability.
"Every time I open it, I kind of have a little pause where I'm waiting to see if it catches that same way," he said.
Justin Smith bought a Duo as a graduation gift for his wife, Roneshia. She said it cracked the following morning, less than 24 hours after purchase.
"We both woke up, and like most people, I grabbed my phone off the nightstand. I went to open it up like a book, and I realized I just could not get it open. It was a lot of resistance," she said.

"When I finally was able to get it opened, that's when we heard the crack noise, like an egg cracking. We just totally just started laughing basically because we were, like, no way, it's been less than 24 hours," Roneshia added.

After taking her device to an Apple Store, she said the staff said they were unable to fix it and that the only option was a replacement. But because the phone is backordered, she's unsure when she'll receive a new Duo. "I'm kind of stuck in this limbo."
What Apple says
Apple told CBS News it is aware that some Duo owners are reporting problems with the phone.

"The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor," the company said in a statement. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement."

Lance Ulanoff, editor at large at technology news website TechRadar, said the Duo's folding screen consists of multiple layers, including an OLED panel, glass, a plastic covering and a mechanical hinge. The ultra-thin glass could be the most fragile part, he said.
Apple's quick acknowledgment of an issue with the device is also unusual, Ulanoff noted.
"I honestly was shocked that Apple responded and acknowledged that they had seen a small number of these things. That's not typical of Apple to do that," he said.

Ulanoff, who said he had been using a Duo for a week and a half, hasn't had trouble with his own device. "I think that this right now looks like a blip. We'll keep an eye on it if it becomes more than that."
Ulanoff said owners with a damaged Duo should go to Apple, and he recommends making an appointment at an Apple Store rather than walking in.
"I would be making a beeline right back to Apple," he said.
The reports came as Apple prepared for another product event in Los Angeles this week, where the company is expected to unveil a touchscreen laptop.

title: Alvin Hellerstein, judge in Maduro and Trump cases, dies at 92
summary: Alvin Hellerstein, a federal judge who for decades oversaw some of the country's most high-profile cases, has died.
story: Alvin Hellerstein, a federal judge who for decades oversaw some of the country's most high-profile cases, counting among his defendants presidents and CEOs, has died, a spokesperson for the Southern District of New York confirmed Wednesday. He was 92.

At the time of his death, he was presiding over the criminal case of one former president, Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela, while steadfastly refusing to allow another president — Donald Trump — to move his criminal case from state court to Hellerstein's Southern District of New York federal courthouse. Hellerstein had faced some criticism for taking on the Maduro case in January, just days after turning 92, and months after reporters observed him appearing to briefly fall asleep during the high-profile trial of Charlie Javice, a 32-year-old CEO who was convicted of defrauding JPMorgan in the $175 million sale of her startup.
Barry Pollack, an attorney for Maduro, said in a text message to CBS News, "We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein's passing and offer our condolences to his family."

Hellerstein was 64 years old when former President Bill Clinton appointed him to the federal bench. In the three decades since, he presided over major lawsuits related to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, a federal lawsuit against convicted sex offender Harvey Weinstein, litigation related to evidence of abuse at Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq, the trial of Ponzi schemer David Hu, and last year ruled against President Trump's use of the Alien Enemies Act in a case involving the deportation of Venezuelans.
During Hellerstein's final years, he was a thorn in Mr. Trump's side.

The no-nonsense judge repeatedly rejected efforts by Mr. Trump to remove his New York State criminal case to federal court. His opinions in the matter frequently scorned arguments made by Mr. Trump's lawyers, who claimed that the facts at the heart of Mr. Trump's "hush money" criminal case involved official acts under the color of his office. Mr. Trump was found guilty by a state jury in that case, which revolved around reimbursements made to former Trump attorney Michael Cohen for a payment just before the 2016 presidential election to adult film star Stephanie Clifford, whose stage name is Stormy Daniels.

"Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to Stephanie Clifford cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty," Hellerstein wrote. "Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty."

A 2024 ruling by the Supreme Court had forced Hellerstein to reconsider that determination. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ordered Hellerstein to reexamine arguments around presidential immunity, factoring the Supreme Court's landmark decision that upended multiple Trump cases. Hellerstein ruled against Mr. Trump in that matter one last time on Aug. 28, writing that "the trial evidence does not infringe on presidential immunity."

Hellerstein presided over cases connected to the Maduro matter since 2014. But his death is unlikely to create significant delays in the case, according to lawyer and former federal prosecutor Duncan Levin.

"There's no automatic pause, and there's really no fixed period of delay. Obviously a new judge is going to need time to get familiar with the case, but they can keep all the existing dates on the calendar or adjust them as necessary," Levin said. "One of the main qualifications of being a judge is that you can read a lot of paper. The fact that there's extra paperwork falls into their skill set."

title: High-speed train crash in Spain kills at least 68, dozens injured
summary: Dozens of people were killed or injured when a high-speed train crashed into another train in central Spain, officials said.
story: A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.

The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.

Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
One passenger said, "We were all thrown into the air." He said he was "reasonably OK" but that his friend was in much worse condition.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.

"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."

Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil, lands in U.S. after election loss
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential election, left the country with his family and State Department official told CBS News they would receive U.S. visas.
story: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family left the country on Tuesday after he lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend, and landed in Miami Wednesday morning.
Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News that Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.

Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, departed Brazil for the U.S. days after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election. En route to the U.S., Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters first arrived in Argentina and then took a private plane to Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to Argentinian officials and flight tracking data.
In a letter to the Brazilian people posted on X, Bolsonaro called the election results illegitimate and accused the government of targeting him for persecution.

"Facing the political weaponization of Justice in Brazil, I decided to move with my family to the United States, where we are safe. I personally thank President Trump and the American government for welcoming us," he said in the letter, translated from the Portuguese. He added, "I want to make it clear: I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil."
Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."
Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."
Mr. Trump told reporters early Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., though he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
"It would be OK with me," Mr. Trump said.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.
"This is what the Bolsonaro family is like: Brazil is their second nation, the U.S. is the first," Lula said Tuesday, according to Reuters.

Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.
The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.
Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.

title: Russell Brand takes the stand at his rape and sexual assault trial
summary: Russell Brand denied all the allegations against him as he took the stand in his trial on rape and sexual assault charges on Wednesday.
story: Actor and comedian Russell Brand took the stand in his trial on rape and sexual assault charges in London on Wednesday.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He started the morning by answering questions on whether he committed each respective charge with a terse "no." Under cross-examination, he said he was innocent.

"My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," Brand said in his initial questioning. Under cross-examination, he said that while he believes he behaved promiscuously during the time period in question, he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
Brand calls consent "more important than sex itself"

One woman alleged she met Brand at a Labour Party conference in 1999. She believed Brand was gay, and invited him to her hotel room to continue a conversation that began after a cabaret show where he performed. She alleged he came out of the bathroom topless before raping her.

Brand said he remembers meeting the victim and chatting with her. When asked if he portrayed himself as gay, he said, "I don't think so." Brand said the victim was the one who suggested returning to her hotel room.

Brand said he believes he would have checked in with the woman during the encounter, and denied raping her. He said he believes "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself."

A woman who was working at MTV in 2001, where Brand was also employed, said she was showing him where the bathrooms were when he grabbed her hard by the forearm and said "come in, go on, come in." Brand said he was only at those offices "between two and five times," does not recall meeting the alleged victim, and does not recall taking her by the arm or attempting to engage in nonconsensual sexual activity.
Another woman alleged Brand grabbed her breasts and orally raped her in a London bar in July 2004, allegations that Brand again denied.

Brand initially told police in 2024 that he "had no memory of meeting" the victim, but he said on the stand that he revisited the alleged location and recalled an encounter. He also said that seeing a video interview between the victim and police helped him recall the encounter. When asked by prosecutors if he waited to give his account until he saw the video interviews from that alleged victim and others to "structure his case" around their comments, he said no.
Brand answers questions about alleged apology

Another victim alleged Brand anally raped her in 2009. She alleged the encounter left blood and feces on bed sheets, which Brand then forced her to clean. Prosecutors say the alleged victim had a threesome with Brand backstage at London's Hammersmith Apollo Theatre before returning to his home for consensual sex.

On the stand, Brand confirmed that he and the woman had anal sex, along with other forms of penetration, and recalled being "excited and enthusiastic" about the "kinky" experience. He said the woman had consented and agreed to the encounter.
Brand said he had no indication that the woman was in pain, and she did not ask him to stop. He said he had a full-time housekeeper who would have cleaned the bed sheets.

Brand said he does not recall texting the victim after the encounter, but she said that she sent Brand a message where she accused him of treating her "like an animal." The woman alleged that Brand texted back "sorry." On the stand, Brand said he did not recall the exchange, but said he would have been apologizing for the "expressed dissatisfaction."
Brand blames documentary for charges

Under cross-examination, Brand blamed a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary program for the allegations against him. He said he believes the media have been unfair to him in the case, and said he was "innocent" of all allegations.

Before the documentary was released, Brand posted a video online denying the allegations. In the video, he noted again that he had been promiscuous during the time period described, but his relationships were "absolutely, always consensual."

He suggested the reports were part of a coordinated attack because of his newfound prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator. The women featured in the documentary said they only felt ready to share their stories after being approached by reporters, with some mentioning Brand's online fame as a factor in their decision to speak.
After the allegations, Brand's YouTube channel was demonitized. He was also dropped by his talent agency and had scheduled performances canceled.

title: No clear winner in Israeli election as polls suggest stalemate
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to early exit polls, but both sides will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
story: No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections on Wednesday with the vote count still under way. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to exit polls on Tuesday night.
With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.

Local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Each would need 61 seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.

"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."
"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

If the opposition breaks their pre-election vow — a common occurrence in Israeli politics — they could take power and remove Netanyahu. A central tenet of Netanyahu's election campaign was keeping the Arab parties out of power.

Another possibility given the current stalemate, analysts say, is a unity government between the pro-Netanyahu and opposition blocs without the Arab parties or the ultra-Orthodox. The question in this scenario is who would be prime minister or whether Eizenkot or Netanyahu could rotate out of the position.

This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis headed to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multifront war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for renewed strikes.
For many Israelis, after three years of war on multiple fronts, the election is seen as existential, and voter turnout appeared to be high.
Netanyahu vs. the "change bloc"

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.
Netanyahu is telling voters that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of parties with different ideologies but one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister," Eisenkot said in a rally late Tuesday, according to Reuters. "A worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics."

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.
What happens next?
In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in the Knesset, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than the 50% of the 120 available.
Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.

title: U.S. cruise ship suspends around-the-world voyage due to fuel costs
summary: The U.S. cruise ship MV Odyssey suspended its three-year, around-the-world voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
story: Sihanoukville, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.

The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting at around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.

Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
The average price for a gallon of diesel fuel the day before the war started, Feb. 27, 2026, was $3.76, according to AAA, and was $6.52 late last month, an increase of $2.76.

"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.

However, a blogger who has been on the cruise, Randy Cassingham, wrote online that "the company has done absolutely nothing to help: we couldn't even walk out of the port, so there were shuttle buses that dropped us in the middle of town, Sihanoukville, Cambodia."
"They didn't even give us a list of hotels, let alone help us get there or pay for them," Cassingham said on his website. The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.

The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.

Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being sidelined by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.

Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.

In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.

After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

title: Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
summary: The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
story: The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.
By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.

The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks.
CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.

The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."

The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war. That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

title: Zookeeper dies after being attacked by leopard, safari park says
summary: The woman was attacked while caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility at the Beekse Bergen park in the south of the Netherlands.
story: A keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park announced on Tuesday.
The woman was attacked while caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility at the Beekse Bergen park in the south of the Netherlands.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure as there are no cameras. The animals were inside due to bad weather and staff are usually kept away from the leopards.
She sustained serious injuries to her head and neck, according to local media. She underwent emergency surgery but died on Tuesday, the zoo said in a statement.

"The keeper started at the Beekse Bergen Safari Park at the age of 17 and worked here, with only a few short interruptions, for nearly 40 years," the park said in a statement on social media. "Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends, and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss."
An independent investigation will be launched to establish the circumstances of the incident, the zoo added.
The leopards were behaving naturally, a park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet.
"They are, and remain, predators," Brabant said.
According to the zoo, the leopard is "a solitary predatory cat found in Africa and Asia" and primarily hunts animals such as deer, monkeys and antelope at night.
Big cats have killed caretakers at other parks around the world in recent years.
Last year, a zookeeper was killed in a lion attack after he stepped out his vehicle at a safari park in Thailand.
In October 2024, a group of lions mauled a zookeeper to death in Crimea after a door inside their enclosure was left unlocked.
In 2020, a 55-year-old keeper at Zurich's zoo was killed by one of the park's Siberian tigers.
In 2018, a lion escaped its enclosure and killed a recent college graduate at a North Carolina conservatory during a routine cleaning.
A Malayan tiger killed a zookeeper at Florida's Palm Beach Zoo in April 2016 after a door that was supposed to be locked was left open and she was attacked.

title: Israelis living abroad spend thousands to fly in to vote in crucial election
summary: Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in just to cast their ballots in an election many voters see as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu.
story: With a consequential election in Israel Tuesday, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad have flown in just to cast their ballots.
Ronnie Teram Gil-Ad left Israel for the U.S. with her family a year ago. She shelled out about $3,000 to come back to vote.
"It is my country. The fact that I'm living abroad doesn't mean that this is not my home here. We wanna make a difference," she said.
Gil-Ad, who will fly back to Boston Tuesday night, will have been in Israel for just 36 hours.
"This is my civic duty," she said. And she's not alone.

Another voter, Yael Natra, told The Associated Press she spent thousands of dollars to travel from Toronto to Tel Aviv to be in the country to cast a ballot. It's the first time in the two decades since she left Israel for Canada that she felt she needed to vote in her home country's elections.

"The Israel that I grew up in is disappearing," she said in an interview from Toronto, citing an eroding democracy and deeply divided society. "If something won't change this time, I don't know what's going to be."

AID Coalition, a U.S.-based nonprofit whose stated mission is strengthening Israel's democracy, estimates that as many as 67,000 Israeli citizens have arrived from abroad to vote, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its "Fly&Vote" initiative. It says about half have been flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Offir Gutelzon helped organize the flights that brought many Israelis to vote with the organization he co-founded, UnXeptable. They say their goal is to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has dominated Israeli politics for 30 years.
Many voters said they see the election — the first national election since the deadly Hamas attack and start of the war in Gaza three years ago — as a referendum on Netanyahu.

Israel has parliamentary elections. The opposition bloc, which polls show will likely have a plurality of votes, is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who left Netanyahu's government in 2024 accusing him of unnecessarily prolonging the war in Gaza and delaying a hostage deal with Hamas.

The mobilization of expats this year is notable, compared with past Israeli elections, Dahlia Scheindlin, an American-Israeli political analyst, told the AP. While many campaigns have focused on anti-Netanyahu sentiment, she said it's unclear overall how those flying in will vote.
"There are also expats coming in to vote for the pro-Netanyahu side," Scheindlin said.
Turnout is expected to be significant with predictions that up to 70% of Israel's roughly 7.3 million registered voters will cast ballots.
But the hard part begins after the polls close: forming a governing coalition that is stable.

title: Israeli police arrest man with knife near left-wing leader
summary: A man with a knife was arrested at an Israeli election event for left-wing leader Yair Golan as Israelis vote in a crucial election.
story: Israeli police arrested a man with a knife at an event for left-wing leader Yair Golan after what his party described as a "suspected stabbing attempt" Thursday, as Israelis went to the polls in a crucial election.
As Golan mobilized voters Tuesday in Tel Aviv, "an unidentified man wearing a jacket approached him in a threatening manner," his party, The Democrats, said.
"Golan's security guards blocked the man, and as they moved toward him, a large knife slipped from beneath his clothing and fell to the ground."
The guards "immediately subdued him before he could do anything. Police were called to the scene and arrested the suspect."
In a statement, Israeli police confirmed they "arrested a suspect in possession of a knife," but added that "contrary to reports, no attempted stabbing took place."
Golan, an ex-military officer, is the leader of Israel's main left-wing party, The Democrats, which is made up of elements of Israel's once-popular Labour Party.
He is in an electoral alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, but sits further to the left.
Golan is the only candidate for a major party in Israel still supporting a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

Israeli police said that while they were escorting Golan, "officers on-site noticed a suspicious object protruding from beneath the coat of an individual standing near the public figure. The officers detained the individual for a search and discovered a knife in his possession."
The suspect, who police say is a resident of Jerusalem in his 20s, was arrested and taken for questioning.
"Incitement and violence will not deter us," Golan said after the incident, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" run by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"I call on everyone who cares about security and democracy to go out and vote now," he added.
Tuesday's incident follows a spat between Golan and the Israeli state. Golan said the security he was offered was insufficient.

"Only after a prolonged legal battle did the Shin Bet assume responsibility for his security, effective yesterday," his party said Tuesday, referring to Israel's counterintelligence and internal security agency.

"We don't want to imagine how this incident could have ended had it not been for the campaign the party waged that resulted in Shin Bet taking responsibility for Golan's security," they added in a later statement.

title: Photos show Ukraine's Starlink was down during fatal strike
summary: Photos obtained by CBS News show Ukraine's vital connection to Starlink was throttled on Oct. 19, inhibiting its interception capacity when a deadly Russian strike hit a park.
story: Kharkiv, Ukraine – Yulia Spichak, a 34 year-old makeup artist in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, dropped her son off at an English-language lesson on Oct. 19 and sat down in a nearby park to send a selfie to her sister, Alina. Seconds later, a Russian drone slammed into the park, killing Spichak and four others, including a 1-year-old girl.

The attack came six days after Elon Musk's SpaceX throttled Ukraine's access to Starlink, which Ukraine has been using to coordinate its defenses against Russian attacks and for some of its offensive operations. In a post on X, Musk accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by also using it for attacks on Russia.

Ukrainian officials told CBS News that the restrictions imposed without advance notice affected ground-based air defense radars and drone interceptors, hindering the military's ability to stop incoming Russian strikes.

"It's an essential part of the air defense infrastructure," Vadym Ivchenko, a Ukrainian member of parliament on the National Security, Defense and Intelligence Committee, told CBS News Monday. "I couldn't say that all other air defenses stopped working, no. But this part is quite essential for the defense of civilians in Ukraine."

CBS News obtained photographs that show Ukraine's ground-based air defense radars' Starlink connectivity dropping to .1 megabytes per second on Oct. 19, the day of the Kharkiv drone attack. That would not be enough to load a webpage, let alone power air defense radars, according to a source familiar with the technology who requested anonymity because he was not permitted to comment on the matter.
On Saturday, Ukrainian officials confirmed that Starlink's access had been restored across the country, with Musk admitting that SpaceX had throttled connectivity.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

Ukrainian officials have also complained of connectivity problems with Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade network, which runs on the same constellation of satellites as Starlink and serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations. But Musk said the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment, and the White House referred CBS News to President Trump's comments last week, during which he told reporters that he did not order the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.

Alina Spichak, the sister of Yulia, the make-up artist who died in the strike in Kharkiv, revisited the park where she died with CBS News on Sunday. She said the Geran-4 Russian jet-powered drone that killed her sister arrived so quickly the victims didn't hear it coming.

"I understand that everyone has their own lives and nobody wants to look at these horrors. But I believe that the whole world has to know what is happening in Ukraine, that there is a war here and we are being attacked," Alina Spichak said. "I really hope that it will end soon."
This story published first on CBS News at 9:54 a.m. on Oct. 27, 2026.

title: Greenhouse gas levels set records again in 2025, U.N. says
summary: Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate​ impacts that will persist for centuries, the U.N. says.
story: Geneva — Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases -- the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide -- all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.

"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO2) has a very long life-time and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Nino's impact
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations -- the amount of those gases in the atmosphere -- rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm); methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them, respectively, to 153%, 267% and 126% of the pre-industrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO2 accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO2 emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm -- smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.

WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Nino," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate for the past decade of 2.6 ppm -- a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.

"We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Nino which will impact land carbon sinks, as it did in 2023/2024," Tarasova warned.
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO2.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.

The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H2) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 has been rising steadily over the past three decades. It is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
Why hydrogen levels have increased over the past decade is unknown but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

title: U.K. charges 2 men linked to alleged terror plot against air base
summary: Two men arrested in connection with the alleged Iran-linked terror plot targeting RAF Fairford in England have been charged with national security offenses.
story: London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.

Abdulkarim was arrested by Counter Terror Police under the National Security Act last week, along with another 25-year-old man — a British-Iranian dual national who was released on bail pending further investigation.

Police are still investigating a suspected terror plot against Fairford after five men were initially detained on Sept. 27 near the base in western England. All five of those men were also released on bail, but police said they remained under investigation and would be monitored.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the base, which prompted the U.S. Air Force to remove all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford. The base had been home to U.S. long-range bombers for many years, and it was used during the war with Iran to launch strikes on the Islamic Republic.

Residents of a nearby town were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police and bomb-disposal experts searched the area on Sept. 27. They found gasoline in three vans that had been driven by the five initial suspects, parked close to an entrance to the base, but no explosives.

Iranian officials have said repeatedly that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. The Iranian Embassy in London, however, said in a previous statement that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.

Police said Tuesday that six men remain free on bail in relation to the incident, four of whom were arrested on Sept. 27 — all U.K. nationals and London residents in their 20s — and two others who were detained subsequently, including the 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national who was detained on Oct. 1.

title: Climber dies in 5,000-foot fall after reaching mountain's summit
summary: Wolfgang Waschiczek fell to his death a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
story: A German climber fell about 1,500 meters (nearly 5,000 feet) to his death on Monday, a day after reaching the summit of Ama Dablam mountain, according to a trekking company operator.
Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, was reported missing from Camp 3, which lies at around 6,200 meters. He had been resting after reaching the 6,812-meter summit on Sunday, before his planned descent.
"After a successful summit, he spent a night at Camp 3 on Sunday, and on Monday morning, his guide found him missing," Gokul Thapa, head of the trekking company Real Himalaya, told AFP.

Thapa said Waschiczek's personal trekking guide, Sonam Lama, had left him in the tent for a few minutes to return borrowed equipment, telling him to stay inside. When he returned, Waschiczek was missing.
Waschiczek's body was spotted by another Sherpa at Camp 2 at around 8 am on Monday at an altitude of about 4,600 metres, Thapa said.
The body was retrieved by helicopter during the afternoon and taken to Lukla, a town known as a gateway for mountaineers and trekkers heading to the Everest region.
It was then flown to the capital, Kathmandu, where a postmortem will be performed at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital.
"Once the postmortem is done, the body will be handed over to his family members through the embassy," Thapa told AFP.
He said this was Waschiczek's second visit to Nepal.
"He had come to Nepal in 2024 for a trek, and his passing saddened us," he added.
Two Japanese climbers died last week on another peak in west Nepal, the Reuters news agency reported.
Ama Dablam lies in Nepal's Khumbu region and is considered a technically challenging mountain with steep faces.
This is the first fatality on the mountain this year.
Last October, two climbers, one French, aged 65, and the other South Korean, aged 66, died during expeditions there.
This climbing season, more than 300 climbers are attempting to scale Ama Dablam.
Mountaineers have died on other peaks this year.
In July, famed British Nepali climber Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers were killed after being swept away by an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak.
In May, two Indian climbers died on Mount Everest during a record-breaking period of ascents via Nepal's southern route.

In May, American climber Shelley Johannesen died in an avalanche on Nepal's Mount Makalu. Johannesen, co-founder of U.S.-based outfitter Dash Adventures, had successfully reached the 27,838-foot summit before she was struck by an avalanche at around 23,600 feet while coming down.

title: TikTok parent ByteDance's founder is China's richest person again
summary: The founder of Tiktok parent ByteDance, Zhang Yiming, reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into AI.
story: Beijing — ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming reclaimed the top spot on a list of China's richest people, driven by his company's push into artificial intelligence.

The rankings released by The Hurun Research Institute on Tuesday reflected that the country's high-tech sectors were rising while others, like the consumer sector and real estate, were under pressure.
The institute, which has published the list annually since 1999, found a record 1,529 people with more than 5 billion yuan (about $750 million), up 6.6% from last year.
The number of billionaires based on their net worth in U.S. dollars rose to 1,176, up 155 people - 176 more than in the U.S. That was slightly below the 1,185 people in 2021.

Zhang topped the list with $100 billion, up 43%, "almost all of it on the back of AI," and the amount was a record high for China's richest person, Rupert Hoogewerf, Hurun Report chairman, said in a statement. Hoogewerf noted that ByteDance's Doubao is China's most used AI assistant.
AI is the biggest single wealth engine on the list: 160 people - one in 10 - now make their money from AI, he said.
ByteDance is the parent company of popular short-video platforms TikTok and Douyin.

TikTok's U.S.-based operations were shifted to a new joint venture in January made up mostly of American investors due to years of national security-related concerns that almost got TikTok banned in the U.S. ByteDance still holds a minority stake in TikTok's U.S. arm.
One of the investors in TikTok's U.S. venture is Oracle, a tech company chaired by Larry Ellison. His son David Ellison is co-CEO of Skydance Corp., the parent company of CBS News.

Bottled water magnate Zhong Shanshan fell to second place on the list with $61 billion, down 23%, while Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, came in third, Hurun said.
Hurun cross-checked its information with entrepreneurs, regulators, industry experts and others to compile the list, while acknowledging limitations.
Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng, a new face on the list, ranked seventh. AI chipmaker Cambricon chair Chen Tianshi was 10th.
Trends in China's economy are reflected on the list

"This year's gains were polarised - entrepreneurs in AI, semiconductors and robotics surged ahead, whilst those in consumer, real estate and traditional manufacturing saw their wealth shrink - a two-speed economy," Hoogewerf said.

China last week said its economy grew 4.5% in the July-September quarter from a year ago, fueled by robust exports, moving closer to meeting its official annual growth target for 2026. For the entire year, Chinese leaders have set a growth target of 4.5% to 5%, down from last year's 5% expansion.

While some industries were thriving thanks to government support for technologies such as AI and electric vehicles, owners of small businesses reported tough times as their customers cut back on spending.
China's domestic demand has been weighed down by a yearslong downturn in its property market.
The Hurun list reflected that, as well.

Hoogewerf said Lei Jun, chairman of Chinese smart consumer electronics maker Xiaomi, was this year's "biggest faller," with his wealth halved to $25.1 billion. Consumer fortunes also fell across the board, Hoogewerf said.
"Today, for the first time ever, not a single mainland property developer remains in the Top 100 - the only property names left at the top are the Hong Kong landlord families," he said.

title: These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate as Israel votes today
summary: Israelis are choosing their next government. The race is wide open, and Benjamin Netanyahu's political fate could hinge on a couple key factors.
story: Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis are casting ballots on Tuesday in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents.

Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent.

Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over.
"It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute.

This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis are heading to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third.

Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes.
The Netanyahu camp

Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.

He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts.
Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.
Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat.
Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb."
Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel.
Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader.
"Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him."
"He's the king of Israel," Abraham added.
The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc"
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.

Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv."
"This time, it won't work for him," he said.
Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas —  something Netanyahu has thus far blocked.
Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu.
"Eisenkot is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said.
The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft
There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side.

One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side.
Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population.
"The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute.

More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News.
"The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future."

There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales —   in either direction —   toward a new coalition government.
Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service.
It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners.
Not all election outcomes are neat and tidy
In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.
Plesner told CBS News that, if all the politicians running effectively stick to their campaign promises and refuse to swap sides in the event of a stalemate "we will roll into another election."
"I'm sure that most politicians are not interested in that," he added.

title: Lula wins 4th term as Brazil's president, but Bolsonaro rejects results
summary: With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon-to-be 81-year-old Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva held an insurmountable lead, but Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the results.
story: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of Mr. Trump and keeps some distance between Latin America's biggest economy and Washington.

With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote. Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.

Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America, where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Mr. Trump have been winning, further extending the United States' influence in the region.

Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders.  It also means the nation with Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, will likely continue defying Mr. Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs he imposed.
The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out of the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with first lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.
Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out in the first round.

A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with first lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.
In addressing supporters, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people, and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro."
"This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said.
He also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty.
"Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard."

In Rio de Janiero, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.
"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."

Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.
Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little to earn the support of his voters.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.
Lula also defended Brazil's sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the U.S. to exert control over Brazil.
He joins Mr. Trump and Nicaragua's president, Daniel Ortega — all age 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.
Judge ruled to extend voting by 2 hours

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he was favored.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.
The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.
Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.
Security and cost-of-living concerns

Lula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.

Both had been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while Lula's supporters chanted in his support.
"The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro said. "Brazil can't go on for another four years on its current trajectory."

In the lead-up to the vote, Lula frequently portrayed Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.

Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives. His government endorsed a debt relief program for small businesses and promised free public transportation on weekends. A major win then came when the Senate backed a popular proposal to end the six-day workweek.

Lula thanked his voters for an outpouring of support while casting his ballot in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he began his political career as a union leader in the 1960s. "It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.
Lula voters respect his past; Bolsonaro voters want change
Lula voters turned out Sunday driven by his history of supporting marginalized people and working to lift Brazilians out of poverty.
"Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it's like to be poor," Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, said. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."
Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia who sported a red shirt in support of Lula, said he worried about Bolsonaro's long-term political vision, which he called "exclusionary."
"It's a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon," he said.
Bolsonaro voters, many of whom wore yellow and green Brazil jerseys in support of the senator, said they wanted change.

"Things are really expensive and taxes are too high," Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said. She added that she once voted for Lula's party but now associates it with corruption.
Issues with public transportation affect the vote

In Bahia state, a stronghold for Lula, whose voters tend to live in areas that depend more heavily on buses, at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving municipal garages during the presidential runoff vote, according to a state electoral judge. He ordered the arrest of the mobility secretary of the capital, Salvador, Pablo Souza, in relation to the case.
Mayor Bruno Reis, a Bolsonaro ally, blamed trade unionists for illegally sticking Workers' Party materials onto transit vehicles for the measure.

President of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, confirmed that electoral authorities received a report on problems with buses in Bahia that is being analyzed. He did not confirm if voting would be extended, which Lula requested in Salvador and Sao Paulo, where issues with public transportation were also reported in the city with a mayor allied with Bolsonaro.
"We will not be robbed by mayors, governors or businessmen," Lula told the press. "These people need to respect democracy."
Bolsonaro did not immediately comment on the issue.
International observers earlier in the day said that voting was occurring peacefully and with transparency and did not immediately comment on the incident.
The Trump administration looms large

Lula criticized the U.S. president before Brazil's election, speaking about the risks of U.S. intervention in Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports and classified drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations. Experts say the moves may have been intended to make Lula look soft on crime.

Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy.
