title: Eric Bauza, 'Looney Tunes' voice actor behind Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dead at 46
summary: Eric Bauza, the voice actor who carried on Mel Blanc's legendary "Looney Tunes" legacy, died Sunday at age 46 of hypertensive cardiovascular disease.
story: Bauza shares what it means to be such a big part of the Looney Tunes legacy & director Dave Green talks about creating the adventure, which in theaters this week following Wile E. Coyote suing Acme for all the faulty gadgets.
Eric Bauza, the voice behind iconic "Looney Tunes" characters including Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died, Fox News Digital has confirmed.
Bauza died Sunday from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. He was 46.

Beginning in 2001, Bauza amassed more than 400 voice-acting credits in a career that gave voice to beloved characters in animated Looney Tunes series including "Puss in Boots," "Muppet Babies," "Avatar: The Last Airbender," and countless others.
The voice actor's family confirmed his death on Instagram, but has not shared any additional details.
HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026
Eric Bauza attends the "Space Jam: A New Legacy" party on June 29, 2021. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Bauza's representative.
Bauza's early breakthrough came when he voiced Stimpy in the 2003 series "Ren & Stimpy: Adult Party Cartoon," taking over the character previously voiced by Billy West.
He became one of Hollywood's most recognizable voice talents, particularly for his work carrying on the legacy of legendary Looney Tunes performer Mel Blanc.

"I’m a fan first when it comes to this franchise, this band of characters. Mel Blanc will always be the original gangsta, the godfather of voiceover," Bauza told Fox News Digital back in 2020. "He was the first voice actor credited on screen as a voice actor. They never did back in the day. And we’re talking about the ‘30s and ‘40s."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Eric Bauza voiced several iconic "Looney Tunes" characters, including Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, and appeared in films such as "Space Jam: A New Legacy" and "Coyote vs. Acme." (Eric Charbonneau/Getty Images)

"So he really paved the way to show the importance of vocal performance, not an on-camera one. And the fact that we’re sitting here now talking about his performance just shows you how incredible, impactful and influential his sound is."

Bauza's Looney Tunes work included feature films such as "Space Jam: A New Legacy" (2021), "The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie" (2024) and this year's "Coyote vs. Acme." Bauza won three Children's and Family Emmy Awards during his career.

Beyond bringing Bugs Bunny to life on screen, Bauza had a deep appreciation for the character's roots and what made him so beloved by generations of fans. Reflecting on Bugs Bunny's signature personality, Bauza once explained how the character's unmistakable New York accent came to be.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Eric Bauza once explained that Bugs Bunny's signature accent was inspired by a combination of Brooklyn and Bronx accents, a creative decision made by original voice actor Mel Blanc. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

"And if you’re wondering where [Bugs Bunny] got that accent from, they say he’s a rascally rabbit," Bauza told Fox News Digital. "So [Mel] thought, he’s gotta be a tough character. And there’s no one tougher than a New Yorker, that’s what he said. He said it’s either Brooklyn or The Bronx. He mixed the two together, those accents. So that’s why he kind of has that street talk."

"I think he represents the everyman, the every rabbit," he added. "He doesn’t have a lot of high demands in life. All he wants is a carrot and a nice afternoon where no one bugs him. And if you get on his bad side, that’s when you gotta look out. That’s when he becomes the trickster. But really, he’s just a simple rabbit, nothing to him. I think that’s why he’s so appealing. And I think that’s why when he gets in trouble, people want him to succeed."

Eric Bauza won three Children's and Family Emmy Awards during his voice acting career. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images)

With hundreds of voice-acting credits across television, film and video games, Bauza built a career introducing classic cartoon characters to new generations while creating memorable performances of his own.
His work helped keep some of animation's most enduring characters alive for modern audiences.

title: Michael Douglas doesn't 'feel bad' about affair revelations from 'before Catherine'
summary: Michael Douglas revealed Catherine Zeta-Jones just got his memoir two days before his podcast appearance, joking their 25-year age gap softens the blow.
story: In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor admitted he had an affair with his "Basic Instinct" co-star, Jeanne Tripplehorn. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Michael Douglas gave a cheeky response when asked how his wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones, had reacted to his new tell-all, "One Helluva Ride."

The 82-year-old actor's new memoir, published Oct. 6, contained revelations about his life, including his secret affairs with his former co-stars Kathleen Turner and Jeanne Tripplehorn, as well as his past cocaine use and struggles with addiction.
During an appearance on the "Happy, Sad, Confused" podcast on the day of the book's release, host Josh Horowitz asked Douglas whether Zeta-Jones, 57, knew "everything" that he revealed in the book.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS GETS EXPLICIT ABOUT HOW HE FILMED SEX SCENES BEFORE INTIMACY COORDINATORS
"I'll be home to ask her because she just got the book two days ago. I told her this was all, as I say, B.C., before Catherine," Douglas said in the interview, which was published on Oct. 19.
Michael Douglas admitted that he "doesn't feel bad" about his wife Catherine Zeta-Jones reading about his affair revelations in his memoir. (Getty Images for The Red Sea International Film Festival)
"And you know, we have a 25-year age difference, so I'm looking at some of these films, like with Kathleen, and Catherine would have been seven years old," he joked.
"I don't feel bad," Douglas added. "I think she understands."
Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones married in 2000. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

In "One Helluva Ride," Douglas confirmed that he and Turner, 72, had an affair in 1983 while filming the hit 1984 romantic adventure movie "Romancing the Stone," a rumor they denied for over 40 years.

At the time, Douglas was legally married to Diandra Luker, with whom he shares son Cameron, though he said in his memoir that they were separated when production on the film began, and they were both having extramarital affairs.
Douglas recalled that he and Turner continued to deny rumors that they were romantically involved during production of the sequel and even years later when they reunited on "The Kominsky Method."
SALLY FIELD SAYS BURT REYNOLDS WAS ‘WONDERFUL’ BUT ‘FRIGHTENING,’ CLAIMS HE TRIED TO CONTROL HER CAREER
The two told the public that while they "had amazing chemistry" and were "both tempted," they never acted on their feelings.
Douglas joked that Zeta-Jones would have been "seven years old" when he and Kathleen Turner had an affair while filming "Romancing the Stone." (20th Century-Fox/Getty Images)

"The truth is that during the production of ‘Romancing the Stone,' Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship," he wrote. "It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen."
PHIL COLLINS GETS FRANK ON MARRIAGE FAILURES AND LIFE REGRETS: 'I REGRET MY MARRIAGES FALLING APART'

He noted that he and Turner kept their affair a secret for 40 years to protect Luker and Cameron. Douglas wrote that the two decided to end their relationship after Luker visited them on set with Cameron "and made it clear to her [Turner] that we were still married."

After reports circulated about Douglas' admission, Turner said in a statement to People, "Good heavens, what a fuss about something 40 years ago! I love Michael, and I look forward to enjoying the book."
Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker were married for 23 years, from 1977 until their divorce was finalized in 2000. (Sygma via Getty Images)
SHARON STONE SAYS SHE 'NEARLY DIED' AFTER 'BASIC INSTINCT' OPENED THE DOOR TO HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE
Douglas also disclosed that he and Tripplehorn, 63, who was almost 20 years his junior, had an affair during the filming of their 1992 movie, "Basic Instinct."
"The truth is, I fell very hard for Jeanne despite our nearly 20-year age difference," he wrote. "In fact, I was ready to officially leave my wife for Jeanne. I was crazy about her."
Douglas also revealed that he had an affair with Jeanne Tripplehorn. (TriStar Pictures/courtesy Everett Collection)
Douglas recalled that his "relationship with Jeanne lasted through production," but that they "went our separate ways" once production ended.
"But I will always think of her as an amazing actress and a truly terrific woman that I was very fortunate to spend time with," he added.
'CADDYSHACK' STAR MICHAEL O'KEEFE CLAIMS COCAINE WAS BUDGETED ON SET, ADMITS FILMING SCENES HIGH
Douglas maintained that he and Luker were still separated at the time. Luker filed for divorce in 1995, and their split was finalized in 2000.

Tripplehorn has not publicly commented on Douglas' memoir, though the actor previously said she approved of him including their relationship in the book. During an interview with Page Six, Douglas said, "I talked to her before I put it in the book," adding that "she was fine" with it.

Cameron Douglas and Michael Douglas attend the 2024 Vanity Fair Oscar Party at the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts on March 10, 2024, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
The memoir also explored Douglas’ struggles with substance abuse, his complicated relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, and Cameron’s battle with addiction.
Zeta-Jones previously confirmed that she had not yet read "One Helluva Ride" during an Oct. 8 appearance on "Today."
"As much as I love my husband, when I’m tired at night, I have no intention of reading about him. At all," she joked.

The Oscar winner cited her exhausting schedule, having just wrapped up seven months of filming the third season of her Netflix series "Wednesday" in Dublin, while also working on her new Prime Video show "Kill Jackie" in London and traveling to Bilbao, Spain, before her press tour.
Zeta-Jones previously said that she has not yet read the book. (Getty Images for Netflix)
"But everyone else should [read it]," Zeta-Jones told the audience. "The book is called ‘One Helluva Ride,’ and I think everyone should hold on to their cowboy hats, because I think it is."
During a subsequent appearance on "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," Douglas was asked if it "was for the best" that Zeta-Jones had not read his memoir.
"Oh, yeah," Douglas quipped.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
In an Oct. 7 interview with Page Six, Douglas confirmed that he had already "talked" to Zeta-Jones about the book and expressed his confidence that she would be "very understanding."

Douglas first fell head over heels for Zeta-Jones when she caught his eye in the 1998 movie "The Mask of Zorro." He went on to meet Zeta-Jones at the Deauville Film Festival in France. title: Christian singer Natalie Grant urges fans not to 'ignore your body' after fall led to emergency surgery
summary: Natalie Grant reveals how a fall outside a restaurant led to kidney bleeding, an ICU stay and emergency surgery that could have ruptured her bladder.
story: The Christian singer told Fox News Digital about the time she tripped while on the way to dinner and suffered internal bleeding.
Christian singer Natalie Grant is opening up about a crazy health scare.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old singer discussed what it meant to her to honor Dolly Parton at the Dove Awards and how she ended up in the hospital with internal bleeding.

Grant explained that after moving her daughter into her dorm room at college, they went out to dinner together with her husband, and on the way, her foot "caught this brick on the ground" and she "belly flopped" onto the ground.

"I thought, 'Oh, maybe I broke a rib' or 'Man, that's gonna leave a bruise' or 'I kind of knocked the wind out of me,'" she said. "But then I got up and I kept walking to dinner. I'm like, I'm sore, but I'm gonna be okay. It wasn't until I realized that I was bleeding internally. And when I realized that it was an emergency, got to the emergency room. And they were like your bladder could rupture, because my kidney was bleeding, and I wasn't able to pass urine."
Grant shared how a simple fall on the way to dinner led to internal bleeding. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

She explained that when she initially arrived at the emergency room, doctors "were kind of confused about what was going on," and it wasn't until she was admitted into the ICU when they realized how serious her condition was.

"I had a catheter so you could see the blood kept filling. I wouldn't stop bleeding, and I think that's when they were like we've got to get you in for surgery and figure out what's going on. But they all let me know like if you wouldn't have come in, like I talked about maybe going to a bigger hospital, and they said, 'No you were really smart to come as fast as you could and get here as quickly as you can,' because if I didn't, my bladder would have actually ruptured, and I wouldn't have known it."
WATCH HERE: NATALIE GRANT SUFFERED INTERNAL BLEEDING AFTER SHE ‘BELLY FLOPPED’ ON HER WAY TO DINNER

The singer went on to say that even through all her pain, she was thinking about her children and how they were feeling, noting that as moms, "we're always concerned about everybody around us," even when bleeding internally.

While in the hospital, she was thinking of her daughter in the hospital with her, who "faints at the sight of blood," as well as her other two daughters back home in Nashville, and how she was going to tell them.
Grant urges her fans to listen to their body when they feel pain. (Tibrina Hobson/Getty Images)
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I was in pain, but I didn't want to miss the moment. I was like, 'No, we are celebrating the fact that she has finished college, and we are going to dinner together, and we're going to make this memory,'" she said. "And I'm kind of like hurting and limping and not able to fully eat my meal. And I was, like, I don't think I can ignore this anymore, but that was just such a picture of what moms do."
After her incident, Grant urges her fans not to "ignore your body," saying, "God created our body in such a way that it gives us signs" and too often, those signs go ignored until "it's too late."
WATCH HERE: CHRISTIAN SINGER NATALIE GRANT IS 100 PERCENT HEALED FROM HER INTERNAL INJURIES SUSTAINED AFTER A FALL
Months after the fall, Grant said she has completely healed, and that, "funnily enough," she did actually break a rib in the fall, and that has been the most painful part.
WATCH HERE: DOCTORS WERE INITIALLY CONFUSED WHEN NATALIE GRANT CAME INTO THE HOSPITAL AFTER HER FALL

"I just last week had my final cystoscopy which checked inside my kidney and my bladder and everything looks fantastic. It's 100 percent healed. You actually can see a scar from where it was and there's I'm like, there's a sermon in that. It's all healed, we still have the scar, but it's healed. And then I just had an ultrasound as well. So internally, everything is 100%. And I just, I thank God because that could have gone 100 different directions. But I'm very, very grateful for good medical care and for the faithfulness of God took care of me."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Amy Grant and Natalie Grant honored Dolly Parton at the Dove Awards. (TBN/Trinity Broadcast Network)
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
The Christian singer recently honored Dolly Parton at the Dove Awards earlier this month, telling Fox News Digital "the most emotional moment for me came in the planning season of it."
The 57th Annual GMA Dove Awards took place on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, at Nashville's Bridgestone Arena, hosted by Tauren Wells.

When putting together the tribute, Grant was left wondering how to honor someone who made such an impact in not just the music industry, but the world, noting, "I'm not gonna sing nine to five or some of her greatest hits, like how do we make this work?"
WATCH HERE: NATALIE GRANT PAID TRIBUTE TO DOLLY PARTON AT THE DOVE AWARDS

"And it was really in looking and reading and remembering and knowing the story of Dolly's faith and how much her faith mattered to her, guided her, led her to the way she lived her life, to the ways she loved people, to the fact she was sure of who she was," she said. "And I think finding that video of her singing ‘How Great Thou Art,’ that was probably the most emotional moment for me was going, wait, this is the anchor of her, the anchor of who she was, was the songs of the faith. And I think that that was really beautiful to get to tell that part of her story."

title: Prince Harry making 'big mistake' that could destroy chance of royal reconciliation: expert
summary: Prince Harry told GQ he wants peace with his family, but royal experts say his public interviews are thwarting any chance of reconciliation.
story: Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham-Turner argues King Charles must take action to bring Prince Harry and Meghan Markle back into the royal fold amid family tensions.
Several royal experts believe Prince Harry is making a "big mistake" that could ruin his chances of reconciling with his family.

In his first major interview since returning to the U.K. with his family, the Duke of Sussex told GQ he wants to make peace with his father and brother. However, royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital that Harry's willingness to publicly discuss his strained family relationships only makes the royals more reluctant to extend an olive branch.

"The peace offering is already undermined as it is public," said Fitzwilliams. "That continues to be his big mistake. He cannot be trusted. [The Sussexes] had already launched brutal attacks on the royal family [with their tell-alls]. Family disputes are bitter. But numerous interventions from 'friends' and interviews like Harry's in GQ make this highly unlikely."
PRINCE HARRY SAYS ‘MOST IMPORTANT THING IS TO RECONCILE’ WITH ROYAL FAMILY

Prince Harry sat down with GQ for an interview recorded in New York in late September 2026 and published Oct. 20. The Duke of Sussex spoke about grief, the death of his mother, Princess Diana, fatherhood, his family's return to the U.K. and his desire to reconcile with his father, King Charles III, and brother, Prince William. (2026 Max Mumby/Indigo)

Speaking about the family rift, Harry told GQ: "Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile — that's the key point."

"Scars stick around forever," Harry continued. "But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past. That’s something that I would encourage everybody to do: If there’s certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that’s harder to let go of. But, for me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives to continue with issues with family."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrives for a visit to the Community Recording Studio in St. Ann's on Sept. 9, 2025, in Nottingham, England. (Getty Images)
Harry also told GQ that he has been "really criticized" for sharing his side of the story.
WATCH HERE: KING CHARLES URGED TO BRING PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE BACK INTO FOLD: EXPERT
"I find it fascinating because everybody else is allowed to tell their version of my story, but God forbid I should be able to tell the other side of it."

Royal broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that although Harry may yearn for reconciliation after years of the Sussexes publicly airing their grievances, "the palace doesn't trust Harry and Meghan." Chard said Harry's decision to speak publicly "proves Prince William's fear — anything said in private will end up in print."
Prince Harry's book "Spare" seen displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)
"Vindication on Megxit and absolution without apology do not equate to reconciliation," Chard added.
Prince Harry told the BBC in 2025 that he's ready for reconciliation. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back from their roles as senior royals in 2020, citing intense media scrutiny and a lack of support from the palace. After moving to California that year, the couple discussed their struggles in interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further strained his relationship with the royals. Several experts told Fox News Digital that Harry and William are still not on speaking terms.
Office workers in London watch the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's "Harry & Meghan" docuseries on Netflix on Dec. 8, 2022. (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)

On Oct. 15, the Sussexes attended a series of charity events in Nottingham, marking their first major joint outing since their reported return to the U.K. The appearances drew attention from royal experts, many of whom compared them to official royal engagements.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit with Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

In January 2020, Queen Elizabeth II made clear following the Sandringham Summit that there would be no "half in, half out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't remain working members of the royal family while pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," Buckingham Palace said in a statement on Feb. 19, 2021.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returned to the U.K. six years after leaving for California. (Getty Images)
In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, poses for a selfie with well-wishers after a visit to Community Recording Studio in Nottingham, central England, on Sept. 9, 2025. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Shortly after the couple returned to the U.K., Buckingham Palace released a letter from the Lord Chamberlain, written on behalf of King Charles III, stressing that there was "no change" to their status. The letter stated that Harry and Meghan are "no longer working members of the royal family" and that their charitable work "is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity."
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter added.
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, arrive at the Endeavour Fund Awards at Mansion House in London on March 5, 2020. Soon after, the couple moved to California. (Justin Tallis/AFP)
A source close to the Sussexes then pushed back against the description of the couple as "private citizens."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince Harry is seen here during a visit to Himmah Hub during the couple's visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
"They are public figures," the source told People magazine. "Members of the public know who they are. The idea that they can live a normal, 'private' life is sadly not realistic."
Another friend of the couple told The Times that Harry and Meghan "hate" the phrase "working members of the royal family."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

"'Working members of the royal family' is a really lazy phrase," the friend told The Times. "He hates it, she hates it. They are not 'working' for the institution, but they are members of the royal family, and they work."

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London, on July 10, 2018. (Getty Images)
The friend said the Sussexes also dislike the term "former royals."

"Things like Nottingham aren't done in the name of the institution or the crown, but Harry is the son of the king, he is still a member of the royal family, he's just not a member of the institution. It's misleading to call them 'former royals.' It has an impact on how they're perceived and the way people talk about them."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle meet well-wishers during a visit to Reprezent 107.3FM in London on Jan. 9, 2018. The "Suits" alum became the Duchess of Sussex when she married the British prince later that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)
A friend of the Sussexes told Hello! magazine that Harry and Meghan never agreed to the late queen's decision to prohibit a "half in, half out" arrangement.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, leave a service of thanksgiving for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II at St. Paul's Cathedral in London on June 3, 2022, during Platinum Jubilee celebrations marking the monarch's 70 years of service. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
"It doesn't trouble them," the friend said. "They never agreed they wouldn't be half in, half out. That was what was decided and foisted upon them."
"They’re just living their lives and they can, because they’re financially independent," the friend added.
Meghan Markle attended a special screening of the documentary "Cookie Queens" in Los Angeles. (Eric Charbonneau/Roadside Attractions via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell for comment.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026 in Nottingham, England. The Sussexes are still non-working royals who are financially independent. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that former palace courtiers were appalled by the unidentified friend's remarks.
"Harry publicly declared he'd accepted the agreement with his grandmother, the queen," Fordwich said.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting Queen Elizabeth II's coffin to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the royal family, often referred to as "The Firm," made "a mistake" by not allowing the Sussexes to resume their royal duties and support the king.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
King Charles III delivers a speech during the ceremonial opening of the seventh Senedd in Cardiff, Wales, on Oct. 15, 2026. (The Welsh Parliament via Getty Images)
"Harry and Meghan are not private citizens — this was decreed by King Charles in the letter created by the Lord Chamberlain which, in my view, was humiliating for the couple," Turner said.

"What that means is that Harry and Meghan can do whatever they want right now. … It just goes to show at the moment that whoever is advising the royal family [is] constantly making mistakes. Because if they really wanted to control Harry and Meghan, they would invite them back so that they can be part of the royal family and could actually control what's going on."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex visit Epic Partners during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images)

"Yet the same accusations are levied against Meghan and Harry when they apparently have decided to do an event for themselves in Nottingham," Turner said. "What is the difference? I ask. Because, in reality, they are allowed to do whatever they want to do now to actually promote their charities and good causes."

King Charles III meets guests during a reception to celebrate the Commonwealth Diaspora ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda at St. James's Palace in London on Oct. 14, 2026. (Getty Images)
Fordwich also suggested there was a "divide" between King Charles III and Prince William over how to handle Harry's return to the U.K.

"The divide is as follows: The king craves family united, keeping the door open and aiming to facilitate some sort of way back, while he is though completely united with Prince William that the Sussexes will never again represent the royal family," Fordwich explained.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, visit The Commons, a project transforming a church into a self-sustaining community centre, during their visit to Northern Ireland on Oct. 9, 2026, in Belfast, Northern Ireland. (WireImage)

"Obviously, from both his actions and words, Harry is rather desperate for reconciliation," she said. "But with every public statement and action, rather ironically, he's actually thwarting any remote chance now of even a familial thawing."
PRINCE HARRY RISKS 'LOBBING A GRENADE' AT PRINCE WILLIAM AS CHANCE TO HEAL YEARSLONG FEUD EMERGES: EXPERT

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Prince William, Duke of Cambridge, watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London, England. (Getty Images)
Fordwich doesn't believe Harry will reconcile with his family anytime soon.

"Writers of 'The Crown' must be sitting with pens poised at this now ridiculous situation escalating," Fordwich said. "Although Harry and Meghan wish to build proper bridges, the king apparently refuses to even discuss the subject."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Donna Mills, 85, draws the line at unexpected OnlyFans request: ‘I’m not going to’
summary: "Knots Landing" star Donna Mills revealed the one surprising everyday activity she refuses to film for her OnlyFans subscribers.
story: Donna Mills tells Fox News Digital what changed her mind about joining the platform — and why she says there's no pressure to bare it all.
"Knots Landing" star Donna Mills is revealing the one unexpected request she refuses to fulfill for her OnlyFans subscribers.

During a Friday appearance on ABC's "Nightline," the 85-year-old actress told correspondent Kayna Whitworth that her content largely consists of glimpses into her daily life but asserted that there is one routine she won’t perform for the camera.

"I do the Peloton," Mills said. "Just, you know, they’re the things of everyday life: having a cup of coffee, you know. They say they like it when you brush your teeth…I’m not going to brush my teeth."
Donna Mills revealed the one OnlyFans request that she won't fulfill. (Disney via Getty Images)
DONNA MILLS DOES 100 SIT-UPS A DAY, PLAYS TENNIS FIVE TIMES A WEEK AT 85 BUT WON'T QUIT DORITOS
When asked if she believes that most of the OnlyFans users who are engaging with her are men, Mills said, "I think so. Yeah. Sometimes you don’t know."

While Mills drew the line at brushing her teeth on camera, she appeared more open to sharing racier content with her subscribers. However, she explained that she does not believe full nudity is necessary to be sexy, pointing to one of her past Playboy shoots as an example.
PLAYBOY'S CELEBRITY-DRIVEN RELAUNCH FACES CREDIBILITY TEST IN ONLYFANS ERA, EXPERT SAYS
The "Knots Landing" star said she plans to sell never-before-seen "Playboy" photos. (2005 CBS WORLDWIDE INC.)

CRYSTAL HEFNER FELT 'ABSOLUTELY BRAINWASHED' DURING HUGH HEFNER MARRIAGE, REVEALS STRICT PLAYBOY MANSION RULES
The "Play Misty for Me" star said she believed that the never-before-seen "Playboy" outtakes could be particularly enticing for her OnlyFans subscribers.

DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME

WHY WWE LEGEND DAWN MARIE IS HEADING TO ONLYFANS AT 55

The actress, who became a television sensation playing the glamorous and ruthless Abby Cunningham on "Knots Landing" from 1980 to 1989, said the platform would give her a chance to connect with fans in a more personal way.
Mills said fans were hungry for a behind-the-scenes look at her life, which she noted wasn't possible during her TV heyday.
Mills said she shared a glimpse at her daily life with her subscribers.  (Photo by Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)
'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS ISSUES URGENT WARNING ABOUT AGING

"They want to know me," she told Variety at the time. "They want to know what I do during the day when I’m home. They want to see my home. They want to know much more about my personal life than we ever experienced back in the ’80s and the ’90s that, you know, the fans were cut off from."

"I've always appreciated the incredible support and encouragement I've received from my fans over the years," Mills said. "Social media has been a wonderful way to stay connected, but I'm excited to join OnlyFans because it offers the opportunity for a more personal and direct connection,"
However, Mills emphasized that she planned to approach OnlyFans on her own terms.
"It’s simply another platform to spend quality time with the people who’ve supported me throughout my career while staying true to who I am," she said.
Andy Bachman, CEO of Creators, Inc., the talent agency that manages Mills' OnlyFans account, noted that the Hollywood veteran isn't switching up her image.

"This is not about changing who she is. It is about giving her longtime fans more access to the personality, style and behind-the-scenes moments they already love," Andy Bachman, CEO of the talent agency Creators Inc., said.
The actress is reportedly making "many six figures." (© 2025 Disney. All rights reserved.)

During an appearance on "TMZ Live" shortly after launching her account, Mills said that she wasn't planning to pose nude but didn't entirely rule out the possibility.
"Who knows? My first answer would be, oh, no, I won’t do that," she said. "But then my second answer is, I don’t know."
"I don’t want to do anything that’s salacious, you know what I mean?" Mills added. "That isn’t my personality. That isn’t what I feel good doing. But if it’s cute and sexy … we’ll see."
In August, Mills appeared on "Creators Inc. Podcast," less than a month after launching her account. At the time, Bachman, who hosts the podcast, shared an update on her page's performance.

Mills teased that her page will be "spicy." (GC Images)
Mills also explained that part of her motivation for launching her OnlyFans was to prove that getting older doesn't mean life gets smaller.

title: Brandi Glanville says doctors are 'taking my face off' in exploratory surgery after years of health issues
summary: Brandi Glanville details the $5,000 exploratory surgery to remove what she believes is something alive moving beneath the skin on her face.
story: Reality star Brandi Glanville explains why her recent financial strain made turning down opportunities more difficult and pushed her to prove she could perform again on FOX's "Special Forces."
Brandi Glanville is taking a major step in her ongoing health battle by going under the knife.

During an episode of her "Brandi Glanville Unfiltered" podcast, shared on Thursday, Oct. 22, the 53-year-old reality star went into detail about the "exploratory surgery" she is scheduled to have on Friday.

"Dr. Carlo Honrado is taking my face off on Friday and going to do an exploratory surgery to kind of do a power wash under my skin," she said. "And then he knows where there's two definite spots, like either fungal balls or something alive. I think it's alive personally cause it moves when it wants."

She explained that after four years of dealing with the issue, she is "super excited" but also "scared to death" because she has "never had facial surgery" and has heard the procedure is "more intensive than a facelift."
Glanville shared that she is undergoing "exploratory surgery." (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)
FORMER REALITY STAR OPENS UP ABOUT NEW DIAGNOSIS AFTER YEARS-LONG HEALTH ORDEAL

While she is nervous, Glanville is hopeful the surgery will be a success, as facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon, Dr. Honrado, "comes highly recommended." She noted that she is "okay" with the $5,000 price tag, telling herself, "what if he actually does take it out and it's done?"
"It started in my face, my cheek and my jawbone, and then it went over my head back in my neck. Now it's down my spine," she explained.
She went on to say that the doctor told her if he is able to "cut that head off the beast", getting rid of the rest of it will be more manageable.
Glanville previously shared that she believed she picked up a parasite after visiting Morocco in 2023. She suffered from facial paralysis and was initially diagnosed with stress-induced angioedema.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Brandi Glanville reveals new diagnoses amid ongoing health battles. (Getty Images/Brandi Glanville Instagram)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

In September, she revealed she had been diagnosed with highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, Demodex dermatitis and mononucleosis, noting her treatment includes daily IV treatments which she estimated would cost $3,300 to $6,000 a month.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" alum revealed she agreed to compete on the current season of "Special Forces" because she needed the money after years of spending on medical treatments.

"The medical system here is broken," Glanville explained. "So I have, like, from 8 a.m. on, I have creditors from, like, medical things calling me, like from Cedars-Sinai. It's out of control. Like I spent hundreds of thousands of dollars that I had saved. I emptied my 401(k). And it's all for medical bills. And I had insurance, and they told me nothing was wrong. I'm so angry. You know, going into my mid-fifties I had a cushion and that's gone. So it's very scary right now."

In addition to her financial situation, Glanville explained she agreed to participate on the show because she was in a place in her life where she "needed to prove to myself that I could do it again."

title: Warning signs that your adult child may be quietly cutting you off
summary: Family estrangement experts reveal the subtle warning signs, from skipped holidays to shifted tone, that may precede a no-contact situation.
story: Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher who focuses on anxiety and family estrangement, said one warning sign may be an adult child’s unwillingness to consider differing views.
Amid a growing trend of parent-child estrangement, experts say recognizing the early warning signs may help families address problems before they escalate into a no-contact situation.

Nearly four in 10 Americans are currently estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults. That includes 24% who reported estrangement from a sibling, 16% from a parent and 10% from a child.
While estrangement can sometimes seem sudden, experts say subtle changes may signal that a family relationship is beginning to unravel.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
The quiet signs
Mary McLaughlin, a licensed couples and family therapist in Vienna, Virginia, said early signs may include an adult child becoming less willing to share details of their life directly with a parent.
Experts say recognizing the early signs of parent-child estrangement may help families address problems before they escalate into a no-contact situation. (iStock)
"You might find out about the trip, the new relationship or a promotion at work at the same time everyone else does," she told Fox News Digital.
The parent may still be in contact with the adult child, McLaughlin said, but the child no longer chooses to share parts of their life directly.
ADULT CHILDREN CUTTING OFF PARENTS AS SOME BLAME THERAPY FOR FAMILY ESTRANGEMENTS

Other potential warning signs may include skipping family holidays, birthdays or weddings; leaving texts and calls unanswered; and reducing communication to brief or sporadic exchanges, according to the expert.
The distance may become so noticeable that siblings, grandparents or other relatives comment that they have not seen or heard from the adult child in a long time.
A child who once readily joined family photos but begins stepping out of them may also be signaling that they are starting to see themselves as separate from the family, McLaughlin said.
The most telling sign may be a noticeable shift in the tone of the relationship, an expert said. (iStock)

Blythe Landry, a Pennsylvania-based therapist and founder of Blythe Landry Coaching, said other early signs may include a child becoming involved with a new social group that encourages estrangement over difficult conversations, or "beginning to rewrite history in a way that seems more damaging than what might have happened."
The adult child may also become less willing to let a parent spend time with their grandchildren.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
The most telling sign may be a noticeable shift in the tone of the relationship, Landry said.
"You know your child, and you know when the energy has shifted in a direction that seems dramatically harsher than in previous interactions."
The shift to independence

Laura Wellington, a Connecticut mother who has been estranged from her adult daughter since 2024, said it can be challenging to distinguish early signs of estrangement from typical moves toward independence.

"It’s confusing to the parent because, a lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone — just pulling away and going off and establishing their lives," she told Fox News Digital.
"That’s what I think confuses many parents, because they want to give them the space to start pulling away and showing signs of their own individuality and carving their path."
"They don’t want to fight every battle, because if they fight every battle, then communication breaks down. So they try to pick and choose."
Loss of respect
One warning sign, according to Wellington, is if the child has an "I know everything, you know nothing" mindset.

"What's happening in our society today is … a lot of ‘I know everything, you know nothing’ toward the parent," she said. "There's no respect for what the parents experience. There's no tolerance for them speaking up and saying, ‘No, this is not what you should be doing.’"
"A lot of times, they look like the general signs of a teenager moving into the young-adult zone."
In some cases, the child may begin treating the parent as a subordinate, according to Wellington.

Some parents begin to notice a shift when their adult children start treating them with disrespect, pushing back on their opinions and positioning themselves as the authority in the relationship, she said.
"They become the authority; they flip it. Anytime you say something, you’ll see them bark at the parent and push back on the parent. They really have no respect for the parent."
Different worldviews
Wellington also pointed to major differences in political, religious or lifestyle beliefs as a possible source of growing distance between parents and adult children.

She suggested that some young people who become estranged are "more liberal in thinking," while acknowledging that the dynamic can also work in the opposite direction when a parent holds especially strong ideological views.
Major differences in political, religious or lifestyle beliefs could be a possible source of growing distance between parents and adult children. (iStock)
"There is extremism sometimes where the parent is extremely something, and then the child … goes the other way," she said.
Richard Blake, Ph.D., a Texas-based psychology researcher who focuses on anxiety and family estrangement, said an adult child’s unwillingness to consider differing views may signal trouble.
He suggested that personality may play a role, with more argumentative adult children who are less willing to consider differing views potentially more prone to family estrangement.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Repeated cutoffs

Another possible warning sign, according to Blake, is if the adult child has begun cutting off other people. He said parents should take note if an adult child has repeatedly stopped speaking to relatives or openly boasts about ending relationships.
"Chances are, they're going to cut off someone else, and it may be the parent," he said. "If you haven’t been cut off yet, you may be in the firing line there."
Communication breakdown
Ongoing communication problems may be an early warning sign, Blake said, particularly when an adult child feels that a parent refuses to listen or acknowledge the child’s point of view.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"They may say, 'My parents just don’t listen. I cannot get through to them. It’s like talking to a brick wall.'"
Parents who consistently dismiss their children’s concerns should not be surprised when conflict develops, he said.
"If you don’t listen to your child, then don’t be surprised if you have conflict with them."
Blake recommends listening actively, avoiding interruptions, repeating back what the other person has said and asking a simple follow-up question: "First, you say, 'Is there more?'"
No clear warning
While there may be some early signs, Blake emphasized that estrangement can sometimes appear suddenly, with no warning.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"A lot of parents will say, ‘My child never told me the issue. We were best friends. And then I got a letter saying, never contact me ever again.’"
"That is a big problem. It's like people don't even know why they get cut off."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Landry noted that recognizing possible warning signs should prompt honest self-reflection, not just concern about the other person’s behavior.
"If there is an imminent estrangement, dig deep," she advised. "Do you have a part? If so, is there a chance of rectifying it before it occurs?"
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Date-rape drug at center of Cornell sex assault allegations can leave victims unaware of surroundings
summary: A former Cornell University student described feeling severe dissociation after taking ketamine before an alleged fraternity gang rape as Dr. Stephanie Widner shared insights.
story: Fox News contributor Dr. Stephanie Widmer explains the dangerous effects of ketamine, including sedation, memory loss and dissociation, and warns parents about the risks of drug use on college campuses.

An investigation into an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity has thrust the illicit use of ketamine into the spotlight, calling attention to the powerful anesthetic’s use on college campuses as a date-rape drug.
A former Cornell student testified before the university’s hearing panel that ketamine made her feel "like her lights were on but no one was home," describing a state of "vague consciousness."

During an appearance on "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday, Oct. 28, Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a Fox News contributor and addiction specialist in New York, warned that the drug’s physiological effects can leave people unable to defend themselves or understand their environment.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM
"When you say the lights are on, but nobody’s home, that’s a pretty good way to describe it," Widmer said.
"You can essentially have no awareness of your surroundings."
The fraternity house at the center of a rape allegation is shown on the campus of Cornell University on Oct. 8, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
Ketamine affects NMDA receptors in the brain and can alter vital signs, according to the doctor.
"It can cause profound sedation, and it can cause dissociation, which is essentially the sensation of your brain not really being attached to your body," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While ketamine has legitimate medical uses — it was used as a battlefield anesthetic during the Vietnam War and remains FDA-approved for general anesthesia — the drug is also abused recreationally at parties, raves and nightclubs.
Due to its ability to induce heavy sedation, impair decision-making and disrupt memory, ketamine is categorized and exploited as a date rape drug. (iStock)

The Drug Enforcement Administration classifies ketamine as a Schedule III controlled substance and identifies it, alongside Rohypnol and GHB, as a drug that can be used to facilitate sexual assault. The agency says these substances can cause sedation, confusion and memory loss, leaving victims vulnerable.
When asked why ketamine falls into the category of date-rape drugs, Widmer said it can affect both cognitive function and physical awareness.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"There are a number of date-rape drugs that are out there, and ketamine does fall into that category because of what it can do to your sensorium," she added.
While ketamine has legitimate medical applications, its illicit recreational misuse poses serious safety hazards, experts warn. (iStock)
Widmer also warned about mixing ketamine with alcohol or other substances, which can compound the drugs’ effects and increase the risk of dangerous sedation and respiratory depression.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"They’re combining them with other substances, they’re combining them with alcohol, and that can compound the effects of these drugs," she said.
"It can cause really profound sedation. It can be incredibly dangerous."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Widmer said her biggest concern is how parents discuss the dangers of drugs with their children, especially before sending them off to college.

"Everybody knows to say drugs are bad and not to do drugs, and you never know what you’re getting, but really understanding what some of these drugs can do is really important. … They’re not benign and they can cause dissociation."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Weight-loss drug could help address nighttime sleep disruptions for millions
summary: Eli Lilly's retatrutide cut breathing interruptions and drove significant weight loss in sleep apnea patients, as well as cardiovascular benefits.
story: Cardiologist Dr. Virend Somers discusses how the weight-loss drug retatrutide significantly reduced obstructive sleep apnea severity and improved cardiovascular risk factors in patients with and without type 2 diabetes.

An experimental obesity drug significantly reduced breathing interruptions and other symptoms of obstructive sleep disorder in two clinical trials, according to new research published in The New England Journal of Medicine.
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects more than 50 million Americans, and about 80% of cases are undiagnosed, according to the National Sleep Foundation.
The study examined whether retatrutide, an investigational weight-loss drug from Eli Lilly, could help treat OSA in adults who were overweight or obese.
EXPERIMENTAL OBESITY DRUG OUTPERFORMS TRADITIONAL WEIGHT-LOSS TREATMENTS IN EARLY RESEARCH
Retatrutide is being evaluated in phase 3 TRIUMPH trials as a potential treatment for obesity and related metabolic conditions. The drug has not been approved by the FDA.
The FDA has warned that unauthorized versions of retatrutide have been illegally marketed and sold online for weight loss.
The researchers measured changes in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), which counts breathing interruptions per hour of sleep. (iStock)
Study details

The two phase 3 randomized trials included 691 adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and a BMI of at least 27. Participants received once-weekly injections of retatrutide at doses of 4, 9 or 12 milligrams, or a placebo, and were followed for 80 weeks.
The trials included 243 participants without type 2 diabetes and 448 with the condition.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF
Participants who received retatrutide lost between 12% and nearly 20% of their body weight and experienced significantly fewer breathing interruptions than those who received a placebo.
About 68% of participants experienced more than a 50% improvement in OSA symptoms, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.
Retatrutide improved more than 50% of OSA symptoms in 68% of participants over the 80-week period. (iStock)

The study also found that hypoxic burden — the severity and duration of low-oxygen episodes caused by breathing disruptions during sleep — fell by about 75% among participants without type 2 diabetes and 65% among those with the condition.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The researchers concluded that retatrutide led to significantly greater reductions in AHI (breathing interruptions) than a placebo among adults with OSA who were obese or overweight, regardless of whether they had type 2 diabetes.
The need for CPAP machines could be reduced by drug therapy, the researchers considered. (iStock)
The researchers noted that retatrutide’s lack of FDA approval was a limitation, and further studies are needed to determine how the drug may affect long-term cardiovascular outcomes.
Expert reaction

Study co-author Dr. Virend Somers, a cardiologist and professor of medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, told Fox News Digital that while the results were expected, he was surprised by the "magnitude of benefit in patients with type 2 diabetes," as well as the significant reduction in sleep apnea.
"OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated."
"This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients," Somers said.

Sleep apnea is associated with a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. In the trial, participants experienced reductions in several cardiovascular risk factors, including systolic blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, systemic inflammation and neck circumference.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"A reduction in these measures would predict whether these patients were at increased cardiovascular risk," Somers told Fox News Digital.
"In diabetics, blood pressure is a key determinant of future cardiovascular risk, and the fact that we were able to reduce it so significantly was both surprising and exciting."
Sleep apnea patients are at higher risk for heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation. (iStock)
Somers said retatrutide also improved several diabetes-related measures.

In participants without diabetes, insulin levels fell by more than 50%. Among those with type 2 diabetes, 40% progressed from diabetes to prediabetes and another 40% no longer met the criteria for diabetes, according to the researcher.
The improvements were largely linked to weight loss, which can lead to better sleep and reduced sleep-related impairment, he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"[The participants] reported much improved sleep beyond just the sleep apnea — what we call sleep-related impairment was significantly reduced," Somers said.

The study included participants who were using CPAP and those who were not. Somers said CPAP use generally declined during the study, suggesting that some patients may eventually require less device-based treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Dr. Wendy Troxel, a RAND senior behavioral scientist in Utah who was not involved in the study, noted that OSA is often under-diagnosed and under-treated, especially among postmenopausal women.

"Although CPAP remains the frontline treatment for sleep apnea, my hope is that greater awareness of treatment options may encourage more people to get screened and seek treatment," she told Fox News Digital.
Somers noted that the condition completely resolved in about 25% of participants without diabetes and 15% of those with type 2 diabetes.
"This is a very exciting time in treating sleep apnea patients."

The study’s findings do not mean patients should stop using CPAP or other prescribed treatments, the researchers emphasized. Additional research is needed to determine retatrutide's long-term safety and effectiveness for sleep apnea.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There’s hope on the horizon," Somers said. "We have the CPAP, we have mandibular devices, we have postural therapy, where you try to avoid sleeping on your back, and now we’ve got drug therapies that can potentially not just reduce your apnea, but also make you sleep better ... and reduce the risk of future cardiovascular events."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Simple exercise done just once a week could help lower blood pressure
summary: Isometric exercise training like home wall squats produced significant blood pressure drops, but a cardiologist says dietary change may matter even more.
story: Tom Shillue discusses a new sprinting study on 'Gutfeld!' showing three minutes of intense exercise beats hours of moderate cardio. Former Navy SEAL Rob O'Neill and Kat Timpf react with their own workout routines.
Holding a wall squat for a few minutes might not feel like an intense workout, but a growing body of evidence suggests it could be one of the most effective ways to lower your blood pressure.

A trial published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine found that isometric exercise training, where muscles contract without moving the joints, leads to meaningful drops in resting blood pressure within just four weeks.
Researchers also found that daily exercise may not be necessary to maintain these benefits, as exercising just once a week was enough to preserve some heart-health improvements.
ANCIENT CHINESE MOVEMENT SHOWS PROMISE FOR REDUCING BLOOD PRESSURE AT HOME, STUDY SAYS
The study followed 100 inactive adults with normal to high-normal blood pressure, defined as a systolic reading between 120 and 140 millimeters of mercury.

For the first four weeks, the participants performed lower-body isometric wall squats three times a week at home. The routine consisted of four two-minute sessions separated by two minutes of seated rest, monitored using heart-rate straps to ensure consistent effort.
The study followed 100 inactive adults with normal to high-normal blood pressure, defined as a systolic reading between 120 and 140 millimeters of mercury. (iStock)

After four weeks, participants’ top blood pressure number (systolic pressure) fell by about 9.5 points on average, while their bottom number (diastolic pressure) also dropped compared with the control group.
Researchers then examined the effects of reduced exercise frequency. During the following four weeks, participants were randomly assigned to train three, two, one or zero times per week.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE
Those who stopped exercising completely saw their blood pressure bounce back to baseline within four weeks, essentially wiping out their progress.
In contrast, participants who kept training just once or twice a week managed to hold onto a significant portion of their blood pressure reductions.
Participants who kept training just once or twice a week managed to hold onto a significant portion of their blood pressure reductions. (iStock)
Only the group that continued training three times weekly retained key improvements in the following metrics.

Total peripheral resistance, which measures the resistance blood encounters as it flows through the vesselsHeart rate variability, the variation in time between heartbeatsReflex sensitivity, which reflects how efficiently the nervous system regulates blood pressure beat by beat
Total peripheral resistance, which measures the resistance blood encounters as it flows through the vessels
Heart rate variability, the variation in time between heartbeats
Reflex sensitivity, which reflects how efficiently the nervous system regulates blood pressure beat by beat

"This is a fascinating study revealing just a little bit of the right exercise even once a week has likely demonstrable cardiovascular benefits in terms of blood pressure reduction," Dr. Aseem Malhotra, a cardiologist and metabolic health specialist at Ovadia Heart Health in Florida, told Fox News Digital.
"It also doesn’t cost anything to do wall squats at home."
Isometric wall squats performed three times weekly produced significant drops in resting blood pressure in just four weeks. (iStock)
Malhotra, who was not involved in the study, noted that physical movement is only one piece of the puzzle.
"In my own personal clinical practice, I regularly see significant improvements in blood pressure with many patients coming off medication just from dietary change alone," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"A low-carb Mediterranean diet is, in my view, the most substantial and effective intervention – not just for blood pressure, but for all metabolic health markers."
Completely stopping the isometric routine caused blood pressure levels to rebound quickly back to their original baseline. (andreswd / Getty Images)
The study cohort was relatively modest in size, consisting of 100 generally healthy, non-smoking adults who were not taking blood pressure medications.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The findings cannot automatically be generalized to individuals with diagnosed hypertension, older populations with mobility limitations, or patients who are already on heart medications, the researchers acknowledged.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Additionally, because the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks, the researchers noted that longer-term trials are needed to see whether a once-weekly session can sustain blood pressure reductions over months or years.
Because the study involved physical activity, participants and researchers knew each person’s assigned exercise group.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Blood sugar spikes may be tied to everyday habits you can control, expert says
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how post-meal glucose spikes, insulin resistance and sleep apnea are deeply connected, plus the 10-minute walking habit.
story: Metabolic health expert Jim LaValle explains how chronic stress, inadequate sleep and everyday dietary choices can affect blood sugar regulation and contribute to insulin resistance.
Everyday habits — from what you eat for breakfast to how much you sleep — can have a significant impact on blood sugar levels, according to a metabolic health expert.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic health, while frequent or prolonged spikes and drops can contribute to health complications.

Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert, told Fox News Digital that understanding how food, exercise, sleep and stress affect blood sugar is key to keeping levels in check.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE
LaValle recommends monitoring blood sugar after meals, known as postprandial glucose, to better understand how different foods, beverages and eating habits affect blood sugar levels.
"Do I spike more from eating rice, or do I spike from eating quinoa? How much can I eat?" he said. "I think that's a foundational issue."
Stable glucose levels are essential for energy, organ function and overall metabolic balance, while spikes and drops can contribute to long-term health effects. (iStock)
The metabolic health expert noted that insulin resistance occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin, a process that can be influenced by inflammation in the body.
Normally, insulin helps move glucose from the bloodstream into muscle cells, where it can be stored as glycogen for later use.
THINK YOUR CORTISOL IS TOO HIGH? EXPERT REVEALS THE TRUTH BEHIND VIRAL WELLNESS CRAZE

LaValle said he’s a "big believer" in eating a higher-protein breakfast rather than one that’s heavy in carbs, pointing to naturally elevated cortisol levels in the morning and their potential impact on blood sugar.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," he added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

One of the simplest lifestyle habits to help lower blood sugar, according to LaValle, is taking a 10-minute walk after eating. Regular exercise is an "obvious" healthy practice, he added, although he acknowledged that it's not easy for everyone.
The expert recommends taking a 10-minute walk after eating to balance blood sugar levels. (iStock)

"It’s easy to say, ‘eat better, exercise, sleep better,’ but then people are working 16-hour days or are single parents, they get home, they open up their pantry and destroy a bag of cookies because that's the first thing they can eat and their blood sugar’s plummeted," he said.
Even a little movement after eating can be beneficial, LaValle said, particularly in a modern world that’s "eliminating the need to move."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
LaValle also emphasized the importance of managing stress, which can contribute to insulin resistance.
Along with healthy eating, exercise and stress management, getting adequate sleep is "huge for glucose regulation," he added.
"You've got to watch how many sugars are in food, how many refined carbohydrates you're [eating]," the expert advised. (iStock)

"When you don't sleep, and you don’t get enough rest to reset your body for the next day ... all those hormones that are supposed to be getting released get skewed," LaValle said, noting that insulin regulation is particularly affected by inadequate sleep.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
LaValle noted that sleep apnea is often associated with conditions such as diabetes, prediabetes, high blood pressure and obesity, emphasizing the importance of healthy sleep habits.
Hyperarousal of the brain can contribute to insomnia, LaValle added.
Sleep hygiene is important for keeping weight and stress in check, the expert said. (iStock)
For someone who’s "jacked up all day long," feeling overcommitted and anxious, that heightened state of stress can disrupt sleep and, in turn, interfere with glucose regulation.
Inadequate sleep can also affect appetite and eating behaviors, potentially making blood sugar management more difficult.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Then you're going to start to put weight on and then, when you don't get enough sleep, you’ve got to eat more to fuel your brain," LaValle cautioned.
"So you eat more, you're not efficient at packaging that fuel up, you're moving less ... and those are the things that you have control over."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Diagnostic test could flag which men need aggressive prostate cancer treatment and which don't
summary: The Decipher genomic test could help doctors decide which high-risk prostate cancer patients need abiraterone hormone therapy and which can skip it.
story: Musician Wayne Singleton shares how a routine physical led to a rare prostate cancer diagnosis at 33 years old, and encourages others to prioritize regular health checks.
A new diagnostic test could improve the prostate cancer experience for millions of men.

Researchers at University College London (UCL) analyzed a tissue-based molecular test called Decipher to determine which men with high-risk prostate cancer were most likely to benefit from stronger treatment — and which might avoid unnecessary medication and side effects.
The analysis focused on abiraterone, a hormone therapy that was shown in the STAMPEDE clinical trial to cut the risk of death in half among men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer.
JOE BIDEN SHARES HEALTH UPDATE AFTER PROSTATE CANCER DIAGNOSIS WHILE ISSUING WARNING TO OTHERS
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Congress 2026 in Madrid, held Oct. 23–27.
Not every cancer is alike, and treating someone more aggressively than necessary could have "increased side effects and poorer quality of life," noted a UCL news release.
Adding a hormone therapy called abiraterone to standard treatment for men with high-risk, localized prostate cancer could cut the risk of death in half, the trial found.
Because prostate cancers differ at the molecular level, not every patient benefits from adding hormone therapy.

To determine whether Decipher could help guide that decision, researchers examined test scores from more than 27,000 patients in real-world data and 401 men with non-metastatic prostate cancer who had participated in the STAMPEDE abiraterone trial.
PATIENTS REMAIN CANCER-FREE NEARLY 3 YEARS AFTER RECEIVING EXPERIMENTAL IMMUNOTHERAPY

Higher Decipher scores predicted worse outcomes, meaning the cancer is more likely to spread and additional treatment may be valuable. A low Decipher score suggested more intensive treatment may be unnecessary.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Howlett of UCL Cancer Institute commented in a statement that for men with very high-risk prostate cancer, preventing spread of the disease is "critical."
"Understanding who benefits most from additional treatment can make a meaningful difference," she added.
A genomic test could help to personalize treatments for prostate cancer patients, the researchers suggested. (iStock)
The findings suggest that genomic testing could help tailor treatment, according to the researcher.

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment.
Identifying the same pattern in both a large, real-world dataset and a randomized clinical trial strengthens the findings, Howlett noted.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE
"But further validation in other datasets is needed before the test is used routinely to make these decisions," she said.

Elai Davicioni, medical director of urology for Decipher test maker Veracyte, also commented, "We believe this growing evidence gives physicians a stronger reason to use Decipher before making decisions that can affect both cancer outcomes and patients’ quality of life."

Men with high-risk prostate cancer and low Decipher scores may face a lower risk of spread and could avoid more intensive therapy, while those with high scores may be the strongest candidates for additional treatment. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel, who was not involved in the study, also commented on the findings.
"Prostate cancer varies from person to person," he said. "Medical science is increasingly aware that it is not one size fits all."
Localized prostate cancer, which has not yet spread, may contain mutations that predict how aggressive the disease will be and indicate whether it could respond to targeted therapies, Siegel noted.
About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, according to the American Cancer Society. (iStock)

Certain targeted therapies are being used more with widespread prostate cancer, according to the doctor, as they include "more powerful anti-androgens, which works not just on the testes, but on the adrenals as well."
Hormone therapies have "significant side effects," including fatigue, and "don’t always help," he added.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Siegel said the study’s strength was its combination of a randomized treatment group with Decipher testing, which helped identify in advance which patients were most likely to respond to intensive hormone therapy.
"This is the personalized, precise approach of the near future," he said.
Many men, but not all with high-risk localized prostate cancer, will have a cancer recurrence after local therapy, according to the doctor. (Getty Images )
Dr. William Dahut, M.D., chief scientific officer at the American Cancer Society, noted that many men with high-risk localized prostate cancer will have a recurrence after local therapy.

"This study shows that by combining drugs that interfere with the male hormone testosterone with standard therapy, the risk of cancer recurrence decreases," the Maryland-based doctor, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Traditionally, if a more intensive therapy benefits some patients, it is offered to all men — even though only a subset may actually benefit, according to Dahut.

"However, a diagnostic test can greatly improve the treatment experience for a patient by potentially only subjecting patients to more intensive therapies whose genomic test predicts the greatest risk of recurrence," he said.
Dahut encouraged patients to speak with their doctors about intensive therapy to decrease the risk of cancer recurrence, as well as to ask about available genomic testing.

The doctor noted that since the study was conducted with a drug to block testosterone and the oral drug abiraterone, it's "unclear whether the Decipher test would be as accurate with other possible combinations that a patient might receive."

Prostate cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death behind lung cancer, according to the American Cancer Society. About one in eight American men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime.
