title: Is that campaign merch store official? Here's how to tell
summary: Attaxion researchers found 30 fake Texas campaign merchandise stores traced to just two sellers hawking gear for competing Republicans and Democrats.
story: George Weiner, CEO of Whole Whale and creator of PACspam.org, tells Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson why blocking political texts rarely works and how a free tool can help you fight back.

You're scrolling online when you spot a campaign T-shirt supporting your favorite candidate. The website looks professional, the merchandise looks legitimate and the address includes the candidate's name. You might even see the word "official" at the top of the page. So, you assume your purchase supports the campaign. But what if the candidate has nothing to do with that store?

With the Nov. 3 midterm elections approaching, new research shared with CyberGuy reveals a troubling discovery in Texas. Researchers at cybersecurity company Attaxion identified 626 unofficial election-related domains, including 30 online merchandise stores presenting themselves as official campaign shops.

Attaxion says it could not verify an official campaign connection for any of the 30 stores. Even more surprising, researchers found that nearly all appeared to come from just two sellers offering merchandise for competing Republicans and Democrats. The findings arrive as the FBI warns about election-related scams involving fake merchandise, fraudulent donations and websites designed to steal personal information. And while this investigation focuses on Texas, the warning signs apply to elections and online shopping across the country.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DON'T LET FAKE ELECTION WEBSITES FOOL YOU BEFORE 2026 MIDTERMS
Websites selling campaign merchandise resemble official campaign shops, but researchers found no verified connection to campaigns for many of the identified websites. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Researchers uncover 626 unofficial Texas election domains

Texas voters are already heading to the polls. Early voting for the Nov. 3 general election began Oct. 19 and continues through Oct. 30. Meanwhile, researchers are finding that candidates' names have become valuable online real estate. Attaxion, a cybersecurity company that helps organizations identify vulnerable websites and other online threats, examined domains connected to the state's U.S. Senate race, governor's race and six competitive congressional districts. The investigation also included websites resembling election offices and voter information pages.

Researchers initially identified 704 domains. After excluding 25 official sites and another 53 domains connected to campaigns or election offices, 626 unofficial addresses remained. Of those, 553 had DNS records when checked. That means the domains had some internet configuration, although it does not establish that each hosted an active website. The Senate race accounted for 323 unofficial domains. Another 75 referenced House candidates, while 70 used gubernatorial candidates' names. The remaining domains referenced election offices or general election-related terms.

Importantly, an unofficial domain is not automatically a scam. Some may belong to supporters, critics or independent businesses. Others may be registered without hosting an active website. However, the researchers identified a smaller group that deserves closer attention.
30 Texas campaign merchandise stores raise questions

Of the 626 unofficial domains, Attaxion identified 30 online stores that presented themselves as official merchandise sellers for Texas political candidates. The stores promoted products associated with Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic opponent James Talarico. Others used the names of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and his Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa.

Researchers also identified stores featuring congressional candidates. Alexandre François, research contributor at Attaxion, worked on the investigation and shared the findings with CyberGuy. "Two things stood out. The first is how little the politics seem to matter to the people selling," François told CyberGuy.

He explained that nearly all the stores appeared to come from the same two sellers, despite promoting candidates from opposing parties. In Texas' 23rd Congressional District, researchers found stores supporting the Republican and Democratic nominees that appeared to share an operator. That raises an obvious question. If a business is selling merchandise for competing candidates, is it really connected to either campaign? According to the investigation, none of the 30 stores could be verified as campaign-operated.
Two sellers appear to control nearly all 30 stores

Attaxion traced most of the merchandise websites to two seller identities: ShirtGoat and madetoprints. ShirtGoat appeared to operate 12 stores and was likely connected to two more. Meanwhile, madetoprints was associated with another 15. The researchers found that both sellers used similar website templates while swapping out candidates' names and merchandise. Some sites also borrowed slogans that appeared on official campaign products.

For example, when Talarico's campaign responded to a political nickname with an "I'm a Talafreako" shirt, similar products appeared in three unofficial stores. "It suggests that the motive is most likely commercial rather than political," François explained. "Someone with a political agenda would be unlikely to sell merchandise for both sides of the same race."

Researchers also noticed that several domains were registered on the same day. Some stores reused identical policies with only the candidate's name changed. A few terms-of-service pages even contained apparent chatbot responses left behind during the creation process. That suggests some operators may be creating these stores quickly and repeatedly. However, the researchers could not establish the legal identities of the people controlling all the websites.
Why these political merchandise websites look legitimate

One of the biggest challenges is how convincing the stores can appear. A website might feature professional product photos and familiar campaign slogans. It may also offer a functional shopping cart with a normal-looking checkout. Those features can create confidence before someone even thinks to check who operates the business. François says that assumption can be risky. "The first thing to know is that appearance is no longer a reliable guide. With AI, anyone can quickly build a polished store with well-written text, so the old signs of poor design and clumsy language rarely apply, and neither does the word ‘official.’"

Attaxion found that none of the 30 unofficial stores included the campaign-related "Paid for by" disclosure the researchers expected to see. However, independent businesses selling political merchandise are not automatically required to display campaign finance disclaimers. The missing disclosure is one warning sign, not proof of fraud or a legal violation. The stores also failed to provide a verifiable company identity and business address. Some listed a seller name or customer service email address. However, those details did not establish an official relationship with a candidate.

To investigate the websites, Attaxion compared them against verified campaign information from the Federal Election Commission and Texas Ethics Commission. Researchers also examined registration records and revisited the stores on Oct. 20 to check their contact pages, policies and checkout processes. None of those checks established a connection to the campaigns.
119,000 FAKE SHOPS COULD STEAL YOUR CREDIT CARD DETAILS
An unofficial Ken Paxton merchandise store is linked to a seller network that researchers found operating websites for candidates from both political parties. (Attaxion)
A former election website now promotes an online casino

The researchers uncovered another unusual example involving an expired election website. The domain elpasoelections.com sounds like it could belong to an election office in El Paso, Texas. However, it previously served El Paso County in Colorado. That county used the address for election information for years before allowing its registration to lapse in February 2026. A domain buyer acquired the address in May.

When researchers examined the website, it displayed an online casino promoting itself to Australian users. The investigation identified a new registrant organization associated with Hong Kong, although that record does not independently establish who operates the casino.
François highlighted the discovery as an example of how a once-legitimate web address can change hands. "It is a good reminder that a familiar-looking address does not tell you who holds it today."

The example extends well beyond politics. An expired website previously used by a government office, nonprofit or business can eventually lead somewhere completely unrelated. For accurate Texas election information, the state's official website is VoteTexas.gov. For voting information elsewhere in the country, you can start with Vote.gov.
FBI warns about election merchandise and donation scams

The Texas findings follow an Oct. 15 warning from the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. The agency warned that criminals exploit political campaigns to target people across the United States. Some scammers impersonate candidates to solicit fraudulent contributions. Others advertise political merchandise that customers never receive.

The FBI also warned about fraudulent voter-registration messages that direct people to websites designed to collect personal information. Artificial intelligence can make these schemes harder to recognize. Criminals can generate convincing written messages and realistic voices that appear to come from legitimate organizations. However, there's an important limitation to the Texas investigation.
Attaxion did not determine whether customers lost money through the 30 stores.
"At this stage we do not know. We did not place test orders, and our research does not include payment records or customer complaints, so we have no evidence either way," François told CyberGuy.

The researchers also did not investigate whether the operators promoted their stores through Google ads, social media or political text messages. They did examine observed DNS traffic and found that some unofficial domains had received lookups. However, those records cannot establish how someone discovered a website or whether they completed a purchase. The findings raise concerns about misleading campaign connections without proving that all the stores committed fraud.
How to protect yourself from fake campaign websites and online scams
These precautions apply to political merchandise stores and fundraising pages nationwide. They can also help you recognize ordinary shopping scams and websites that impersonate trusted organizations.

Before buying political merchandise or making a donation, find the candidate's established campaign website. Look for the merchandise or contribution page linked directly from that website. For federal candidates, you can also use the Federal Election Commission's database to verify campaign committees and find their reported information. If you're shopping from an unfamiliar retailer, visit its official website independently rather than following a promotional link. This approach also works when someone claims to represent a bank, charity or government agency.

Scammers and unauthorized sellers can register web addresses that closely resemble legitimate ones. Look for misspellings or added words that make an unfamiliar address appear trustworthy. Don't assume a website belongs to an organization simply because the address contains its name or the word "official." You can also use a WHOIS lookup to investigate when a domain was registered. A newly created website deserves closer attention, especially when it claims to represent an established organization. However, domain age alone cannot establish whether a website is legitimate. And remember, HTTPS encryption protects information while it travels between your browser and a website. It does not prove that the site's operator is trustworthy.
WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM
This unofficial James Talarico merchandise store uses a nearly identical layout to the Ken Paxton store, with both linked to the same seller contact. (Attaxion)

Before contributing to a political campaign, confirm the organization receiving the payment. Federal political committee websites generally must include a disclaimer identifying who paid for the communication. When applicable, the disclosure also identifies the campaign or committee that authorized it. Look for a "Paid for by" statement and compare the information with official campaign records. Many political campaigns use fundraising platforms such as ActBlue or WinRed. Others use different payment systems. The key is reaching the contribution page through the campaign's verified website. Independent businesses may legally sell political merchandise without supporting a campaign. However, they should not mislead you about who receives your money. A missing or suspicious disclosure deserves attention, but a disclaimer alone does not guarantee legitimacy.

Take a closer look at any online store you've never used before. Search for the company name along with terms such as "reviews," "complaints" or "scam." Read its return and refund policies. Look for a legitimate way to reach customer support. The Better Business Bureau at bbb.org/ can be another place to check for complaints, although the absence of complaints does not prove a company is trustworthy. If you cannot establish who operates a website, consider buying elsewhere.

A scammer may send a message claiming that your voter registration needs attention. Another might pressure you to contribute immediately or purchase merchandise before an offer disappears. The same tactics appear in fake bank alerts and fraudulent delivery notifications. Avoid clicking payment or account-verification links in unsolicited messages. Instead, open the organization's established website yourself. For election-related messages, check information through Vote.gov or your state election office. Be especially cautious about messages asking for passwords, Social Security numbers or payment details.

When shopping online, paying with a credit card generally gives you stronger protections if an order never arrives or a charge is incorrect. Avoid unfamiliar sellers that insist on payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency or wire transfers. Those methods can make recovering your money difficult. Keep your purchase confirmation and review your statements after paying. Also, check whether a political contribution involves recurring payments before submitting it. The FTC's online shopping guide explains how to research sellers and protect yourself when making purchases.

A suspicious shopping site may ask you to create an account before checking out. Never reuse a password from your email, banking or other important accounts. Use a password manager to create unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) when available. Strong antivirus software can also help detect malicious downloads and block some dangerous websites. However, it cannot verify whether a political merchandise store is actually affiliated with a campaign. Be selective about the information you share, especially when you cannot verify who operates the website. What to do if you already paid a suspicious website
If you've purchased merchandise or sent money through a questionable website, act promptly when something appears wrong.

Contact the seller if an order never arrived. If the seller doesn't resolve the problem, contact your card issuer about disputing the charge. If you suspect fraud or see unauthorized charges, contact your bank or card issuer immediately.Save your records. Keep receipts, confirmation emails and screenshots showing the website address and payment details.Review your accounts. Look for unfamiliar transactions or recurring payments you did not authorize.Change reused passwords. Update any other account where you used the same login information.Report suspected fraud. File a report with the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. You can also contact your state attorney general's consumer protection office.

Contact the seller if an order never arrived. If the seller doesn't resolve the problem, contact your card issuer about disputing the charge. If you suspect fraud or see unauthorized charges, contact your bank or card issuer immediately.
Save your records. Keep receipts, confirmation emails and screenshots showing the website address and payment details.
Review your accounts. Look for unfamiliar transactions or recurring payments you did not authorize.
Change reused passwords. Update any other account where you used the same login information.

Report suspected fraud. File a report with the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. You can also contact your state attorney general's consumer protection office.
If you entered sensitive identity information into a suspicious website, visit IdentityTheft.gov for personalized recovery guidance.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stands out to me about this investigation is that the people behind these stores appear willing to sell merchandise for candidates on both sides of the same race. That raises serious questions about what shoppers are being led to believe. I have no problem with an independent business selling political merchandise. But I do have a problem when a website gives people the impression they're supporting an official campaign without making clear who's actually taking their money. And here's something else worth remembering. The FBI is already warning about election scams involving merchandise that never arrives and fake donation requests. Meanwhile, AI makes it easier than ever to create a convincing website. I wouldn't judge a store by its design or the word "official" in its address. I'd go straight to the organization I want to support and use the links it provides. The same advice applies when you're shopping online or responding to an unexpected request for money. A few extra moments of checking can make a difference.

title: GM wants drivers to take their eyes off the road by 2028
summary: GM plans to debut eyes-off driving in the Cadillac Escalade IQ by 2028, but safety testing reveals how long distracted drivers take to regain control.
story: GM plans to introduce eyes-off driving in the Cadillac Escalade IQ by 2028, allowing drivers to look away from the road under approved conditions. (General Motors)

Would you feel comfortable watching a movie while your car cruises down the highway at 70 mph? General Motors is betting that someday you will. The automaker plans to introduce technology in 2028 that could let drivers take their hands off the steering wheel and their eyes off the road. That means you could potentially answer emails, watch a show or attend a virtual meeting while your vehicle handles the driving.

The technology is expected to debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ electric SUV. However, GM still has plenty to prove before drivers can safely look away from traffic. The company is testing how people react when a vehicle suddenly needs their attention. That research could help GM determine how much warning drivers need before safely taking control.

IKEA TURNS TO DRIVERLESS SEMIS WITH NOBODY IN THE CAB
(GM already offers Super Cruise across Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC and Buick.)
How GM plans to make eyes-off driving possible

GM already offers Super Cruise, a hands-free driving system available on more than 20 models across Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC and Buick. It can manage steering, acceleration and braking on compatible roads under certain conditions. However, drivers must continue watching the road and remain ready to take control.

The next version of Super Cruise would remove that constant attention requirement when the eyes-off feature is active. GM plans to introduce it on compatible highways before eventually expanding to other roads. The system will use lidar, radar and cameras to monitor its surroundings. Turquoise lights on the dashboard and exterior mirrors will signal when eyes-off driving is available and active. GM says the technology could arrive as early as 2028. However, the launch depends on further development, safety testing and other requirements. Availability will also depend on state laws.

GM's ambitions are also growing. On Oct. 21, the company announced plans to bring autonomous highway driving to its full-size SUVs and light-duty pickup trucks, including gas-powered vehicles. Those vehicles represent some of GM's biggest sellers. However, the automaker has not announced when the technology will reach those additional models.
Why GM is putting drivers inside a virtual world

Before asking drivers to trust a vehicle with their safety, GM wants to understand what happens when people stop concentrating on driving. At its Global Technical Center in Warren, Michigan, hundreds of volunteers have climbed into real GM vehicles, including the Cadillac Lyriq. However, instead of driving onto an actual highway, they enter an immersive simulator that recreates different road conditions. Researchers can introduce sudden traffic changes, construction zones and hazardous situations.

Meanwhile, sensors monitor drivers' eye movements, heart rates and stress responses. The tests help GM understand how people behave when the technology encounters something unexpected. GM also tests its automated driving technology on closed courses and public roads with trained safety drivers. According to the company, its simulation tools can reproduce the equivalent of 100 years of driving in a single day. That gives engineers opportunities to study dangerous situations without exposing everyday drivers to those risks.
Why Candy Crush is part of GM's driving tests

Here's something I didn't expect to see in automotive safety research. GM is asking some participants to play Candy Crush while researchers study their reactions. The game creates an engaging distraction. Players become focused on improving their scores, which gives researchers a way to measure what happens when they must suddenly shift their attention back to driving. According to reporting by The Associated Press, Maureen August, a senior manager at GM Research & Development, explained that the game helps researchers draw participants into an activity before interrupting them.

That interruption is especially important. Consider how long it takes to understand what's happening around you after you've been concentrating on your phone. Now consider making that adjustment while sitting behind the wheel of a moving SUV. At 70 mph, a vehicle travels roughly 103 feet every second. Even a five-second delay means it covers more than 500 feet. That's a lot of highway to travel while someone figures out why the car needs help.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS?
Turquoise lights on the Cadillac's exterior mirrors will signal when GM's planned eyes-off driving system is active. (General Motors)
What happens if the car suddenly needs you to drive?

This may be the biggest question surrounding GM's plans. What happens when an automated vehicle encounters a situation it cannot safely handle? Perhaps there's debris blocking the highway. Maybe road markings disappear during construction. An unexpected maneuver by another driver could also create a dangerous situation.

GM's engineers are studying how much warning drivers need before taking control. Researchers also examine whether people understand the system's alerts and feel comfortable trusting the technology. However, an eyes-off system must be designed around the possibility that someone cannot respond immediately. That's why the vehicle's ability to handle unexpected conditions and safely manage a failed takeover becomes especially important. GM has not yet publicly detailed every situation its planned system will handle or exactly how it will respond when a driver fails to take over.
How GM compares with Tesla and Ford

Several automakers already offer systems that reduce the work involved in highway driving. However, their capabilities vary considerably. Ford's BlueCruise allows hands-free driving on compatible roads, but drivers must continue paying attention. Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) can handle many driving tasks, although it still requires active human supervision.

Mercedes-Benz previously introduced its DRIVE PILOT system, which allowed conditional eyes-off driving in limited situations. However, the automaker has since pulled back from that technology in the U.S. as it develops its next generation of automated driving systems. GM's larger ambition is to make eyes-off driving available at highway speeds across a broader network of compatible roads. The company hopes to expand the capability to additional models after the Escalade IQ.
Will GM charge drivers to take their eyes off the road?

There's a financial incentive behind the push toward automated driving. Automakers increasingly offer advanced features through paid software subscriptions. GM already charges for continued Super Cruise access after the included service period expires. According to the company's August 2026 update, equipped vehicles include three years of service, followed by plans starting at $39.99 per month.

GM has not announced pricing for its future eyes-off technology. Some industry analysts believe drivers will be more willing to pay for technology that frees up their time behind the wheel. Still, there's a practical question for buyers. If you're already paying a premium for a luxury SUV, how much more would you be willing to spend each month to use its most advanced driving features?
WAYMO RECALLS ROBOTAXIS OVER CONSTRUCTION-ZONE RISK
GM is developing technology that could eventually let drivers watch videos or answer emails while their vehicles handle highway driving. (General Motors)
What GM's eyes-off driving technology means to you

If you're considering a vehicle with advanced driving technology, pay attention to what the manufacturer actually promises. Today's hands-free systems generally require you to keep watching the road. GM's planned eyes-off feature would allow you to look away only when the system is properly engaged under compatible conditions. Before paying for that capability, you'll want to know where it works and how the vehicle handles emergencies. It's also worth asking what happens if the system requests your attention while you're distracted.

Also, don't overlook the ongoing cost. Subscription fees could make a vehicle more expensive to own than its original purchase price suggests. And remember, GM's planned system remains under development. Until a manufacturer explicitly authorizes eyes-off operation under the appropriate conditions, keep watching the road and follow the system's instructions.
Kurt's key takeaways

I love the idea of a less stressful drive, especially on those long stretches of highway where you're staring at the same traffic for miles. But handing over control is one thing. Taking my eyes off the road while traveling at highway speed is another. GM's research is encouraging because the company is studying how people actually behave when they're distracted. Still, I want to know what happens when the car encounters something it wasn't expecting. And if automakers plan to charge us every month for this technology, they'd better be able to show that it's safe and dependable. I'd be curious to try it, but I'd want a lot more evidence before settling in to watch a movie.
Would you trust your car enough to watch a movie while it drives at 70 mph, or would you always want to keep an eye on the road? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Data brokers don't just collect facts. They guess about you
summary: Data brokers assign labels predicting your health, finances and religion based on browsing and purchases, then sell those profiles to businesses.
story: Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson explains how algorithms track browsing history and location to estimate what shoppers are willing to spend on ‘Fox & Friends.’

They know where you live. They may know your phone number, your relatives' names and roughly what your house is worth. By now, most people have at least a vague sense that data brokers collect personal information. What many don't realize is what happens next.

Data brokers also analyze that information. They use algorithms, compare records from different sources and sort people into categories that predict their interests, circumstances and behavior. Those predictions can involve your health, finances, religious beliefs and potential vulnerabilities.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Data brokers analyze personal information to identify patterns and predict your finances, health and behavior. (Neil Godwin/Future via Getty Images)

Some may be wrong. Others could reveal sensitive details you never intended to share. And depending on the company and the type of information involved, those profiles may be sold or shared with businesses you have never heard of. Here's a closer look at the labels data brokers assign to you, how they come up with them and what you can do to protect your personal information.

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. Here's what data brokers' labels actually look like

Data brokers do far more than maintain databases of addresses and phone numbers. Some build detailed profiles designed to help advertisers identify specific audiences. The Federal Trade Commission documented this practice years ago. Its investigation found that brokers combined information from multiple sources to infer sensitive characteristics, including income, religion, political views and health conditions.

Acxiom, a major data company, developed a segmentation system called PersonicX that grouped households into lifestyle categories. One documented historical category was called "Rural Everlasting." According to the FTC, it described older adults with relatively low income and educational attainment. Other categories included "Urban Scramble" and "Mobile Mixers."

These were classifications built from data, not personal descriptions written by the people involved. The FTC also documented how companies used location information to create even more specific advertising audiences. For example, InMarket offered audience categories such as "Christian church goers," "parents of preschoolers," and "wealthy and not healthy." The FTC subsequently restricted InMarket's use and sale of sensitive location data.

Then there was Oracle's BlueKai advertising business, which helped advertisers use extensive consumer data for targeting. Oracle shut down its advertising products in September 2024. Still, its history illustrates how sophisticated this industry became. The important point is that a label doesn't have to be accurate to influence how a company views you.
Want to see how much of your personal information may already be exposed? Get a free scan to find out what data brokers may have on you at CyberGuy.com.
The categories data brokers can put you in
Some of these classifications sound harmless. Others are surprisingly personal. Here are examples of the information brokers have historically inferred or used to create consumer segments.
Data broker research and enforcement cases have documented categories involving:
Diabetes and related health interestsPregnancyHigh cholesterolHealth and wellness behaviorFinancial status combined with health-related assumptions
Diabetes and related health interests
Pregnancy
High cholesterol
Health and wellness behavior
Financial status combined with health-related assumptions

A major concern is that these classifications can originate outside the medical system. HIPAA protects health information handled by covered healthcare organizations and their business associates. However, health-related information independently gathered or inferred by other businesses may fall outside HIPAA's protections.

For example, searching for information about diabetes doesn't mean you have diabetes. You could be researching the condition for a family member. Yet advertising systems may still use that activity as one of several signals when building a profile. Other federal and state privacy laws may apply, but they don't necessarily provide the same protections as HIPAA.
AMAZON ABOUT YOU MAY KNOW YOU A LITTLE TOO WELL
Your online activity can help data brokers build detailed profiles, even when you're simply browsing the internet. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

Data companies have also offered categories based on estimated income, spending behavior and financial circumstances. These can include people classified as affluent, price-sensitive or likely to respond to certain financial offers. One particularly troubling example comes from the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management. According to federal prosecutors, Epsilon used sophisticated modeling to identify consumers likely to respond to solicitations. The company sold information about more than 30 million Americans to operators of fraudulent schemes, including fake sweepstakes promotions. Epsilon agreed to pay $150 million as part of its deferred prosecution agreement. This is a documented example of consumer data being used to help fraudsters identify potential victims.

Data brokers have also inferred people's religious interests and political leanings. These predictions may draw on information such as location patterns, purchases, public records and other available data. For example, the FTC documented the use of a "Christian church goers" advertising segment. A person visiting a church doesn't necessarily belong to that faith. Similarly, someone researching a political candidate doesn't automatically support that candidate. Nevertheless, profiling systems can use these signals to group people into audiences.

Another category focuses on what may be happening in your personal life. Data companies have developed segments involving parents with young children, empty nesters and households at different stages of life. These classifications can help businesses decide what products or services to advertise. However, they can also reveal potential pressure points. Someone approaching retirement may receive different financial offers than a young parent. A household believed to be managing health expenses may attract another type of marketing. And when those assumptions are wrong, the resulting profile may still influence what someone sees.
How data brokers make guesses about you

Consider what you've done online recently. Maybe you searched for joint pain relief. Perhaps you compared retirement plans or looked up treatment options for a relative. Individually, these activities might reveal very little. However, companies can combine information from websites, apps, purchase histories, public records and commercial databases.

Then predictive models look for patterns. For example, a company may consider your age range, estimated income and browsing activity when deciding whether you fit a particular advertising category. These classifications are often called modeled attributes or inferences. They represent predictions rather than verified personal facts. And here's the problem: a company buying access to an audience segment may use the prediction without knowing how accurately it describes each person.
How scammers use personal data to make attacks more convincing

Basic information helps a scammer contact you. More detailed personal information can help make the approach believable. For example, someone who knows your name and address could send a convincing-looking financial notice. Now suppose that same person also has information suggesting you're approaching retirement or researching medical expenses. A criminal could use those clues to tailor a fraudulent Medicare offer, investment pitch or fake medical service.

This doesn't mean every scammer buys sophisticated consumer profiles. However, the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management shows how targeted consumer information can end up in the hands of fraudsters. The company sold consumer data to operators of fraudulent schemes, helping them identify people more likely to respond.

Meanwhile, the FBI reported that Americans age 60 and older lost approximately $7.7 billion to internet crime in 2025, up from $4.9 billion in 2024. While those losses weren't all connected to data brokers, the documented sale of targeted consumer lists shows how personal information can help criminals identify potential victims and make their scams more convincing.
Can you see what data brokers have predicted about you?

Finding every profile attached to your name can be difficult. Unlike a credit report, there isn't one centralized system where you can review all the marketing predictions companies have generated about you. However, some state privacy laws give residents rights to access, correct or delete personal information, including certain inferences.

California provides one important example. Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, eligible residents can request information held by covered businesses, subject to legal exceptions. California also launched its Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, known as DROP at privacy.ca.gov/DROP/, in January 2026.

It allows eligible California residents to submit one deletion request covering registered data brokers. Those companies began processing requests in August 2026. Matching records, including inferences, generally must be deleted unless an exception applies. Other states have different privacy protections, so your options depend on where you live.
IS YOUR PERSONAL DATA CHANGING WHAT YOU PAY ONLINE?
Scammers can use personal information to create targeted attacks that appear more convincing and trustworthy. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
How to reduce what data brokers know about you
You may not be able to eliminate every prediction about yourself. However, you can take practical steps to reduce how much personal information remains available.
Here's where to start:

Search for your personal information. Look up your name, phone number and home address on people-search websites.Submit removal requests. Use the opt-out processes offered by data brokers and people-search services.Review your privacy rights. Check whether your state allows you to request access, correction, deletion or an opt-out from data sales.Limit unnecessary sharing. Review the information you provide to apps, shopping websites and online services.Check your family members' exposure. Relatives' names, addresses and phone numbers can appear together in people-search databases.Consider an automated removal service. Ongoing removal requests can help address information that reappears over time. Submit removal requests. Use the opt-out processes offered by data brokers and people-search services.
Review your privacy rights. Check whether your state allows you to request access, correction, deletion or an opt-out from data sales.
Limit unnecessary sharing. Review the information you provide to apps, shopping websites and online services.
Check your family members' exposure. Relatives' names, addresses and phone numbers can appear together in people-search databases.

Consider an automated removal service. Ongoing removal requests can help address information that reappears over time. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Reducing publicly accessible personal information can make it harder for unfamiliar businesses and scammers to build detailed profiles. However, removal services cannot guarantee that every existing inference will disappear or prevent companies from collecting new information.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've warned you before about data brokers collecting your personal information, but I find the predictions they make about us even more troubling. Think about it. You could search for a medical condition on behalf of someone you love and end up in a category suggesting you have that condition yourself. Someone buying access to that profile may have no idea the assumption is wrong. And when personal information gets into the wrong hands, it can help scammers make their pitches sound much more convincing. What concerns me is how little most of us know about the profiles being built around our names. You may never see every label a company assigns to you, but you can start reducing the information available to build those profiles. I recommend checking what appears when you search for yourself and taking advantage of the privacy protections available in your state. A reputable data removal service can also help by automatically sending removal requests to data brokers and continuing to check when your information reappears. You won't disappear from the internet, but you can make it harder for strangers to assemble a detailed profile of your life.

title: Elon Musk vows to give every US child SpaceX stock
summary: Elon Musk says he'll give one SpaceX share to every kid in America in 2027, but key details about eligibility and distribution remain unclear.
story: Elon Musk announces a plan to give one share of SpaceX stock to every child in America. The 'Big Money Show' debates the business and charitable aspects of this multi-billion dollar giveaway, contrasting it with Anthropic's decision to commit five percent of its equity to a public benefit fund. Panelists discuss the motivations behind these high-profile corporate charity initiatives.

You probably don't expect Elon Musk to show up in your child's investment portfolio. But that's exactly what could happen next year. The billionaire behind SpaceX has made a remarkable promise. He says he'll give one share of his space company to every kid in America.

We're talking about a potential giveaway worth more than $10 billion. Free SpaceX stock for kids sounds appealing, especially when you're thinking about your child's financial future. But before you start looking for a way to sign up, there are some pretty important details Musk has yet to explain.

NEW BOOK ON ELON MUSK EXAMINES THE BILLIONAIRE’S MIND, MOTIVATION AND MAKING LIFE MULTI-PLANETARY

Elon Musk has pledged to give one share of SpaceX stock to every child in America in 2027, a potential giveaway valued at more than $10 billion. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Elon Musk promises SpaceX shares to every US child

Musk recently announced on X that he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every kid in America in 2027. "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk wrote.

That's a sweeping commitment. SpaceX, which went public in June 2026, operates the Starlink satellite internet network and develops rockets for commercial spaceflight. Now Musk wants millions of American children to own a tiny piece of the company. The promise has already attracted attention because of its enormous potential cost. However, Musk hasn't provided a detailed plan explaining how the shares would reach families or which children would qualify.
How much would the SpaceX shares be worth?

For perspective, SpaceX shares closed at $147.49 on Oct. 23. There are just over 72 million Americans under age 18. Using that closing price, giving every one of them a share would cost approximately $10.6 billion. For a family with two eligible children, that could mean roughly $295 worth of SpaceX stock based on the Oct. 23 valuation. Of course, that amount could change considerably by 2027. Stock prices rise and fall, and owning a single share offers no guarantee of future profits. Still, there's something intriguing about the idea of a child becoming an investor before graduating from high school. If SpaceX continues to grow, that share could become more valuable over time. On the other hand, families could also watch its value decline.
Why Musk's SpaceX promise followed Anthropic's announcement

The timing is especially interesting. Just one day before Musk made his announcement, artificial intelligence company Anthropic revealed a major philanthropic commitment of its own. The company behind Claude AI announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval. The fund could support nonprofit organizations or provide direct financial assistance to certain populations, including workers affected by AI-driven economic changes. The company also described a structure that could increase its contribution as its valuation grows, subject to future board decisions.

Musk responded to Anthropic's announcement by recommending that companies give shares directly to the public. He then followed up with his own pledge involving SpaceX. This exchange raises an interesting question about the enormous wealth accumulating around AI. As technology companies become increasingly valuable, executives are facing greater scrutiny over how that wealth should benefit the public.
SEN DAVE MCCORMICK: TRUMP ACCOUNTS GIVE ALL AMERICANS A STAKE IN PROSPERITY

A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket launches with NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope onboard from Launch Complex 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla., on Aug. 30, 2026. (NASA via Getty Images)
Could SpaceX shares be connected to Trump Accounts?

Under the Trump Accounts program, the Treasury Department began automatically enrolling eligible children in tax-advantaged investment accounts on Oct. 1. Parents or guardians must still claim and activate those accounts before managing them. A separate federal pilot program provides a one-time $1,000 contribution for qualifying U.S. citizen children born between Jan. 1, 2025 and Dec. 31, 2028. Families must make an election to receive that contribution.

SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell and her husband, Robert Shotwell, previously pledged to donate one SpaceX share to the Trump Account of each of more than 2 million children. Their contribution targets children ages 11 to 17 in areas with lower-than-average household incomes, with additional emphasis on communities near their home in central Texas.

New Treasury regulations that took effect Sept. 30 also allow qualifying donations of publicly traded company shares into Trump Accounts. Under those rules, donated shares generally must be held for five years or until the account's special growth period ends, whichever comes first. Musk's proposal could potentially use this system, but he has not publicly explained the exact distribution process. That's an important unanswered question because Trump Accounts have established eligibility requirements and investment rules. Musk's announcement appears to cover a much broader population of children, although he has yet to define exactly who qualifies.
What questions remain about Musk's SpaceX giveaway?

A pledge this large naturally comes with logistical challenges. For starters, Musk hasn't clarified whether every child under 18 would qualify or whether the giveaway would be limited to U.S. citizens. It is also unclear how children would receive their shares.

If the giveaway uses Trump Accounts, families would need to understand how eligibility and account requirements apply. If Musk chooses another distribution method, parents may need some type of custodial account to hold stock for a minor. But Musk has not identified a specific process for families to claim his promised shares.

There are also financial questions. Would families face any tax consequences? Could children sell their shares immediately, or would restrictions apply? And when during 2027 would the transfers happen? For now, there's no confirmed application process for Musk's nationwide pledge. Parents should be cautious of anyone claiming otherwise.
UKRAINE'S STARLINK RESTORED AS ELON MUSK CLAIMS KYIV VIOLATED TERMS OF SERVICE 'TO KILL PEOPLE'

Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Technologies, and his wife Susan speak alongside President Donald Trump during the announcement of a $6.25 billion donation from the Dell family to "Trump Accounts" in the Roosevelt Room of the White House on December 2. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images)
What this means to you

If you have children or grandchildren, this is certainly a development worth following. A free share of SpaceX could introduce young people to investing and give them a financial interest in a company developing space technology. But I'd encourage parents to be patient. Musk has not announced an official enrollment process for his proposed giveaway. That means you should be especially suspicious of websites or social media messages claiming you can already register your children for free SpaceX stock.

We have previously reported on scams using Elon Musk's name to promote questionable products. A high-profile stock giveaway could provide another opportunity for impersonators to target families. Avoid sharing your child's Social Security number, financial information or other sensitive details with anyone promoting an unverified giveaway. For legitimate information about Trump Accounts, visit the IRS website at irs.gov/trumpaccounts directly. That official program already has an established enrollment process, but signing up for a Trump Account does not guarantee your child will receive a share from Musk's pledge. If SpaceX eventually announces a formal process, review the eligibility requirements and any account restrictions before participating.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've seen Elon Musk make some pretty ambitious promises over the years, but offering a piece of SpaceX to every child in America is certainly an attention-grabber. What interests me most is the idea of giving young people an ownership stake in a company helping shape the future of space exploration. There could be real financial value in that over time. Still, I want to see the details before getting too excited. A promise involving billions of dollars and millions of children deserves a clear explanation of how it will work. I also find the timing fascinating. With Anthropic making its own massive commitment to public benefit, we're beginning to see tech billionaires debate who should share in the wealth their companies create. I'll be watching to see whether Musk follows through and how much of that wealth actually reaches American families.

title: Giant robotic claws will grab dead satellites in space
summary: ClearSpace UK's robotic spacecraft with giant claws will chase down dead satellites at 17,000 mph, with a 2029 launch from Scotland planned.
story: Peter Doocy reports on the Pentagon's public confirmation of US space weapons. Former NASA astronaut Butch Wilmore joins to analyze the growing space arms race. Wilmore discusses the strategic importance of controlling the exo-atmosphere and explains the challenges of kinetic and non-kinetic weaponry as Russia and China expand their space capabilities.

Space is getting crowded, and I'm not talking about astronauts. Thousands of pieces of junk are circling Earth at incredible speeds. Some are dead satellites. Others are leftover rocket parts or fragments from past collisions. Any one of them could cause serious trouble if it hits a working spacecraft.

Now Britain has a pretty wild solution. It's developing a robotic spacecraft with giant claws that can grab dead satellites and move them toward a fiery end in Earth's atmosphere. Think of a garbage truck in orbit, except this one has to track down its trash while both objects are traveling thousands of miles per hour.
The UK is putting roughly $81 million behind the project. And if everything goes according to plan, the mission could change how we deal with the growing mess above our heads.

WILL A FOUR-ARMED ROBOT REPLACE ASTRONAUTS IN SPACE?
ClearSpace's robotic capture technology could help remove abandoned satellites before they collide with working spacecraft. (ClearSpace)
Britain's $81 million plan to clean up space

The UK Space Agency has selected aerospace company ClearSpace UK to develop a spacecraft specifically designed to remove dead satellites from orbit. The contract is valued at approximately $81 million. The project is part of Britain's Active Debris Removal mission, known as UK ADR. The spacecraft is targeted for launch in 2029 from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland's Shetland Islands.

Its first job will be to remove two defunct UK-registered satellites from low Earth orbit. The government wants both satellites removed by 2032. If successful, the mission would demonstrate that one spacecraft can capture and dispose of multiple dead satellites without being sacrificed after its first cleanup. That could make future operations far more practical, especially as the number of satellites in orbit continues to grow.
How giant robotic claws will grab dead satellites

Catching a satellite sounds straightforward until you consider what's happening in orbit. Objects in low Earth orbit typically travel at roughly 17,000 mph or faster. Some dead satellites may also tumble, making them difficult to approach safely. That's where ClearSpace's robotic technology comes in. The spacecraft will use a specialized capture system to approach and secure an inactive satellite. First, it must carefully coordinate its movements with the target. Then its robotic capture mechanism will take hold of the object.

Once the satellite is secured, the spacecraft will move it into a lower orbit and release it. Atmospheric drag will eventually pull the abandoned satellite down, causing it to reenter Earth's atmosphere, where it is expected to burn up. The cleanup spacecraft itself is being designed for potential refueling and reuse. That means it could remain in orbit for future work instead of ending its mission after disposing of one satellite. Of course, engineers still have to prove the technology can handle these demanding operations safely.
Why space junk is becoming a serious problem

You might assume there's plenty of room in space for a few broken satellites. Unfortunately, some of the orbital regions where satellites operate are becoming increasingly crowded. According to the European Space Agency's space debris statistics, updated October 14, 2026, approximately 47,140 objects are regularly tracked in Earth's orbit. That figure includes functioning satellites, inactive spacecraft, rocket bodies and debris.

And those are only the objects large enough to track reliably. ESA estimates that millions of smaller pieces also surround Earth. The danger comes from their enormous speeds. A piece of debris measuring just one centimeter can carry enough energy to disable a spacecraft. ESA has also warned that an impact of that size could penetrate the protective shielding of the International Space Station.

Now consider what happens when two large objects collide. They can break apart and produce many additional fragments, each capable of damaging something else. Scientists call this potential chain reaction the Kessler syndrome. If enough collisions occur, certain orbital regions could become extremely hazardous for future missions. ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report warns that active debris removal will be necessary to prevent long-term debris growth driven by collisions.
TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY
An ESA visualization shows how abandoned satellites and other debris crowd Earth's orbit, increasing the danger of collisions. ((European Space Agency (ESA))
Space junk also threatens astronauts

The danger extends beyond expensive satellites. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station face risks from debris traveling through orbit. In November 2021, crew members took shelter inside their spacecraft after a Russian anti-satellite weapons test created a dangerous cloud of debris. NASA confirmed that astronauts and cosmonauts closed hatches and sheltered inside docked Dragon and Soyuz spacecraft while teams evaluated the threat.

Fortunately, the station and crew remained safe. The incident demonstrated how quickly debris from a satellite breakup can disrupt operations in orbit. A serious impact could damage critical systems or puncture a spacecraft's pressurized structure. That's why space agencies continuously monitor debris and sometimes adjust spacecraft orbits to avoid potential collisions. Removing larger abandoned satellites could help prevent future collisions that create even more fragments.
Could space junk fall back to Earth?

Here's another concern that deserves attention. Some space debris eventually returns to Earth, and certain components can survive the intense heat of atmospheric reentry. Most smaller debris burns up. However, larger objects and components made from heat-resistant materials can sometimes reach the ground. As rocket launches increase, researchers are paying closer attention to this danger.

Space environmentalist Ewan Wright, from the University of British Columbia, told Space.com that approximately 124 rocket stages reentered Earth's atmosphere uncontrolled in 2024. He estimated that if that annual level continued for a decade, there would be a 33% probability of at least one person somewhere in the world being killed by falling rocket debris. That estimate describes a cumulative global risk from rocket stages, rather than the danger posed by Britain's two satellite-removal targets.

ESA also reports that the risk of casualties from uncontrolled reentries has increased in recent years, although the overall probability remains low compared with many everyday risks. The takeaway here is that removing debris from orbit requires careful planning. Operators must consider what happens when that material eventually returns to Earth.
A new space cleanup industry could be taking shape

Britain's mission could have implications well beyond the two satellites it plans to remove. For years, many satellites were designed primarily to complete their missions and then be retired. Some remain in orbit long after they stop functioning. Now companies are developing spacecraft capable of approaching other satellites and performing tasks that once seemed incredibly difficult.

ClearSpace's mission could help prove that robotic spacecraft can safely capture objects that were never designed for servicing. Its planned refueling capability is particularly interesting. Instead of launching a new cleanup vehicle for every job, operators could eventually service an existing spacecraft and send it after more debris.

That could open the door to a new commercial industry. Satellite operators might eventually pay specialized companies to remove aging equipment or extend the useful lives of working spacecraft. However, the UK mission remains in development. Its long-term commercial potential will depend on whether the technology performs as expected.
The International Space Station faces ongoing risks from high-speed orbital debris that could damage critical equipment and threaten astronauts. (NASA)
What this means to you

You probably don't spend much time thinking about abandoned satellites while checking the weather or following GPS directions. But the technology operating above Earth plays an enormous role in everyday life. Satellites support communication networks, provide navigation signals and deliver information used for weather forecasting. They also help scientists monitor changes on Earth and support emergency response operations.

GPS satellites operate in medium Earth orbit, much higher than the low Earth orbit debris targeted by Britain's mission. Still, the broader effort to keep orbital regions safer helps protect the infrastructure that supports satellite-based services. A collision that disables an important spacecraft could disrupt operations and force companies or government agencies to rely on backup systems. Replacing a damaged satellite can also be expensive.

Britain's robotic cleanup mission won't eliminate the space junk problem overnight. But successfully removing two abandoned satellites could help establish a practical way to deal with dangerous objects already in orbit. And with thousands of additional satellites being launched, finding a reliable way to retire them safely could become increasingly important.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to admit, the idea of a spacecraft chasing down dead satellites with giant robotic claws sounds like something Hollywood dreamed up. But I find the technology fascinating, especially when you consider how much we depend on satellites without giving them a second thought. What really caught my attention is the possibility of reusing the cleanup spacecraft. That could make removing space junk a routine service rather than an occasional experiment. Still, I wonder whether we're moving fast enough. With companies launching more satellites every year, cleaning up two abandoned spacecraft feels like a small start. I'd like to see satellite operators take greater responsibility for what they leave behind. After all, we wouldn't tolerate companies abandoning broken equipment on our highways. Why should Earth's orbit be any different?

title: Fake Social Security statement email hides a scam
summary: A fake Social Security statement phishing email uses the SSA logo and a convincing layout, but the sender's domain instantly exposes the scam.
story: Following the arrest of an alleged leader in the Netherlands, a top FBI cyber official released an unusual public address urging the remaining cybercriminals to turn themselves in "while the choice is still yours."

There's something about an email from Social Security that makes you pay attention. After all, we're talking about your retirement benefits and years of earnings. So when a message lands in your inbox saying your statement is ready, clicking to take a look might seem perfectly reasonable. That's exactly what scammers are counting on.

Take a look at this email below that recently landed in an inbox. It looks professional, carries the Social Security Administration (SSA) logo and includes a button to view a statement. However, a closer inspection reveals something the sender probably hoped you wouldn't notice. The message came from an email address with no apparent connection to the federal government.

Even more concerning, the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General warned in February 2026 about a significant increase in fraudulent emails using this same type of trick. Here's how to spot the warning signs in this email and protect yourself before scammers get their hands on your personal information.

FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
A fake Social Security statement email uses the agency's logo and an official-looking design to trick recipients into clicking a suspicious link. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How this fake Social Security statement email works

The message arrives with the subject line "Statement Support Was Posted to Your Account Details Report." The sender appears as "Social Security Administrator," which immediately gives the impression of an official government communication. Inside, the email announces, "Your statement is ready." It goes on to say your 2025 Social Security statement is available and invites you to review your earnings record and benefit estimates online.

There's even a neatly formatted box showing the year as 2025 and the status as "Ready." Below that sits a prominent blue "View statement" button. The message also displays what looks like the official Social Security website address. For someone quickly checking email before work or while getting through a crowded inbox, this could easily pass as a routine government notification.
The sender's email address exposes the scam

Here's where the message falls apart. Although the sender's display name says "Social Security Administrator," expanding the sender information reveals an address using the domain loradmiadministraciones.com . That's a major red flag. The address has no apparent relationship to Social Security, and the sender's domain does not end in .gov. Scammers can customize their display names to impersonate government agencies or other trusted organizations.

According to the Social Security Administration, most legitimate SSA emails come from government email addresses. However, the agency does use some authorized outside services, including certain communications from echosign.com and approved marketing firms. That means you should examine the complete sender address and verify any unexpected request independently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed.
FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC
Expanding the sender's details reveals an email address unrelated to the Social Security Administration, exposing a major warning sign of the scam. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why the View statement button raises concerns

The email encourages the recipient to click "View statement" to access what appears to be a routine financial document. That button is a central concern. A phishing link can redirect you to a fraudulent website designed to steal account credentials or sensitive personal information. Some malicious links can also lead to malware downloads.

We haven't verified the destination behind the button in this particular email. However, the suspicious sender address and resemblance to known SSA phishing campaigns make the message unsafe to trust. The SSA's inspector general has specifically warned about fake statement notifications containing dangerous links. Those links could expose personal information or compromise devices.
Why this Social Security scam looks so believable

One interesting thing about this example is how little pressure it puts on the reader. There's no demand for immediate payment or warning that benefits will disappear within 24 hours. Instead, the message offers something people might genuinely want to see: their Social Security statement.

It also uses the generic greeting "Dear Beneficiary," despite appearing in an inbox associated with a named recipient. That lack of personalization provides another reason to investigate, although generic greetings alone cannot prove an email is fraudulent. The professional appearance does much of the work. The SSA logo and government-style formatting create an impression of credibility. Yet none of those visual elements establishes who actually sent the email.
Does Social Security really send statement emails?

Yes, and that's what makes this scam particularly convincing. According to the SSA's official guidance, people with a personal my Social Security account generally receive an annual email reminder approximately three months before their birthday. The agency also sends certain notifications about new messages and notices. Scammers take advantage of these legitimate communications by creating messages that resemble official SSA reminders.
How to check whether a Social Security email is legitimate
Before opening a statement or following instructions in an unexpected email, take a few seconds to investigate the message.

On a computer, click the sender's name or expand the message details to reveal the full email address. On an iPhone or Android phone, tap the sender's name or address to view additional information. The exact method depends on your email app. Look closely at the domain. Watch for unfamiliar company names, extra characters or addresses unrelated to Social Security.

On a computer, hover your mouse over a button or link without clicking. Your browser or email app may display its actual destination. On a phone, some email apps let you touch and hold a link to preview its address. Be careful because certain apps may open or begin loading a preview. When in doubt, skip this step and visit the official SSA website yourself. Remember that a website beginning with HTTPS can still be fraudulent. Encryption alone does not prove that a website belongs to the government.

The most reliable approach is to open a new browser window and visit ssa.gov yourself. You can also contact Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 using the number published on its official website. Avoid using contact details provided in a suspicious email.
How to safely access your Social Security statement
You can check your earnings record and estimated retirement benefits without clicking an emailed statement link.

Open your browser and type ssa.gov/myaccount directly into the address bar.Select the option to sign in to your personal my Social Security account.Use Login.gov or ID.me , the supported sign-in services.Complete any required authentication or identity verification.Once signed in, open your Social Security Statement to review your earnings history and estimated benefits.
Open your browser and type ssa.gov/myaccount directly into the address bar.
Select the option to sign in to your personal my Social Security account.
Use Login.gov or ID.me , the supported sign-in services.
Complete any required authentication or identity verification.
Once signed in, open your Social Security Statement to review your earnings history and estimated benefits.
If you don't already have an account, follow the official registration instructions. Creating an account can also help you monitor your Social Security information for unexpected activity.
Retirees can reduce their online exposure by checking where their personal information appears and requesting its removal. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
7 ways to protect yourself from Social Security phishing scams
A convincing email can catch anyone off guard, especially when it concerns retirement benefits or personal financial information. These practical steps can help protect your identity and accounts.
Even when an email looks authentic, use the SSA website independently to access your information. Avoid downloading unsolicited statement attachments or documents that claim to come from the agency.

Use a unique password for your Login.gov or ID.me account and keep multifactor authentication enabled. Also protect the email account associated with your Social Security profile because criminals may target it to reset other passwords.

Strong antivirus software can help identify dangerous websites and block known malware downloads. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated to protect against newly discovered threats. Never provide your Social Security number or financial account information through an unexpected email link. If someone claims to represent Social Security and requests sensitive details, contact the agency through its official website.

Review your earnings history periodically through your personal SSA account. Look for unfamiliar earnings or changes to account details. If you notice something suspicious, contact Social Security directly for assistance.

Scammers can collect personal details from people-search websites and data brokers to make their messages more convincing. Consider removing your information from these websites or using a reputable data removal service to handle supported requests. Although this won't stop every phishing attempt, it can limit some of the personal details criminals find online. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

The SSA Office of the Inspector General accepts reports of Social Security impersonation scams at oig.ssa.gov/report/ . Save the suspicious sender address and relevant screenshots. You can also report the message through your email provider's built-in phishing-reporting feature. Once you've preserved the information needed for a report, delete the email.
What to do if you clicked a fake Social Security statement link
Your next steps depend on what happened after you clicked. Here's how to respond.

Close the suspicious website immediately. Avoid interacting with additional prompts or downloading files. If the site attempted a download, check your device's Downloads folder without opening the file. Simply visiting a phishing page does not automatically mean your information was stolen. However, keep your browser and operating system updated, and run a security scan with strong antivirus software if you notice anything unusual.

Change the affected password immediately through the legitimate website, preferably using a trusted device. If you reused the password anywhere else, change it on those accounts too. A reputable password manager can help you create strong, unique passwords for each account and alert you to passwords that may have been exposed in a data breach. Next, review account activity and recovery settings. Check for unfamiliar sign-ins or unauthorized changes. Contact Login.gov, ID.me or the affected service through its official support channels if you believe someone accessed your account.

Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan. Consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. This can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts using your information. You should also review your credit reports and monitor financial accounts for unauthorized activity.

Avoid opening the downloaded file if you haven't already. If you ran it, disconnect the affected device from the internet and perform a scan with strong antivirus software. If you suspect malware installed successfully, use a separate trusted device to change sensitive passwords. Consider getting professional assistance before signing back into financial accounts on the affected computer.

Contact your bank or financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about securing your accounts or disputing unauthorized transactions. You should also report the incident to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/ and the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ . The SSA's inspector general recommends these reporting channels for victims of Social Security impersonation scams. If you experienced financial loss, consider filing a report with local law enforcement.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me about this particular scam is how routine the email feels. There are no dramatic threats or wild promises. It simply tells you that your Social Security statement is available, something millions of Americans have a legitimate reason to check. And the design is convincing enough that someone could click before thinking twice. I've said it before, and I'll keep saying it: A polished email doesn't tell you anything about who's really behind it. In this example, checking the sender's actual address exposed a serious warning sign immediately. My advice is simple. When an email involves your Social Security information, go directly to the government website and check for yourself. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache.

title: Your credit can look normal while someone steals your identity
summary: A clean credit report doesn't mean your identity is safe. Six ways criminals can steal from you without triggering a credit monitoring alert.
story: JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson for the ‘Beyond Connected’ podcast.

You check your credit score, see nothing unusual and assume your identity is safe. But what if someone has already stolen your personal information, and your credit report shows absolutely nothing? That's entirely possible.

Credit monitoring can help detect certain types of identity theft, particularly fraud involving new credit accounts. However, criminals can also target your existing bank accounts, retirement savings, government benefits and phone number without triggering a traditional credit alert. As a result, a clean credit report can give you a false sense of security. Here's what credit monitoring can catch, what it might miss and how to better protect yourself.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
