title: DHS investigates massive data breach exposing 40,000 employees, including ICE and Border Patrol agents
summary: The Department of Homeland Security is investigating a breach that exposed roughly 40,000 employees, including 10,000 ICE agents and CBP personnel.
story: The Department of Homeland Security is investigating a massive data leak reportedly exposing the personal information of roughly 40,000 employees, including thousands of ICE and Border Patrol personnel and several undercover agents.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is investigating a potentially massive data breach that may have exposed the identities and contact information of tens of thousands of employees, sources told Fox News.

The suspected breach, which sources described as a "catastrophic" security incident, may have exposed the names, titles, locations and, in some cases, phone numbers and email addresses of approximately 40,000 DHS employees and contractors, including roughly 10,000 ICE personnel, according to sources familiar with the data.
The data also includes records associated with more than 20,000 U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) employees, including Border Patrol personnel.
Multiple sources confirmed the authenticity of portions of the data.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET

U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin speaks during a press conference at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) headquarters on October 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
The data leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said Wednesday it had released information about the employees.
Fox News independently confirmed that the leaked records include the names of several undercover ICE agents working in different parts of the country.
An anti-fascist hacking group calling itself the "Department of Peace" claimed responsibility for obtaining the data.
"DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively," a department spokesperson told Fox News.
NY COP CALLS FOR POLICE PROTECTIONS AFTER PROTESTER HE ARRESTED SHOWED UP TO HIS HOUSE, HARASSED HIS FAMILY

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents walk down a street during a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago, Ill., on Jan. 26, 2025. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the statement continued. "We will update the public when more information is available."
Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said in a statement that a tool had been developed to allow the public to search the data, saying it would "replace anonymity with accountability."

The Department of Peace said in its own statement that DHS employees "have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs" and that it hoped the data "can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction."
The reported breach comes amid broader concerns about the security of government personnel records.
FOREIGN ENEMIES HAVE A SHOCKINGLY SIMPLE WAY TO TRACK US TROOPS OVERSEAS, LAWMAKERS WARN
The U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) headquarters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, May 10, 2023. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Last month, a Pentagon personnel database breach exposed sensitive personal information belonging to more than 2.76 million living U.S. military and civilian personnel and 294,000 deceased individuals.

Unauthorized users accessed unencrypted files containing Social Security numbers and military or civilian employment information between October 2025 and July 2026, a Pentagon official previously confirmed to Fox News.

title: Emergency declared at South Carolina nuclear site after fire erupts at lab
summary: A fire at a massive Department of Energy nuclear site triggered emergency measures, though officials reported no contamination outside the facility.
story: A fire at the Savannah River National Laboratory in South Carolina prompted officials to declare a Site Area Emergency, leaving one employee with minor injuries, though authorities reported no radiological contamination.
An emergency was declared at a massive Department of Energy nuclear site in South Carolina after a laboratory fire left one employee with minor injuries, officials said.

The Savannah River Site (SRS) declared a Site Area Emergency at 5:39 p.m. Wednesday after a fire broke out at the Savannah River National Laboratory near Aiken, South Carolina, according to the Department of Energy (DOE).
The emergency was terminated at 9:45 p.m. after the fire was extinguished and radiological surveys found no detectable levels of contamination, according to an updated notice from SRS.
One employee was taken to a hospital with minor injuries, a DOE spokesperson told Fox News.
STARTUPS BRING INNOVATION TO DEFENSE INDUSTRIAL BASE
A file photo shows the Savannah River Site near Aiken, S.C. (The State/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
"No radiological contamination has been reported," the spokesperson said.
All protective actions were lifted, and site barricades have reopened, officials said.
"There are currently no operational emergencies or scheduled delays for the Savannah River Site," an SRS notification update stated.
Oncoming shift workers were instructed to report as usual, while all other employees were told to return to work as scheduled on Thursday, Oct. 29.
Shift workers who had been directed to shelter in place were also allowed to return to work as usual.
Highway 125 remained open following the incident and traffic at site entrances resumed after officials temporarily barricaded them as a precaution, according to SRS.
SRS earlier announced restrictions on all rail, river and air traffic near the vicinity of the site.
SRS officials continued directing response efforts and notified the appropriate state and local government agencies.
Local residents were previously advised to monitor local radio and television stations for updates and any instructions from state officials.
FROM MOJAVE TO BEIJING: HOW AMERICA QUIETLY CONCEDED THE RARE EARTH RACE
A boat travels the Savannah River in Savannah, Ga. (Amy Galo)
The SRS is a major installation in the nation’s weapons complex that has supported the U.S. military’s strategic deterrence mission for more than 75 years, according to the SRS website.
The installation manages nuclear materials and radioactive waste, with cleanup operations aimed at protecting the surrounding environment, according to the Department of Energy.

U.S. Department of Energy headquarters at the James V. Forrestal Building in Washington, D.C., on May 28, 2026. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

"While serving as one of the nation’s most critical pieces in the weapons complex, the site is also one of the safest major industrial sites in the world. Ensuring national security, protecting workers, the public, and the environment, are our highest goals," the SRS website states.

The facility was constructed in the 1950s, when five reactors were built to produce materials used in nuclear weapons, primarily tritium and plutonium-239. Several support facilities were also built, including two chemical separation plants.

title: Convicted murderer got over 5-hour head start after prison escape before local police were notified: official
summary: Jacob Allen Morley had at least a five-hour head start before Tiptonville police were notified he escaped the Northwest Correctional Complex.
story: Former federal prison Warden Cameron Lindsay says Jacob Morley’s escape raises serious questions about staff failures after video showed the convicted murderer moving through the facility seemingly unimpeded.

FIRST ON FOX: The convicted murderer who escaped from a Tennessee prison had at least a five-hour head start before local police were notified he was missing, the local police chief told Fox News Digital.
Jacob Allen Morley broke out of the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, Sunday, although authorities have not disclosed the exact time of his escape.

Staff at the prison noticed Morley was unaccounted for at around 11:30 p.m., and a review of surveillance footage subsequently revealed him crossing through the prison's perimeter fence. According to Tennessee Highway Patrol dispatch audio, Morley was last seen at the prison around 4 p.m. Sunday.

Surveillance footage recorded Morley taking a pickup truck from the 400 block of Keystone Drive, a location roughly 2 miles south of the prison, at around 1 a.m. Monday, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said. The truck was found abandoned by law enforcement officials early Tuesday morning in Marion, Illinois, but Morley wasn't located.
TENNESSEE INMATE CONVICTED OF MURDER ESCAPES FROM PRISON, STEALS PICKUP TRUCK, MANHUNT UNDERWAY: OFFICIALS

Surveillance footage shows convicted murderer Jacob Allen Morley inside Northwest Correctional Complex before his escape Sunday. Authorities said Morley was captured on security video breaching a prison fence. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Tiptonville Police Department Chief Joe England said his department wasn't notified about a potentially missing inmate until 4:40 a.m. on Monday, over 5 hours after prison staff first realized Morley was unaccounted for.
Officers responded to the prison and worked with staff to assess the situation. At 5:14 a.m., England said, officers alerted the rest of the department that the inmate's escape had been confirmed.
At 6:20 a.m., prison officials formally notified Lake County Central Dispatch, which handles 911 calls and coordinates law enforcement services, that an inmate escape had been confirmed.
The notification set off a broader search for Morley in the area surrounding the prison.
ESCAPED TENNESSEE KILLER'S ABANDONED TRUCK OFFERS CLUES TO WHAT HE MAY DO NEXT: RETIRED FBI AGENT

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield when he escaped from a Tennessee prison Sunday, according to correctional officials. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

"The Tiptonville Police Department immediately coordinated with the Tennessee Department of Correction and the Lake County Sheriff's Office to conduct a search of the surrounding area," England said. "The Tennessee Highway Patrol, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and numerous other state, local and federal law enforcement agencies also participated in the search efforts."

While Morley stole the pickup truck at around 1 a.m. Monday, England said his department wasn't made aware of a potentially missing truck until 2:15 p.m. Monday, which was confirmed missing at 2:30 p.m. He noted that the pickup truck wasn't stolen within city limits.
Jacob Allen Morley escaped from prison in Tennessee and stole a pickup truck, which was found abandoned in Illinois. (Fox News)

A map shows key locations in the manhunt for escaped Tennessee murderer Jacob Allen Morley, including the prison he fled, where he allegedly stole a pickup truck, a reported sighting and where the stolen vehicle was found abandoned in Illinois. (Google Maps)
In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Tennessee Bureau of Investigation spokesperson said the agency was notified of the prison escape on Monday morning but didn't elaborate on an exact time.

The Lake County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to Fox News Digital when asked when the agency was first alerted of the prison escape. The Tennessee Department of Correction didn't respond to multiple requests for comment to Fox News Digital.
Former federal prison Warden Cameron Lindsay told Fox News Digital the delay in notifying police of an inmate escaping prison is "100% unacceptable."

"Part of any correctional facility's basic tenets of operations should include emergency plans. And one of those plans that you have for an emergency is an escape. And part of your escape plans entails notifying law enforcement, local law enforcement, state law enforcement, U.S. Marshals Service and everybody in the community. You need to get that word out immediately. So, for them to have that kind of delay raises a huge red flag," Lindsay said.
"And it begs the question, why, why did they delay? Because it is 100% unacceptable in the profession of corrections."
The stolen Ford F-350 authorities say escaped Tennessee inmate Jacob Morley drove after fleeing prison was found abandoned in Marion, Ill. (Tennessee Bureau of Investigation)
Lindsay said local law enforcement should have immediately been contacted once prison staff realized the inmate was unaccounted for.
Retired FBI Special Agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital the community should have been notified much sooner.

"That community should put out an emergency text to everyone to make sure none of their family members are missing as he could have killed or kidnapped someone after ditching the truck," Gilliam said.
TBI said Wednesday afternoon that the reward in the search for Morley is now $15,000 — $7,500 from the governor’s office, $5,000 from the U.S. Marshals and $2,500 from TBI.

Morley is described as 5 feet, 11 inches tall, and 240 pounds, with brown hair and green eyes. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said he should be "considered dangerous," adding Morley is now on the state's most wanted list.

In addition to the first-degree murder conviction, he was also found guilty of burglary, vandalism, tampering with evidence and evading arrest.
Morley was serving a life sentence for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield.

title: Woman wearing burka escorted out of Florida county meeting after playing call to prayer recording
summary: A woman wearing a burka played an Islamic call to prayer recording at a Pinellas County commissioners meeting before a sheriff's deputy escorted her out.
story: A woman covered in a veil was escorted out of the Pinellas County Board of County Commissioners meeting after refusing to shut off the recording (Credit: Pinellas County Board of County Commissioners).

A woman wearing a burka was escorted out of a Florida county commissioners meeting on Tuesday after playing a recording of the Islamic call to prayer during the public comment period where residents spoke against the potential expansion of a local mosque amid concerns from some over its wording on zoning and agenda materials.

The incident occurred as the Pinellas County Board of County Commissioners was listening to residents address the board. A woman covered head-to-toe in black, with only her left eye visible, and approached the podium. Rather than making a verbal statement, she activated a recording of the call to prayer.
It was not immediately clear whether the gesture was a protest or a prank.
PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'

A woman wearing a burka was escorted out of a Pinellas County Board of County Commissioners meeting on Wednesday after playing what appeared to be an Islamic call for prayer. (Pinellas County Board of County Commissioners.)
The audio played for nearly a minute before Board Chairman Dave Eggers interrupted, pointing out that county rules require public speakers to deliver verbal comments rather than play recordings.
"Ma’am, you’re going to have to stop … stop the music, stop the tape," Eggers said.
TEXAS POLICE ADMIT OFFICER MADE INACCURATE FIRST AMENDMENT REMARKS AFTER PREACHER CITED AT PRIDE EVENT
When the woman refused to comply, a Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office deputy approached the podium and escorted her out of the meeting room and the building.
Her removal sparked immediate friction in the room, with several audience members shouting and arguing with Eggers over the decision.
"Please. Just please exercise some decorum and kindness of your own," Eggers told the audience. "We’re all people living together here."
He further clarified the board’s rules to the crowd.

"We don’t allow taped things," he said. "You can record the meeting, but we don’t allow taped activity like that. We ask you to come here and make comments, and that was not a comment. That’s why she was asked to step out."

The incident came during a public period where multiple residents decried an Oct. 13 vote in which the board voted 4-3 to approve a land-use amendment for the expansion of the Masjid Al Rahman mosque, which was referred to in presentations and documents as a "community assembly facility."
LAWSUIT ACCUSES DEARBORN, MICHIGAN, OF BEING 'HOSTILE TO CHRISTIANS AND JEWS' WITH ISLAMIC DISPLAYS
The vote changed the property's land use from residential rural to public and semi-public, which would allow the facility's owner to replace the building with a newer structure 1,000 feet larger.
During Tuesday's meeting, public speakers spoke out against the facility, some citing the treatment of women in Muslim-majority countries.

"It is about the big picture and the long term," one woman told the commission. "By allowing this mosque to expand in our area, you are participating in the expansion of a totalitarian ideology which is fundamentally opposed to Western American values. Expansion of the ideology of Islam is not good for women's rights."

Another woman supported the mosque: "They want to turn it to face Mecca, and they want it to look a little more like a mosque instead of a house," she said. "We have no problems with them. We've been their neighbors for many years."
Commissioner Vince Nowicki reportedly questioned why the mosque wasn't described in plain language in government documents.

"Residents read these materials to understand what is being proposed near them, and they should get the same plain description in every case, no matter the applicant," Nowicki wrote in an email to County Administrator Barry Burton, Florida Politics reported.

title: Dolores Huerta, United Farm Workers co-founder who accused César Chavez of sex abuse, dead at 96
summary: The longtime labor organizer and civil rights activist helped build a national movement advocating for agricultural workers after beginning her career as a schoolteacher.
story: Dolores Huerta attends a film premiere in Los Angeles, California, in July. The pioneering labor organizer died at the age of 96 on Oct. 28, 2026. (Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)

Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor activist who co-founded the United Farm Workers union and spent decades fighting for better working conditions for America's agricultural workers, has died. She was 96.
Huerta died at her home on Wednesday in Bakersfield, California, surrounded by her close family, her foundation announced.

Svante Myrick, president of the progressive advocacy group People For the American Way, where Huerta served on the board of directors for 22 years, remembered her as "unstoppable," in a statement remembering her legacy.

"Dolores Huerta was one of the fiercest and most consequential activists in our nation’s history," Myrick said. "She was the first to get started in the morning and the last to quit at the end of the day."

Born in New Mexico and raised by a single mother in California's San Joaquin Valley, Huerta began her career as a schoolteacher before helping establish a local chapter of a grassroots organization that challenged segregation and police brutality.

Dolores Huerta waves to fans before throwing out the first pitch during Mexican Heritage Night at Dodger Stadium on May 26, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
CALIFORNIA DEMOCRATS DISTANCE THEMSELVES FROM FAMED PRO-UNION ACTIVIST AFTER BOMBSHELL REPORT

Eventually, her focus turned to labor organizing, and together with César Chavez, whom she'd later accuse of sexual abuse, she built the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. Four years later, that association merged with another organization to form the United Farm Workers union.
Six decades after its founding, the United Farm Workers remains the nation's longest-standing labor union representing agricultural workers.
Huerta herself was one of the most enduring and influential labor leaders in the country, becoming known for her rallying cry, "Sí, se puede!"
In English, the slogan translates to "Yes, it can be done," reflecting her sincere belief that ordinary people can affect political change.

Beyond her work to improve the lives of those working in America's fruit and vegetable fields, many of whom are immigrants, Huerta became a prominent civil rights and women's rights advocate, combating discrimination and fighting for gender equality in a labor movement that was dominated by men at the time.

Dolores Huerta attends a demonstration after the Women's March Foundation and Feminist Majority deliver 15,000 letters, postcards and printed emails to Senator Kyrsten Sinema on Aug. 2, 2021 in Phoenix, Arizona.  (Matt Young/Getty Images)
DOLORES HUERTA RECEIVES NATIONAL PRIZE FOR PUBLIC SERVICE

Huerta was one of the leaders behind the Delano grape strike, which lasted from September 1965 to July 1970. She, along with a coalition of Mexican and Filipino farmhands, accused grape growers in Delano, California, of exploiting their workers by underpaying them.

Thousands of farmworkers walked off California's grape fields in 1965, sparking a labor movement that gained momentum in the years that followed. Huerta played a pivotal role in expanding the strike into a nationwide consumer boycott of grapes.
In the summer of 1970, the strike ended after the United Farm Workers union signed off on collective bargaining agreements that covered 10,000 workers.

Huerta received numerous awards throughout her career, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. Presenting her with the award in 2012, then-President Barack Obama praised her decades of activism and joked that he had borrowed her famous slogan, "Sí, se puede," for his 2008 presidential campaign.
Dolores Huerta receives the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama in the East Room of the White House on May 29, 2012 in Washington, D.C. (Leigh Vogel/WireImage)
DEMS FACE RECKONING AFTER PUTTING DECEASED LABOR LEADER ON PEDESTAL AS SEXUAL ABUSE ALLEGATIONS EMERGE
Earlier this year, Huerta publicly accused César Chavez of raping her in 1966 after driving her out to a grape field in Delano, where the strike was unfolding.
Huerta's account was published in The New York Times in March alongside two other women who say Chavez sexually abused them as girls during the 1970s.

Huerta also told The Times there was another incident between her and Chavez in August 1960, when he allegedly pressured her into having sex with him in a hotel room while on a work trip in San Juan Capistrano in Southern California.

Huerta said she became pregnant following both encounters with Chavez, who died in 1993, and later arranged for the children to be adopted and raised by other families, according to a statement she released addressing the allegations.
Dolores Huerta on Oct. 13, 1969, at the height of the Delano grape strike. She was 39 years old. (Bill Young/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She said she kept both the alleged assaults and the children secret for decades out of fear that others in the Latino civil rights movement would not believe her. She also worried that speaking out against Chavez, one of the movement's most prominent figures, would ultimately damage the cause and their shared objectives.
Despite her revelation, Huerta encouraged people to continue fighting for their rights and said the labor movement was bigger than her or Chavez.
Huerta's lifelong partner starting in the early 1970s was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, whom she had four kids with. She also had seven children from two previous marriages.
Even into her 90s, Huerta remained politically active, delivering speeches, attending rallies and speaking out on issues ranging from civil rights to national politics.

title: US military kills five in eastern Pacific strike on suspected drug-trafficking vessel
summary: Video shows a go-fast vessel erupt into a massive fireball as SOUTHCOM confirms five narco-terrorists were killed in the eastern Pacific strike.
story: U.S. Southern Command released footage of an Oct. 27 strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific that officials said was involved in drug trafficking, killing five people the military identified as narco-terrorists (Credit: X@Southcom).

The U.S. military on Tuesday carried out a lethal strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific that it said was involved in drug trafficking, killing five people it identified as "narco-terrorists," according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM).

"On October 27, under the direction of SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific," SOUTHCOM said in a statement.
"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the statement continued.
SOUTHCOM said five people it described as narco-terrorists were killed during the operation.
US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3
U.S. Southern Command released footage of a military strike on a suspected drug-trafficking vessel in the eastern Pacific on Oct. 27, 2026. (U.S. Southern Command)

Tuesday's strike was the latest in the Trump administration's monthslong campaign targeting suspected cartel vessels, which has now resulted in at least 240 deaths from more than 70 strikes, according to The Associated Press.
Video of Tuesday's operation released by SOUTHCOM shows a vessel in the water before it erupts into a massive fireball.
SOUTHCOM did not specify where the strike occurred beyond identifying the eastern Pacific and saying the vessel was operating along established drug-trafficking routes.
US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK
A vessel erupts into flames after being targeted by a U.S. military strike in the eastern Pacific that killed five people, according to SOUTHCOM. (U.S. Southern Command)

Throughout its campaign targeting suspected drug-trafficking networks, the military has released videos and statements describing those aboard the targeted vessels as "narco-terrorists" or alleging links to designated terrorist organizations. However, it has generally not identified those killed or provided evidence that the vessels were carrying narcotics.

The strikes have generated scrutiny from lawmakers, legal experts and human rights groups who have questioned the legal basis for using lethal military force against suspected traffickers outside a traditional battlefield.

SOUTHCOM's continued operations in Latin America and the Caribbean come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the U.S. was increasingly seeking to conduct counter-narcotics operations in cooperation with regional allies and in accordance with their laws.
Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has "the capacity to act unilaterally," it would rather work with its allies because that is "the most effective way to do it."
THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the United States prefers to work with regional allies on counter-narcotics operations while maintaining the ability to act unilaterally. (ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)
Rubio also said the U.S. military would "still blow up ships if need be" and that decisions would be made on "a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation" basis.

In recent months, SOUTHCOM has also released several videos showing military personnel intercepting and boarding vessels it said were involved in narco-trafficking before removing their crews and sinking the boats.

title: Halima Salman convicted of receiving ISIS military training in Syria, faces 10 years in prison
summary: Halima Salman, a former Brooklyn resident and U.S. citizen, was convicted in federal court of receiving ISIS military-style training in Syria.
story: Halima Salman, 27, was seen leaving a Brooklyn federal courthouse after a jury found her guilty of receiving military training from ISIS in Syria.
A federal jury on Tuesday convicted Halima Salman of knowingly receiving military-style training from ISIS while living in Syria, bringing an emotional end to a closely watched terrorism trial.
The case was believed to mark the first time a woman accused of joining ISIS stood trial in a U.S. federal court.
Salman, also known as "Umm Khattab al-Muhajir," is a 27-year-old U.S. citizen and former Brooklyn resident who faces up to 10 years in prison. She is scheduled to be sentenced Feb. 2.
According to federal prosecutors, Salman's parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States in 2016, ultimately taking the family to ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.
NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

(Reuters/Jane Rosenberg)
The Justice Department said she was 18 years old when she married an ISIS fighter and voluntarily sought military-style training from the terrorist organization.
Prosecutors said Salman pledged loyalty to ISIS and willingly participated in its activities.

She received authorization from ISIS to carry an assault rifle and was given a document certifying that she had completed the training. That document was later recovered from her husband's cellphone, officials said.

Halima Salman shields her face as she leaves federal court in the Brooklyn borough of New York on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

"With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization," U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York said in a statement.
"ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign," Nocella continued.
Following the reading of the verdict at the federal courthouse in Brooklyn, Salman broke down crying and was consoled by members of her defense team.

Her mother, who arrived after word came that the jury had reached a verdict, also broke down and was seen crying on her knees in the gallery. Multiple members of Salman's defense team were also visibly emotional, including her lead attorney, Mia Eisner-Grynberg.
SHE WAS MARRIED TO AN AL QAEDA MEMBER. NOW ONE WOMAN IS FIGHTING THE TERRORISM SHE SAW UP CLOSE

Halima Salman, charged with knowingly receiving military training from a foreign terrorist organization, the Islamic State, attends her trial as a rifle is shown on screen at Brooklyn federal court in New York City, New York, October 13, 2026, in this courtroom sketch. (Reuters/Jane Rosenberg)
Tuesday's verdict came after jurors previously indicated that they were struggling to reach a unanimous verdict and were sent back twice to continue deliberations.
Salman's defense team portrayed her as a teenager who was drawn into Syria's civil war through her father and later her husband.
Salman, who was born in Brooklyn, testified that she believed the family was traveling to visit relatives in Turkey when her father instead took them across the border into Syria.
"I do blame my father for a lot of things that happened," she testified.
She also said she didn't want to be "married off" at age 18 and had tried to get a divorce.
DEPROGRAMMED: HOW A MAN RADICALIZED BY THE TALIBAN BECAME A COUNTERTERRORISM FORCE SAVING LIVES FROM EXTREMISM
Halima Salman covers her face while departing a federal courthouse in Brooklyn, New York, on Oct. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)
"You try to leave, it is death," Salman testified.
Salman testified that she eventually fled with other refugees and separated from her husband.
She was detained in Baghouz, Syria, in 2019 by forces fighting ISIS and was arrested by U.S. authorities after returning to New York in 2024.

Salman's attorneys have asked the judge to set aside the verdict and acquit her, arguing that the evidence presented at trial was legally insufficient to sustain the conviction, according to The Associated Press.

title: Man accused of threatening to hijack United flight says it was a drunken joke
summary: Cockpit audio captured a pilot explaining the diverted United Airlines flight while Dante Milne allegedly slept, unaware he caused the emergency.
story: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley praises the crew's response after a passenger allegedly sent text messages threatening to hijack a Newark-bound flight, prompting an emergency return to Las Vegas.

A New Jersey man accused of sending a text threatening to hijack a United Airlines flight over the weekend told investigators he had been drinking and described the message as poorly worded banter with a coworker, according to an arrest report.

Dante Milne, 25, allegedly sent the threatening message Saturday while aboard United Airlines Flight 1681, a Boeing 737 carrying 150 passengers and six crew members from Las Vegas to Newark, New Jersey.
"I’m gonna hijack this b---- and crash ur row only," Milne allegedly wrote, according to an arrest report cited by FOX5 Vegas.

United Airlines planes at Newark Liberty International Airport in Newark, N.J, Nov. 3, 2025. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The message was allegedly spotted by a flight attendant shortly after departure, and the crew alerted the captain, who secured the cockpit and diverted the aircraft back to Harry Reid International Airport, where it landed at approximately 11:05 p.m.
The flight was delayed overnight after the crew reached its permitted working hours and departed for Newark the following morning, United Airlines previously told Fox News Digital.
Authorities later charged Milne with one count of making threats or conveying false information concerning an act of terrorism.
According to an arrest report, Milne told investigators he had consumed a beer and several shots at an airport bar before boarding.

He said he then fell asleep aboard the plane and woke up to discover the aircraft was returning to Las Vegas.

Milne initially acknowledged texting someone aboard the flight but said he could not remember the messages. When investigators specifically asked about the alleged hijacking threat, he described it as poorly worded "banter between coworkers," according to the arrest report.
Milne reportedly said he never intended to take control of the aircraft and apologized for what happened.
He told detectives he was returning home after spending three days in Las Vegas for an apprenticeship training program involving underwater welding, according to the report.

Air traffic control audio previously obtained by ATC.com and reported by Fox News captured the pilot explaining the situation as the flight returned to Las Vegas, including that the passenger suspected of making the threat apparently did not realize the aircraft had turned around because of him.

Travelers wait for luggage at Harry Reid International airport in Las Vegas Sept. 20, 2025. (Michael Anthony for Fox News Digital)

"The passenger does not know anything is going on," the pilot told air traffic controllers. "The flight attendant saw him texting that he was going to hijack the aircraft and called me and we went lockdown. … No restraint, passenger is compliant because he’s unaware."
Milne was later released on $10,000 bail, and his attorney told a judge Tuesday that he intended to plead not guilty, according to KLAS-TV.
Milne is due back in court on Jan. 5.
After the incident, United Airlines said the flight had returned to Las Vegas to address a "potential security concern."
"United Flight 1681 from Las Vegas to Newark on Saturday, Oct. 24, safely returned to Las Vegas to address a potential security concern," United Airlines previously told Fox News Digital.
"The flight was delayed overnight due to crew timeout, and departed for Newark this morning."

title: Suspected shark knocks fisherman off kayak a mile off California coast, forcing swim to shore
summary: A fisherman swam to shore after a suspected shark struck his kayak near Leffingwell Landing in Cambria, puncturing the hull and capsizing it.
story: Soren Stevenson shares how a spontaneous decision to record every wave during an early morning trip to Newport Beach led to the discovery of a massive great white shark only after reviewing the footage hours later.

A California fisherman was forced to swim to shore after a suspected shark struck his kayak about a mile offshore, capsizing the vessel and leaving it too damaged to stay afloat, according to fire officials.

The fisherman was near Leffingwell Landing in Cambria around 9:30 a.m. Monday when something struck the underside of his kayak, throwing him into the water, the Cambria Fire Department said in a Facebook post.
He managed to climb back aboard and paddle toward shore, but punctures in the hull caused the kayak to fill with water, forcing him to swim the rest of the way.
SHARK BITES FISHERMAN TWICE DURING KAYAKING ENCOUNTER ALONG CALIFORNIA BEACH
A great white shark swims underwater. A California fisherman escaped injury after a suspected shark encounter off the coast of Cambria. (iStock)
The fisherman reached shore without injuries, according to the department.
Firefighters responded after he reached land and launched a rescue boat to recover the damaged kayak, along with his fishing gear and personal belongings.

Dr. Chris Lowe of California State University, Long Beach's Shark Lab reviewed photographs of the damage and determined it was reasonable to suspect a shark was responsible, according to the fire department.
However, officials emphasized that shark involvement has not been definitively confirmed.
CALIFORNIA SCIENTISTS DEVELOPING SHARK-SPOTTING ROBOT AHEAD OF 2028 LOS ANGELES OLYMPICS

The area has seen similar encounters before. In May 2012, a shark struck a fishing kayak near Leffingwell Landing, throwing fisherman Joey Nocchi into the water and damaging his vessel. Nocchi escaped without injuries, according to California Department of Fish and Wildlife records and reports from the time.

Another fisherman, David Zamora, reported a similar encounter near Cambria in 2019, when a roughly 10-foot great white shark bit his kayak about two miles offshore from Leffingwell Landing, according to local news outlet KSBY. Zamora was thrown into the water but managed to climb back aboard before a nearby boater rescued him. He was not injured.

California has documented 233 shark incidents since 1950, including 36 involving kayaking or canoeing, according to Department of Fish and Wildlife figures updated in January 2026. The agency's records include encounters in which sharks make contact with kayaks, surfboards or other equipment, even when no injuries occur.

State wildlife officials say some white shark encounters may involve exploratory bites as the animals investigate unfamiliar objects in the water, including kayaks. Such behavior does not necessarily indicate that a shark was attempting to prey on a person.
SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS
A great white shark swims in a file photo. (Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Following Monday's suspected encounter, the Cambria Fire Department urged ocean users to exercise additional caution, remain aware of their surroundings and avoid entering the water when sharks are visibly active.

The department also encouraged anyone facing an immediate threat or emergency to call 911.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Escaped Tennessee killer's abandoned truck offers clues to what he may do next: retired FBI agent
summary: A retired FBI agent told Fox News Digital Jacob Allen Morley's abandoned truck in Marion, Illinois, may reveal the escaped killer's next move.
story: Retired FBI Special Agent Jonathan Gilliam explains what Jacob Morley’s abandoned truck could reveal about where he may go next as authorities continue their manhunt.
A convicted killer’s abandoned truck could offer clues about his next move after he escaped a Tennessee prison and triggered a multi-state manhunt, a former FBI special agent told Fox News Digital.

Jacob Allen Morley broke out of the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, Sunday, although authorities have not disclosed the precise time of his escape. Staff at the prison noticed Morley was unaccounted for at around 11:30 p.m., and a review of surveillance footage subsequently revealed him crossing through the prison's perimeter fence.

Surveillance footage recorded Morley taking a pickup truck from the 400 block of Keystone Drive, a location roughly 2 miles south of the prison, at around 1 a.m. Monday, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said. The truck was found abandoned by law enforcement officials early Tuesday morning in Marion, Illinois, but Morley wasn't located.

The manhunt has drawn assistance from multiple agencies, and an Illinois State Police spokeswoman told Fox News Digital the agency has "offered its assistance to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation." TBI separately confirmed that the U.S. Marshals Service is assisting in the search for Morley.
MULTISTATE MANHUNT UNDERWAY AS MURDER VICTIM'S CLOSE FRIEND FEARS ESCAPED KILLER COULD STRIKE AGAIN

Surveillance footage shows convicted murderer Jacob Allen Morley inside Northwest Correctional Complex before his escape Sunday. Authorities said Morley was captured on security video breaching a prison fence. (Tennessee Department of Correction)
Retired FBI Special Agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital he thinks the abandoned truck offers clues to what Morley's next move might be.
"But when he got the truck, now they found that 2½ hours north. He is probably gonna lay low, or he's gonna try to get another vehicle," Gilliam said.
"That vehicle in particular that he took is a work truck [that] just absolutely screamed work truck," he added, saying it "would have been easy to identify."
TENNESSEE INMATE CONVICTED OF MURDER ESCAPES FROM PRISON, STEALS PICKUP TRUCK, MANHUNT UNDERWAY: OFFICIALS

Surveillance footage shows Jacob Allen Morley, 28, inside the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, before he allegedly escaped Sunday. Morley was serving a life sentence for murder, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction. (Tennessee Department of Correction)
Gilliam said if Morley managed to steal another truck that isn't as identifiable as the work truck, it could dramatically expand the search area.
"If he's in a vehicle that's nondescript and nobody reports it missing, he could go a very long ways without being caught," Gilliam said. "He could be halfway across the country."
Gilliam said Morley’s lack of money could limit how far he can travel, unless he obtains additional resources by committing another crime.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield when he escaped from a Tennessee prison Sunday, according to correction officials. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

Unless Morley is receiving outside help, something authorities have not indicated, Gilliam said his movements suggest he may simply be trying to put as much distance as possible between himself and the prison.

"I think the fact that this guy went north reduces his chance of familiar resources. So, family resources are all east. He went north," Gilliam said. "If I had to just look at the totality of what I know right now at this point, I would think that the guy is probably more just trying to put distance between him and the prison."
Jacob Allen Morley's stolen truck was found in Illinois after he escaped from prison in Tennessee. (Fox News)

Morley is described as 5 feet, 11 inches tall, and 240 pounds, with brown hair and green eyes. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said he should be "considered dangerous," adding Morley is now on the state's most wanted list.
