In 2025, Putin offered to host Zelenskyy for talks in Moscow, but the Ukrainian president rejected the invitation as Russian forces continued attacking Ukraine.
"He can come to Kyiv," Zelenskyy told ABC News at the time, saying he could not visit Moscow while Ukraine remained under Russian missile attacks.
In September, on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, Russian journalists pressed Zelenskyy on when he would visit Moscow. He replied, "On a missile."
ZELENSKYY CONGRATULATES TRUMP ON TURNING 80 IN BIRTHDAY CALL, VOWS MORE UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AT G7 ON TUESDAY

Russia's President Vladimir Putin seen Monday at a ceremony to present state awards to mentors and teachers of participants in Russia's war in Ukraine at the Kremlin in Moscow. Putin has tightly suppressed the flow of information to the outside world, observers have said. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Mendel, however, argued that personal animosity between the two leaders has become the main obstacle to diplomacy.
"Today there are diplomatic efforts to try to stop this brutal and bloody war that Russia started," she said.

"But what we see now is a personal opposition between Zelenskyy and Putin that continues to grow into constant escalation in which people suffer tremendously, Ukraine's infrastructure, energy grid, and businesses are in ruins, and refugees are fleeing."

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. More than four years later, peace negotiations are deadlocked over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a lasting ceasefire.
Moscow has demanded territorial concessions from Ukraine, including areas Russian forces do not fully control.
Kyiv has rejected ceding sovereign territory and insists that any agreement include enforceable security guarantees against another Russian attack.
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN

President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Dec. 28, 2025, a Ukraine peace deal is nearing completion after Florida talks, though disputes over territory remain. (Volodymyr Zelenskyy X)

Mendel went on to praise President Donald Trump's efforts to break the diplomatic deadlock, calling him the first Western leader to "challenge the status quo" and consistently push for an end to the war.
"For this reason, many Ukrainians place great hope in his ability to bring peace," she said.
"A sustainable peace deal cannot be reached solely between Zelensky and Putin; it requires the involvement and initiative of a strong third party to halt the ongoing devastation."

On Friday, the White House announced that first lady Melania Trump had helped broker a temporary ceasefire in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries, demining operations and civilian evacuations.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in the devastated front-line town, many of them facing severe shortages of food, medicine and other essentials.
The White House said the ceasefire would begin Oct. 29, although Ukrainian and Russian officials have indicated that operations could begin Oct. 27.
Pope Leo also reportedly spoke with Zelenskyy and Putin about the humanitarian crisis, according to Vatican News.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE

First lady Melania Trump visits the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art on Sept. 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The visit took place during Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States. (Finn Gomez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Melania Trump has become synonymous with the words of a saver and a hero, since she has brokered the deal for Oleshky," Mendel said. "This is something that is going to save around 2,000 people and that neither Ukraine nor Russia could have solved for months and months."
"That is why, you know, what Melania Trump has done is actually a case to show that where two men are fighting, a woman can actually save lives," she added.
"And this is the new approach that would show that peace really should focus on human lives, not on maps and territories."
Mendel also criticized the influence of Zelenskyy's longtime ally Andriy Yermak on his diplomatic approach, arguing that the Ukrainian president has favored confrontation over compromise.
"Mr. Yermak was teaching Zelenskiy to be a strong man in diplomacy. And what today we see is actually diplomacy that doesn't exist," she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's a diplomacy of humiliation, diplomacy of constant threats, diplomacy of demands," Mendel added.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado makes surprise return home after nearly a year abroad
summary: María Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could reshape opposition dynamics as Edmundo González vows to join her and push for democratic elections.
story: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado joins Rachel Campos-Duffy in Panama to warn Americans about the dangers of socialism ahead of the midterms. Machado shares a direct message to President Donald Trump, praising his leadership and stating that capturing Maduro would be his legacy. She also criticizes Delcy Rodriguez over the response to devastating earthquakes in Venezuela.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado made returned to her home country on Sunday after nearly a year abroad, re-entering a political landscape transformed by the U.S. ouster of Nicolás Maduro.

"I'm here. With you all," Machado wrote on social media, announcing her return for the first time since December. Her homecoming comes as Venezuela remains under the leadership of acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a longtime Maduro ally backed by the Trump administration, with no presidential election scheduled.
President Donald Trump, asked about Machado's return by reporters in Port Huron, Michigan, said he was unaware of the development but expressed hope for her safety.
TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado arrives at a church after returning to the country following nearly a year abroad, in Lara, Venezuela, Oct. 25, 2026. (Vente Venezuela Press/Handout via REUTERS)

"I don't know anything about it, but I think she's a very nice woman," Trump said. "She gave me her Nobel Prize. So how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe. She's a very nice woman. But we're doing really well in Venezuela."
Machado presented the Nobel Peace Prize she won to President Trump last week. (White House handout via Reuters)
Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025 for her peaceful opposition to Maduro's government, did not disclose her exact location or provide details about how she returned.
Fellow opposition leader Edmundo González, who ran for president in 2024 after Machado was barred from seeking office, confirmed her arrival on social media and said he would join her "very soon."
"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González wrote on X. "You know it, this is until the end."
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado speaks during a news conference at The Heritage Foundation in Washington, DC, on Jan. 16, 2026. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Machado's return comes nearly 10 months after U.S. forces captured Maduro in January, removing the longtime leader from power.
Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice president, has remained in power with the Trump administration's support, despite exceeding the period she was initially authorized to serve as acting president.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado displays vote tally sheets during a protest against the reelection of President Nicolás Maduro one month after the disputed presidential vote which she says the opposition won by a landslide, in Caracas, Venezuela, Wednesday, Aug. 28, 2024. (Cristian Hernandez/AP Photo)
Trump has repeatedly praised his administration's relationship with Rodríguez, highlighting agreements involving Venezuelan oil production and other business ventures with American companies.
NICOLAS MADURO AND WIFE CILIA FLORES FACE NEW CHARGES OF CONSPIRACY TO TORTURE AMERICANS

In September, Trump said it was too soon to consider holding democratic elections in Venezuela, with U.S. officials prioritizing economic stabilization. Machado and her allies, meanwhile, have pushed for an election date, arguing that democratic governance is essential to the country's long-term stability.
Her return could complicate relations between the Venezuelan opposition, the interim government and Washington. Reuters reported in June that U.S. officials had asked Machado to delay her return.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gestures at a protest ahead of the Friday inauguration of President Nicolas Maduro for his third term, in Caracas, Venezuela January 9, 2025. (REUTERS/Maxwell Briceno)

Machado spent much of 2025 in hiding after being briefly detained following an opposition protest that January. She later secretly left Venezuela and resurfaced in Norway in December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

Meanwhile, a faction of the Venezuelan opposition and Rodríguez's government held another round of talks this month focused on reforms to the country's Supreme Court and electoral authorities ahead of eventual elections, Reuters reported.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Machado's political movement has not participated in those negotiations.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Who is Itamar Ben-Gvir, the Israeli firebrand rising with the populist right across the globe?
summary: Itamar Ben-Gvir’s law-and-order agenda has made him one of Israel’s most controversial politicians — and potentially a pivotal player in the country’s next government.
story: Knesset candidate Yishai Fleisher discusses party leader Itamar Ben-Gvir, one of Israel’s most controversial politicians, who could have a major say in Netanyahu’s political future as Israelis prepare to vote on Tuesday.

Polling ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election projects that National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit Party will win between seven and ten seats in the 120-member Knesset, potentially making any future government led by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud Party contingent on his support and positioning him to secure senior ministerial portfolios.

His political rise mirrors a broader trend across Europe and the West, where parties such as Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella's National Rally in France, Geert Wilders’ Party for Freedom in the Netherlands, Australia's One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, Italy’s Matteo Salvini and Germany's Alice Weidel of the AfD have all gained ground on traditional conservative political parties.

The highly controversial Ben-Gvir, as national security minister, oversees the ministry responsible for internal security, including the Israel Police, Israel Prison Service and civilian firearms licensing.

"I always say that Minister Ben-Gvir, if he were in America, he would just be called a Texan," Yishai Fleisher, international spokesman for the Jewish community of Hebron and a candidate ranked No. 12 on the Otzma Yehudit list, told Fox News Digital.
NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE

Israel's Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir speaks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, during a session at the Knesset, Israel's parliament, before it dissolves ahead of the 2026 Israeli elections, in Jerusalem, July 16, 2026.  (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

In a video interview with Fox News Digital, Fleisher continued, "Meaning law and order, the death penalty for murderers, tough conditions for jihadists in our prisons and gun rights for the average Jewish person to be able to defend themselves in our national state. That’s what Itamar Ben-Gvir stands for," he added.
Fleisher said that mass immigration had fueled Islamist extremism and unrest in parts of Europe, saying Israelis want to avoid similar developments.

"There is a jihadist takeover that has come in through immigration, and now the streets of Paris are burning, and the people of Belgium and the U.K. want their countries back," Fleisher said. "In Israel, we don’t want to see Tel Aviv burning," prompting politicians to embrace what are known in the United States as "law-and-order" and "tough-on-crime" candidates.

Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir visits the Al-Aqsa compound, also known to Jews as the Temple Mount, during Jerusalem's Day, in Jerusalem's Old City May 26, 2025.  (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

FORMER IDF CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGERFormer Israeli Ambassador to Washington Danny Ayalon said that Ben-Gvir had missed an opportunity to change course despite his lack of military service and past conviction, arguing that his tenure had instead had a damaging impact, including on Israel’s diplomatic standing.
"Ben-Gvir spoke in a way that turned the entire world against Israel, portraying it as a racist country by making statements that made Israel a pariah state," Ayalon said.
"I always say that Minister Ben-Gvir, if he were in America, he would just be called a Texan...Meaning law and order, the death penalty for murderers.

Fleisher praised Ben-Gvir, who he said has cracked down on protection rackets in southern Israel and made significant progress toward what he described as greater equality for Jews on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, Judaism’s holiest site.

"Minister Ben-Gvir was an activist from a very young age. He saw the dangers and evils of the Oslo process with the Palestinians and tried to stop it. He was arrested and stopped many times because of that, and he faced the court many times. It was then-Chief Justice Aharon Barak who once told him, ‘Why don’t you go study to be a lawyer?’" Fleisher said.

Leader of the Party for Freedom (PVV) Geert Wilders speaks to the press after a meeting with Speaker of the House at the House of Representatives in The Hague, on November 24, 2023. After his shock election win, far-right Dutch firebrand Geert Wilders on Friday kicked off the formal process of building a government coalition, battling to convince reluctant rivals to serve under him as premier.  (Sem van der Wal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images)
"Ben-Gvir spoke in a way that turned the entire world against Israel, portraying it as a racist country by making statements that made Israel a pariah state."

Ben-Gvir, who studied law, became active in public and political affairs and was first elected to the Knesset in 2021. Following the 2022 elections, he was appointed minister of national security by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

His many critics have taken issue with his firebrand style and what many view as a lack of political correctness.  Ambassador Ayalon, a former deputy foreign minister, told Fox News Digital that he also viewed Ben-Gvir’s performance as national security minister negatively.
EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT VOTES TO CONFRONT MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, 'ISLAMIST ENTRYISM' IN OVERWHELMING VOTE

Security attempted to prevent Knesset member Itamar Ben-Gvir from holding up signs reading "Shame' during a session at the Israeli Parliament (Knesset), which had convened to vote on the country's next government under Naftali Bennett, who became Israel's new Prime Minister by leading a fragile coalition of eight parties. Jun. 13, 2021  (Ilia Yefimovich/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)

"During his tenure, Israel has become less secure internally because crime is rising. Many young people believed in the last election that he would bring governability and authority to areas such as the Negev and the Galilee, on the outskirts of the country, where there is almost no law," Ayalon said.
In 2007, Ben-Gvir was convicted of supporting a terrorist organization and inciting racism.

His campaign told Fox News Digital that the conviction stemmed from displaying a sticker of the late Rabbi Meir Kahane, whose Kach party was outlawed in 1994, and reflected his support for a Jewish nationalist movement.
"As a young man, Minister Ben-Gvir was an intense Jewish nationalist. He has said many times, publicly, that he has matured since then and moved on from those positions."
ABBAS DELAYS PALESTINIAN ELECTIONS AGAIN, MAKING MORE THAN TWO DECADES WITHOUT VOTE

A demonstrator holds a sign with an image of Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and the words "The Bedouins against the murder, You failed" as members of Israel's Arab minority protest, calling on the Israeli government to protect Arab communities of the Negev desert from crime and killings from within the community through effective law and order, outside the Prime Minister's Office in Jerusalem, January 11, 2026. REUTERS/Ammar Awad  (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Recent posts on Ben-Gvir’s social media accounts, along with statements issued through Netanyahu’s and Likud’s official channels, have raised questions about whether the two remain fully aligned.

On Oct. 15, Ben-Gvir shared a Hebrew-language media report quoting Netanyahu as saying that he would not serve again as national security minister. In response, Ben-Gvir wrote: "Dear Prime Minister, only the people will decide. Ben Gvir is strong, Israel is strong!"
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE

Last Wednesday, Netanyahu's Likud party appeared to reverse course, posting a message on its official WhatsApp channel stating: "Ben-Gvir is a senior minister in our government, and he will remain so in the next government — provided that the bloc consisting of the Left and Arab parties does not win."

Despite the public statements, Ayalon said Netanyahu could opt not to include Ben-Gvir in the next government, even if it meant forming an alliance with opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar.
"Netanyahu is brilliant. He kept Ben-Gvir because it suited him. If he could, he would get rid of him in a minute. Bibi is capable of changing his mind on a dime," Ayalon said.

Election banners with images of Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of Likud party, in Sderot, near Israel's border with Gaza, in southern Israel, Oct.18, 2026.  (Reuters/Amir Cohen)

Fleisher credited Ben-Gvir with tripling the number of personal firearms and firearms licenses issued to Israelis over four years, establishing 1,000 rapid-response teams, overhauling the prison system and demolishing 9,000 illegally built homes, particularly in the Negev.
In March, the Knesset approved a death-penalty law sponsored by Otzma Yehudit and other lawmakers, a measure Ben-Gvir has strongly championed.
"No more hotel-like conditions in our prisons. You’ll know you are being punished for your crime, and these simple policies ultimately deter jihadism," Fleisher told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They understand that he represents a full-throated pushback against the jihadist takeover of our land. Ben-Gvir also represents a strong Jewish identity, strong policies and strong laws to ensure that we don’t lose control of our country," he said.
The latest polls show Netanyahu’s bloc slightly behind the opposition, led by Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot, but neither side has a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a governing majority.
Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: From arrests to crackdowns, how Europe’s leaders are responding as protests rock the continent
summary: Emmanuel Macron vows rioters will pay as 70,000 police deploy across France, while Italy, Belgium and Albania face escalating protest violence.
story: Senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on the ongoing protests in Paris after 70,000 police officers were deployed to maintain order in France. Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo discusses the President of France Emmanuel Macron's response to the protests and Iranian threats.

From mass arrests in France to troop deployments in Italy, European leaders are taking varied approaches to protests and clashes across the continent. The unrest began in France in mid-September with student demonstrations over school conditions, then spread to other countries, where protests have centered on local grievances.
President Donald Trump has used the unrest to press his hard-line immigration message, blaming France’s protests on immigration and urging the country to close its borders.
PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE
French President Emmanuel Macron pushed back, calling foreign leaders' comments "unacceptable and even stupid" and accusing them of exploiting France’s crisis for political gain.
Here’s how leaders across Europe are responding.
Demonstrators occupy the sculptures and ledges of the Monument a la Republique in Paris, France, on October 17, 2026. (Aruallan / Hans Lucas /AFP/Getty Images)

Macron has vowed that those who loot or destroy property will be held accountable and made to pay for the damage. French authorities deployed 70,000 police officers nationwide Saturday as demonstrations took place in Paris and other cities.

Some clashes broke out in several cities, including Paris, Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes. Police used tear gas, sound grenades and water cannons, and the Interior Ministry reported more than 1,300 arrests.
VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED

Most union-organized marches were peaceful, though clashes broke out later in Paris and several other cities. Separately, a French intelligence assessment reportedly identified Antifa and other far-left groups as instigators of some of the violence, according to a French outlet.
Demonstrators light flares during an anti-government protest organized by the Italia in Piazza movement, at Piazza Duomo in Milan, on October 17, 2026. (Piero Cruciatti/AFP/Getty Images)
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned what she called "gangs of thugs" who used demonstrations to "sow chaos," and voiced support for police facing violence in several Italian cities.

Meloni moved quickly after the previous weekend’s looting and clashes, sending 500 additional soldiers to Milan and approving tougher penalties for minors involved in vandalism. She said destroying and stealing was a crime and that the state's response would be firm.
The measures put Meloni among the European leaders taking the most visible steps to deter further violence.

A protester holds a lit flare and shouts slogans as students, teachers and civil servants take part in a rally to protest against the high cost of living, saying they face the same problems that sparked violent demonstrations in France at the weekend, in Greece on October 21, 2026. (Sakis Mitrolidis/AFP/Getty Images)
While Greece has seen less unrest than France and other European countries, officials have been monitoring the risk of clashes as student and teacher demonstrations spread.
Government spokesperson Pavlos Marinakis said the right to protest must be respected as long as demonstrations remain lawful, while condemning violence, looting and occupations.
Police still kept a visible presence at demonstrations earlier in the week, which largely passed without major violence.
A Belgian police officer faces young protesters during clashes near Brussels-South railway station on October 12, 2026. (Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images)

Belgium's demonstrations began over education reforms and budget cuts, with young protesters taking to the streets in Brussels and Liège. Earlier clashes injured police, damaged public areas and blocked roads. Nearly 200 people were arrested, according to Belgian officials.
Interior Minister Bernard Quintin accused far-left activists, including people linked to Antifa, of infiltrating demonstrations and encouraging young people to commit violence.

In Albania’s capital, Tirana, student-led protests have grown into a broader challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama, with demonstrators demanding his resignation and accusing his government of corruption and neglecting schools and public services.
US LAWMAKERS SOUND ALARM AS VIOLENCE GRIPS NATO ALLY ALBANIA AMID ANTI-GOVERNMENT PROTESTS
Police used tear gas and water cannons as more than 2,500 officers were deployed. Rama placed chairs outside his government headquarters and invited protesters to talk, but they rejected the gesture.
He said his government would address their concerns and warned that people responsible for violence could face criminal and financial consequences.
In Spain, the unrest was largely concentrated in Barcelona, unlike France, where protests and clashes spread across multiple cities.

Police arrested 128 people in Barcelona after fires, vandalism and looting. Catalonia, the northeastern Spanish region that includes Barcelona, saw its regional president, Salvador Illa, condemn the violence and back the police response.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

Meanwhile, Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni said the city would take legal action against those responsible and warned that parents or guardians could face consequences for damage caused by their children.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Brazil becomes next test for Latin America’s surging conservative movement
summary: Lula da Silva seeks a fourth presidential term in Brazil in a closely contested second round election with Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as security and safety concerns weigh heavily.
story: Flavio Bolsonaro joined supporters in Santa Barbara D'Oeste to lead a motorcade. Polls in Brazil show a tight presidential race with incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. (Video: Reuters.)

Brazil's estimated 158 million voters could advance Latin America's conservative wave in Sunday's election as the continent's most populous nation could elect conservative Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro as its next president.

The first round election three weeks ago saw a strong performance by Bolsonaro, proving the polls wrong. While incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (Lula) had been predicted to take the first round by single digits, Bolsonaro ended up winning 47% to Lula's 45%. As neither candidate won a majority, the election went to a second round.

Brazil's election follows a long string of victories for the Latin American right across Central and South America that started with the election of Libertarian outsider Javier Milei in Argentina in 2023.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, left, and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, right, face off in a presidential election runoff. (Getty Images)
BOLSONARO WINS FIRST ROUND OF BRAZILIAN PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION, AS TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATES CONTINUE RED WAVE
2025 saw a right-wing sweep across the region, as Ecuador, Bolivia, Honduras and Chile all voted for conservative heads of state.

In 2026, Keiko Fujimori narrowly defeated a left-wing candidate to win the Peruvian presidency, while most recently, in Colombia, conservative attorney Abelardo de la Espriella bested left-wing Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Bolsonaro's slate of congressional candidates also fared well, ensuring that Brazil will have one of the most conservative congresses in years, and a legislative branch aligned with Bolsonaro's goals, or ready to thwart Lula's agenda.

The two candidates met Friday night for the final debate in Rio de Janeiro, which featured a series of questions organized around Brazil's five geographic regions. While the debate featured some heated personal exchanges, it appears unlikely to have moved the needle in either direction heading into a close race.

Colombian President Abelardo De la Espriella holds a press conference with the mayor of Bogota and newly appointed city manager Clara Lucia Sandoval in Bogota, on Aug. 25, 2026. (Sebastian Barros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
TRUMP'S WAR ON DRUG CARTELS COULD GAIN POWERFUL NEW ALLY AFTER PIVOTAL ELECTION

President Donald Trump has heralded these electoral results as vindication for his hardline approach to security, crime, and migration policies, as well as a stamp of approval for the new Shield of the Americas initiative.
The Trump administration counts on considerably more close allies now than it did at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Yet, the question remains: why is the region resoundingly rejecting the left and progressivism?
Argentina's President Javier Milei arrives for the inauguration of Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella in Cali, Colombia, Friday, Aug. 7, 2026.  (Matias Delacroix/AP Photo)

Many of the elections have been won by narrow margins, with Brazil being a case in point: Lula bested Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 by just 1.8%. While many Latin American nations remain deeply polarized, there is no denying a right-wing resurgence.

Commentators appear to be expressing a rejection of progressive movements amid growing concerns over safety and security, giving approval to proposals to dramatically ramp up police and military presence to combat crime and drug trafficking.

Meanwhile, leftist parties seem unable to capitalize on recurring concerns over inflation and kitchen table economics, which have played into the hands of the Latin American right, as working class and middle class voters have felt the pinch of rising food, housing and energy costs.

In addition to social and economic concerns, the specter of Jair Bolsonaro also looms over the election.  Flavio Bolsonaro has pledged to free his father, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence on house arrest for allegedly plotting a coup in the wake of the 2022 election.

Lula was also sentenced to a 12-year prison sentence on corruption charges stemming from the infamous Operation Car Wash, until he was freed on a technicality by the Brazilian Supreme Court, and rose from the ashes to win the 2022 presidential election.

Brazil's right-wing senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) gestures next to federal deputy and candidate for governor of Rio de Janeiro, Douglas Ruas (L) during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in Campo Grande neighborhood, in the western zone of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on Oct.r 4, 2026 (Douglas SHINEIDR / AFP via Getty Images)
BRAZIL’S RAPID ELECTION COUNT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON VOTING SECURITY AHEAD OF US MIDTERMS

Bolsonaro has narrowly led in recent polls, and enters the second round with some structural advantages. Most importantly, he enjoys the backing of three of the four other major candidates in the race, who failed to advance to the second round.
Self-help author Augusto Cury, former Goias Governor Ronaldo Caiado, and former Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema all officially backed Bolsonaro in the second round.

Entrepreneur Renan Santos, candidate for the Mission Party, declined to endorse either candidate. However, as his political movement is characterized as free-market and libertarian, these voters are also more likely to trend to Bolsonaro.
Thus, Lula needs to win a significant majority of first round voters who backed right-wing or center-right candidates. It's a daunting, but not impossible, proposition.
The entire election may hinge on voters who are voting against a candidate, as much as for a candidate.

Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (C) waves next to Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin (L) and to his candidate for Sao Paulo's governor, Fernando Haddad during a campaign rally on the eve of the general election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil on October 3, 2026. Brazilians go to the polls on October 4, 2026, in a tight race led by leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving house arrest.  (Luis Robayo/AFP Via Getty Images)
Another question looming over the election: has Lula finally worn out his welcome with the Brazilian electorate?
This will be Lula's seventh time in 40 years appearing on a presidential ballot: he lost elections in 1989, 1994, 1998, won in 2002, 2006, and 2022.
Lula famously promised to serve only one term when he ran to oust Jair Bolsonaro in 2022.

President Trump sent a letter to former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro calling for an immediate end to the ‘unjust’ trial against him for allegedly starting a coup. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci and Evaristo Sa/AFP via Getty Images)
On October 25, 2022, just five days before the last second round presidential election, he posted on his official X account: "If elected, I will be a single-term president."
It was a promise that he did not keep.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Various polls have shown that voters are not happy with the course of Lula's third term, and even a sizable percentage of Lula backers in 2022 responded with pessimism on the prospect of an unprecedented fourth term.
However, a large percentage of the Brazilian electorate also consistently rejects the prospect of voting for another Bolsonaro for president.

Lula is unquestionably the dominant figure in Brazilian politics over the past half-century. But will his magnetism and charisma be enough to overcome the right-wing resurgence sweeping the continent?
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot emerges as Netanyahu’s leading election challenger
summary: A decorated former Israeli army chief has emerged as a leading election challenger after serving in the war cabinet and suffering devastating personal losses following the Oct. 7 attacks.
story: Fox News Digital speaks with three experts on Israel’s high-stakes election and the fight over Netanyahu’s political future. The election is set for Oct. 27, 2026.

JERUSALEM — Israel’s high-stakes election on Oct. 27 pits the longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, against the highly decorated retired Lt. Gen. Gadi Eisenkot. While fairly new to politics, Eisenkot has an impressive resume that could help him become the Jewish state's next leader.

According to a number of polls, Eisenkot's centrist political party, Yashar, has a narrow lead over Netanyahu's Likud. To form a government, Yashar or Likud will need to cobble together a 61-seat majority of parties to be able to form a new coalition government.
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, speaks from behind a podium with a banner reading "Yashar with Eisenkot" during an event presenting the party's full candidate list ahead of October's general election on Sept. 7, 2026 in Rosh HaAyin, Israel. Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.  (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)
He was born in Tiberias in Israel’s north to a Jewish-Moroccan family who relocated to Israel’s southernmost city, Eilat, on the Red Sea when he was a toddler.

A career soldier, he opted to serve in the infantry. He was part of the elite Golani Brigade and reached the zenith of the military with his 2015 appointment to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff in 2015 until 2019.

Yossi Melman, one of Israel’s most respected journalists on intelligence and defense reporting, told Fox News Digital that Eisenkot, "Is 100% a soldier. He is very brave and humble. He is an officer and gentleman."

Melman noted that when Eisenkot was chosen to be the next IDF chief of staff, he declined because he felt that then General Benny Gantz should receive the appointment. Melman asked, "How many people would do that? He was selected after Gantz. It shows his traits of modesty, honesty and not arrogant."
Melman said, "It is a miracle he is leading in the polls. He is the antithesis of a what a politician should be. He is not a great orator when you compare him to Netanyahu. He radiates honesty."
BENJAMIN NETANYAHU'S LEGACY AND POLITICAL FUTURE ON THE LINE IN ISRAEL'S OCT 27 ELECTION

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot attends the Jerusalem Residents Conference on Aug. 12, 2026 in Jerusalem. Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of the Israel Defense Forces and current leader of the Yashar party, has emerged as the foremost challenger to Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of October's general election. (Erik Marmor/Getty Images)

Eisenkot’s Mizrahi background — Jews who originate from North Africa and the Middle East — would mean, if he prevails, that he would be the first Israeli Prime Minister of Moroccan origin. The Prime Minister’s office has been held by Israelis of Eastern European descent (Ashkenazi) since the rebirth of the Jewish state in 1948.
After Hamas invaded Israel on Oct. 7, 2023 and slaughtered over 1,200 people, including more than 40 Americans, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet as a minister without portfolio.

Melman said Eisenkot "did not set any political conditions" and "his presence in the cabinet saved Netanyahu." After eight months of serving in the war cabinet, Eisenkot resigned, blaming the prime minister for failing to implement a comprehensive strategy.

The war against the Iran-backed terrorist movement Hamas took an enormous toll on the battle-hardened General Eisenkot and his family. Hamas killed his son, 25-year-old Master Sergeant Gal Eisenkot, in Dec. 2023. The terrorist organization also killed two nephews of Eisenkot. Netanyahu and his wife Sara said at the time that they were devastated by Gal’s death and Eisenkot was a "true hero."
ZIONISM EXPLAINED FROM ITS BIBLICAL ORIGINS TO THE REBIRTH OF THE STATE OF ISRAEL

Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, is seen at the Black Arrow memorial site near Kibbutz Mefalsim during a visit to deliver a statement near the border with the Gaza Strip on Oct. 15, 2026, ahead of the Israel's legislative election.  (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images)

Danny Orbach, a military historian from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, gave his take on the leading contender to replace Netanyahu. "I think his military record and his prospects as a national leader have both significant strengths and serious weaknesses. He bears considerable responsibility for shaping the IDF that existed on Oct. 7, 2023. And that was, paradoxically, both the army that proved capable of defeating Hezbollah, striking Iran and achieving unprecedented military successes in the extraordinarily difficult, tunnel-ridden battlefield of Gaza and the army that failed so miserably on Oct. 7."

He continued that, "Like other chiefs of staff, Eisenkot bears responsibility for the decisions that reduced the army's size and for the infamous ‘conceptzia’ [Hebrew word for concept] regarding Hamas. In that respect, I consider him just as culpable as Netanyahu."

Israel’s military, intelligence and political establishments bought into the ‘conceptzia’ that Hamas could be housebroken with massive infusions of economic aid. Hamas, however, was wedded to its radical Islamist ideology —the destruction of the Jewish state — and used the funds to advance its war aims.

Orbach noted that "I don't think most of Eisenkot's support stems from his energy, enthusiasm or even his political platform. My impression is that Eisenkot has emerged as the default ‘non-Bibi’ candidate, the politician who currently channels much of the camp's hopes and expectations."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli Chief of Staff Gadi Eizenkot (L) give a press conference in Tel Aviv, on Dec. 4, 2018. Israel's army said today it has discovered Hezbollah tunnels infiltrating its territory from Lebanon and launched an operation to destroy them, a move likely to raise tensions with the Iran-backed group.  (Jack Guez/AFP Via Getty Images)
Orbach added that "I also doubt that Eisenkot would have had the political determination to stand up to the Biden administration on such matters."
Netanyahu and former President Biden repeatedly clashed over Biden’s attempts to rope in Israel’s efforts to defeat Iran’s seven-front war against the Jewish state.

The military historian, however, noted that "I believe an Eisenkot government could address several of Israel's most urgent problems. It would remove Ben Gvir from power, confront the growing problem of Jewish extremist violence and terrorism in the West Bank, and begin repairing Israel's severely damaged international legitimacy."

Itamar Ben-Gvir is a controversial right-wing firebrand politician and the current minister of national security since 2022, who has outraged many Western European and foreign leaders with his heated rhetoric against the Palestinians.
TIMELINE OF DECADES-LONG ISRAELI-ARAB, PALESTINIAN CONFLICT

Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot attends the funeral for his son, First Sergeant Major Gal Meir Eisenkot, 25 years old, at the Herzliya cemetery on Dec. 8, 2023 in Herzliya, Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said the 25-year-old major, son of the cabinet minister and former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, died on Thursday in Gaza. (Dima Vazinovich / Middle East Images / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images))

Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, comes from an American Jewish family. U.S. General Joseph Dunford awarded Eisenkot the Commander of the Legion of Merit because of his "exceptionally meritorious service as chief of the General Staff of the IDF" and his "contribution to the strategic cooperation between the United States and Israel [that] will have a lasting effect on both countries," according to the Washington Institute, where Eisenkot served as a military fellow in 2019.

Nadav Eyal, an Israeli analyst and journalist for the mass circulation Israeli paper Yedioth Aharonoth, told Fox News Digital, Gadi Eisenkot is widely considered one of the most successful Chiefs of Staff that Israel has had in the last thirty years."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Israel's new Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot delivers a speech during his swearing-in ceremony at the Prime Minister's Jerusalem offices on Feb. 16, 2015.  (Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images)
He continued that "Chiefs of Staff in Israel, unlike in other countries, are really extremely capable, in general, to be prime minister. They are leading the country’s biggest organization, the IDF."

Eyal, who writes extensively about the IDF, credited Eisenkot’s military planning against the Iran-backed Hezbollah terrorist organization in Lebanon and the significant defeats the Lebanese Shiite entity experienced, including the "discovery of tunnels that Hezbollah built" to enter Israel. Hezbollah immediately joined Hamas’s war against Israel in Oct. 2023.

Given the nature of Israel’s electoral system, an outright winner won’t likely be known for several days, since the leading party will need to form a coalition to get to the 61-seat mandate to run the country.
Benjamin Weinthal reports on Israel, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Europe. You can follow Benjamin on Twitter @BenWeinthal, and email him at benjamin.weinthal@fox.com

title: Alaska governor orders investigation into Peltola camp after report they recruited second Dan Sullivan
summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it recruited a candidate with the same name as her Republican rival, Sen.
story: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it recruited a candidate with the same name as her Republican rival, Sen. Dan Sullivan, onto the ballot in an effort to dilute his votes.

The Department of Public Safety would seek to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted,” Dunleavy said in an overnight post to X. “The evidence will determine what happens next.”

Dunleavy, a Republican, referred to Wednesday’s revelations from a bombshell New York Times report as “disturbing new evidence” and said that “anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”

The Times published an explosive report detailing the campaign and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s alleged efforts to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent, citing interviews with 12 people who were involved with or were told about the plan, or were contacted as potential recruits. The report also cited dozens of text messages among participants.

The Times’ report included information from Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August. Rios later contacted the Times and “retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race,” the outlet reported.

The revelations have rocked the critical battleground race. Republicans have widely condemned Democrats for allegedly trying to manipulate the ballot, which they argue could confuse voters, and the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan loses.
NBC News has reached out to the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment on Dunleavy’s announcement.

Reached for comment Wednesday on the Times report, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also pointed to instances of Republicans allegedly propping up “spoiler” candidates.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
A spokesperson for the DSCC, the campaign arm of Senate Democrats, said in a statement that the group “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit challenger Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law.
Following the report, President Donald Trump called for Peltola and the challenger Sullivan to be “removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Asked by a reporter whether he agreed that Peltola should be prosecuted, Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that “we should certainly look into whether she committed election fraud.”

“She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he said later. “So whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her.”

title: California judge denies Trump DOJ request to segregate alleged noncitizen ballots
summary: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.
story: A federal judge in California on Wednesday refused the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots from individuals it alleges are noncitizens.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” U.S. District Judge David Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”

What the administration was asking for, he wrote, “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”
He also questioned whether the government’s claims of over 20,000 noncitizen voters were accurate.

“Given the vagueness of Plaintiff’s descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states, the Court cannot conclude that Plaintiff’s process is credible,” Carter wrote, pointing to similar allegations the administration had made in a neighboring state.

“In Nevada, DHS initially identified up to 15,903 registered voters as noncitizens based on ‘high-confidence’ matches, but later reduced that number to 6,218, and then to 185 after conducting its manual review. Nevada officials later confirmed that all 185 individuals were citizens,” the judge wrote.

“Had Nevada officials accepted Plaintiff’s allegations there as true, 185 citizens would have been deprived of their vote. This Court will not deprive Californians who have met the requirements for voter registration of their fundamental right because of Plaintiff’s unfounded allegations.”

The Justice Department filed the suit Oct. 15, seeking a court order that the state “set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens” and not count them until their citizenship is confirmed.
The department said it had compiled “a list of over 20,000 names of people” the government “believes are likely non-citizens.”

Attorneys for the state countered that the government’s numbers are unreliable. In a July letter, it put the number of suspect voters at 190,000 and has refused to release information about how it has generated its lists.
“Where is the evidence?” an attorney representing California, Christina McCall, said at the hearing Tuesday, calling the government’s allegations “vague” and “not reliable.”

Another attorney for the state, Anne Bellows, told the judge “the stakes here are enormous,” arguing the government was trying to force California to initiate an unclear investigation into the citizenship of tens of thousands of people without any clear standards shortly before an election.
It “is a recipe for disenfranchisement,” Bellows said.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told Carter: “We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling them what they can’t do.”
Essayli said that once the state is made aware of potential noncitizens on its voter rolls, “they need to do something.”
“What they cannot do is do nothing and proceed to count the votes,” he said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The judge said that if the government believes there is noncitizen voting, which is a crime, it should bring charges.

“Don’t you have the power of indictments?” Carter asked Essayli. “You brought 28 indictments,” he said, referring to a recent announcement by prosecutors of people who have been found to have voted illegally in California in recent years. “You may find others. You have the right to bring that indictment against them.”
“You’ve got a remedy, for goodness’ sakes,” Carter said. “Go out and indict.”
Essayli on Wednesday bashed the judge’s ruling and said an appeal is underway.

“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” he said in a statement. “The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit.”

The Justice Department has already been to a federal appeals court once in the case. It filed a motion to expedite the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals last week, after Carter did not act on its request to rule in the matter by Thursday.
The appeals court held an emergency hearing Sunday and ruled against the administration 2-1 on Monday.
The majority found it did not have jurisdiction because Carter had not yet ruled, but it found the government’s “claimed emergency” was at least partly “a self-constructed one.”
“At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’s own delay in filing suit,” Circuit Judge Mark Bennett wrote in the ruling.

“The United States has taken issue with California’s voter rolls since at least July 16, when it sent a letter to California’s secretary of state citing its ‘[p]reliminary’ analysis of California’s voter rolls. And neither California’s law permitting the processing of ballots twenty-nine days before an election, nor its law providing for the issuance of mail-in ballots to registered voters, is new,” he wrote.

Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in a concurring opinion that the government was asking the “court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.”

The dissenting judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, wrote, “We should’ve granted the federal government relief — federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”

title: RFK Jr. takes shortcut to make some unapproved peptides available for use
summary: HHS is pausing legal action against compounding pharmacies that make certain peptides, effectively allowing them to offer the unapproved drugs immediately.
story: The Department of Health and Human Services is giving compounding pharmacies a temporary green light to make six peptides while the agency continues to work on a formal rule change.

In a notice filed Wednesday, the agency said it would exercise “enforcement discretion,” meaning it will not take legal action against compounding pharmacies that make the six unapproved peptides. In practice, that means these pharmacies can start offering them now, even though the peptides aren’t yet on the Food and Drug Administration’s list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make.
The six peptides are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500.

They’ve been promoted online as treatments for everything from faster healing to younger-looking skin and a longer lifespan. None are approved by the FDA, and the agency’s own scientists concluded there is insufficient data to prove they are safe and effective.
The FDA said compounding pharmacies must certify the identity and purity of the compounds. They must also now report side effects, which was not previously mandated.

The move comes as a growing “gray market” has sprung up around peptides, where retailers sell them labeled “for research use only,” a legal workaround that lets them claim they aren’t meant for humans. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others have argued that allowing peptides to be compounded would move people away from this gray market and toward safer products.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, HHS is working to put prevention and patient safety at the center of health care—and that includes confronting the risks of black-market peptides,” Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said in a statement.

Dr. Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now leads the Center for Science in the Public Interest watchdog group, said the FDA was essentially “turning a blind eye” to widen access to drugs that have not been proven to work.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Compounding pharmacies generally may use only ingredients the FDA has added to an official list known as the bulk drugs substances list. Adding an ingredient requires the FDA to propose a rule, take public comment and issue a final rule, a process that can take several months.

The agency took a step toward that process in July, when an FDA advisory panel narrowly voted in favor of adding six peptides to the bulk list. The panel included six new appointees with ties to the peptide industry and another who is the son of a U.S. representative who has pushed Kennedy to make peptides more available. (During that meeting, some committee members expressed concerns that the recommendation could make it harder for the FDA to say no to other unapproved drugs in the future.)

On Tuesday and Wednesday, the FDA was scheduled to meet outside groups, including Medivant Healthcare, a compounding pharmacy that offers peptides, according to Reginfo.gov, a federal website that tracks government regulations.

Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, which researches the dangers of counterfeit medicines, said both the enforcement discretion and upcoming rule change would expose Americans to “untested, dangerous substances.”
“Imagine what it means for the nation’s top drug regulator to announce they won’t enforce the laws on people making completely untested compounds and distributing them to the public,” Safdar said.

title: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
summary: HONG KONG — Hong Kong’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades.
story: HONG KONG — Hong Kong’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades.

The Nov. 26, 2025, fire at Wang Fuk Court, a high-rise housing estate in the suburban district of Tai Po, swiftly engulfed seven of its eight towers, killing 110 women and 58 men ranging in age from 6 months to 98 years old. Thousands of others were displaced from their homes at the complex, which was undergoing major renovations at the time of the blaze.

The tragedy provoked widespread public grief and anger and was widely seen as the first major test for the Hong Kong government since Beijing imposed a sweeping national security law in 2020 in response to pro-democracy protests. Critics say the law, which Hong Kong and Chinese officials say was necessary to restore stability, has been used to stifle dissent in the former British colony.

Calls for accountability and transparency after the fire were quickly met with warnings from Hong Kong and Chinese officials, who said that “external hostile forces” were trying to re-create the chaos of the 2019 protests, which sometimes turned violent.
John Lee, Hong Kong’s top leader, said he was “deeply saddened” by the fire’s impact on the community.
“After self-reflection, I have considered that the government should roll out a large number of measures for reform, and a lot of work has to be carried out,” he said at a news conference.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“In my capacity as chief executive, I apologize to all the victims and members of the public,” said Lee, who bowed in apology with seven other senior Hong Kong officials.

Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho had resigned on Wednesday, making her the first official to lose her job over the fire. Ho “should bear political responsibility” for the disaster, he said, despite no evidence of personal wrongdoing.

title: The former youth pastor leading one of the NFL’s best offenses
summary: Nate Scheelhaase, the Los Angeles Rams’ offensive coordinator, is a former youth pastor. He credits time in the church for his success in professional football.
story: When Nate Scheelhaase was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams last winter, he stepped into one of the NFL’s most auspicious jobs, and for a Super Bowl contender, no less.
Not bad for a former youth pastor.

Fresh out of college, Scheelhaase moved to Louisville, Kentucky, in 2014 to work with teenagers at Southeast Christian Church, one of the largest megachurches in the U.S. During that time, he regularly stopped by a few dozen high schools to visit with students. For two high schools’ football teams, he volunteered as a chaplain. The role entailed building trust, finding common ground and helping those he spoke with work for something bigger than themselves.
“An impactful year,” said Scheelhaase, 35.

It wasn’t the typical starting point for a career in coaching — because even though Scheelhaase had been a four-year starting quarterback at Illinois, he wasn’t initially interested in that career path at all.
Without intending to, though, Scheelhaase honed skills while he was a youth pastor that he says helped him rise quickly within the coaching industry.

“I would say that there’s a lot of carryover,” Scheelhaase said in an interview. “From a ministry standpoint, just being around people from all different walks of life, different journeys, being able to meet them where they’re at — that’s also a football locker room. That’s a staff locker room.”

The growth of sports in the U.S. is often a story of their crossover with faith. James Naismith, basketball’s inventor, is said to have believed he could better embody what it meant to be a Christian using sports than the pulpit. Many of football’s conventions, including the huddle, numbered jerseys and padded goalposts, came from Amos Alonzo Stagg, who had gone to Yale to study divinity and began coaching to fulfill a vision of “muscular Christianity.”

Careers in sports have often led to careers in religious roles. Rocky Seto won national championships at the University of Southern California and a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks during 16 years on Pete Carroll’s coaching staffs. In Seattle, Seto’s role eventually evolved to include a weekly address delivered in front of the entire roster and staff. He obsessively prepared his material.
“How am I going to capture the whole room?” Seto said. “It’s basically convincing them that if you learn this, this is going to help us win, help us be better.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

That experience made him feel prepared to give his first sermon. It was 2017, and Seto had just left the Seahawks to become the pastor-in-waiting at Evergreen Baptist Church, in suburban Los Angeles. Standing in front of another packed room of congregants, Seto felt his new job’s mission mirrored that of his last one — to deliver hope.

“You come to church in some ways to take a peek into heaven for a moment, and then we break. It’s like a huddle, and then we break out to basically fulfill the Great Commission outside this building, right?” he said. “And so coaching is no different. The information has to be almost like, ‘This is the greatest thing you need to know.’”
As Scheelhaase’s career was ending in late 2013, all he knew was that he didn’t envision a future in coaching.

He had gotten married a few months earlier, and he had seen enough coaches get fired and hired to question raising a family in an industry with fleeting job security and a nomadic career path. Meetings with Illini alumni in corporate jobs in Chicago also failed to inspire him. Unsure what to do, Scheelhaase called Jason Epperson, a local pastor who served as Illinois football’s team chaplain.

Epperson had just taken a job at Southeast in Louisville, where there was a youth pastor role open. The idea intrigued Scheelhaase, who had grown up outside Kansas City, Missouri, as a devout Christian. When he arrived at Southeast in early 2014, he was trying “to figure out different ways to just connect with people in the area and show them that I was interested in just who they were more than just what they were doing,” Scheelhaase said. “Which I think is always a good spot to start.”

Chris Burke, an ESPN baseball analyst who lived in the area, first noticed Scheelhaase because of his athleticism during pickup games inside Southeast’s gym. Other things about Scheelhaase soon stood out, too.
“He looked perfectly suited for that job,” Burke said. “You can tell he got a kick out of being around young people. He communicated well with them. He had the patience.”

When a local mother told Scheelhaase that her eighth grade son’s father had recently died and that she needed others to be there for her son, Scheelhaase gave him rides and went to practices. The son was Nate Hobbs, the future San Francisco 49ers defensive back whom Scheelhaase still describes as one of his closest friends.

Scheelhaase stopped by Trinity High School, a local powerhouse, with a “confident humility,” said Andrew Coverdale, Trinity’s offensive coordinator at the time, who is now the passing game coordinator at Kentucky. Scheelhaase didn’t expect students to listen to him just because he had been a college quarterback.

“As somebody who taught in high school for a long, long time, I can’t really emphasize enough that kids need every form of mentorship and positive adult presence they can have, because it is brutal to be a teenage kid right now,” Coverdale said. High schoolers are “just dealing with so much and carrying so much. And so I just think having a guy like that around that you can talk to, who has life experience that he’s willing to share in a really winsome way, it was just great.”

Scheelhaase spent a relatively brief year and a half in Louisville, but he said that time shaped him immeasurably. Scheelhaase, who now has three children, said spending time around church leaders and attendees gave him role models for how he wanted to act as a husband and a father. It also changed his career path.

While he was leading a chapel service for football players at Eastern High School in 2014, he gave what he thought was a compelling, relatable speech that pulled in his athletic background and life story. It was received, he said with a smile, by proverbial crickets.
Taking a seat, he was stunned to see the reaction when the school’s head coach stood up to deliver his own pregame speech.

“Everybody was on the edge of their seat,” Scheelhaase said. “And in that moment, I thought, man, there is a cool ability to impact as a coach. And it was probably the thing that triggered the thought of, man, what would it look like to be able to impact in that way and influence in that way.”

By the start of the 2015 football season, Scheelhaase was at Illinois coaching running backs. Technically, he was new to the profession. Yet recruiting players to campus and developing them once they were on the roster didn’t feel any different, at its core, from how he’d worked to build trust in Louisville.

“You are going to ask people to do really hard things as a coach, things that are counterintuitive to what you want to do,” he said. “Stand in a pocket where you know somebody’s going to hit you in the side of your helmet. To be somebody who loves to catch the football, but you got to go and block. To be somebody that’s willing to do the dirty work, and you’re going to ask them to do it, and the only way I know how to do that is to connect with them on a deep level. They know I not only understand what we’re asking them to do, but I care and I see them in that. And so connection, fortunately for me, it’s how I’m wired. That’s the part I enjoy the most about my job. ...

“And there probably is an element of that’s what I enjoyed even about the job as a high school pastor in Louisville, too, is just connecting with people and seeing there’s oftentimes more common ground than you think.”

In 2023, he became a coordinator at Iowa State. A year later, he left to become an offensive assistant for Sean McVay and the Rams, which to some may have seemed like a backward step; his job revolved around using software to manually draw the plays McVay wanted called each week. In the NFL, however, just being around McVay is a career springboard: The last four Rams offensive coordinators are now head coaches, and Zac Taylor was drawing McVay’s plays before Cincinnati hired him as its head coach. In 2025, a full year before Scheelhaase’s promotion to Rams offensive coordinator, McVay had called him “a special coach” and “a rising star, without a doubt.”

Last winter, as Scheelhaase was interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs, he called interim Stanford coach Frank Reich to ask about the school’s opening. The two had more in common than football. After he retired from a long career as a backup NFL quarterback, Reich attended seminary and worked as a pastor before he became an NFL head coach.
He saw carryover between the two industries, too.
“In coaching or seminary or pastoring, there are a lot of hours,” Reich said in 2019.
The hours Scheelhaase put in in Louisville have paid off in ways he didn’t expect, he said. There, his life revolved around Sundays. In ways he could never have predicted, it still does.

title: Google-parent Alphabet’s stock price plunges, erasing more than $500 billion in value
summary: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank by as much as 15.8%, on course for the company’s worst single-day drop in history.
story: Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank on Thursday by as much as 15.8%, putting the company on course for its worst single-day drop in history.

The plunge also instantly wiped out more than $550 billion in market capitalization, also ranking as the company’s worst one day market value loss ever. It also ranks as the second-worst wipeout in market history, only behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025.
Google is still America’s fourth largest company by market value, and its shares are worth more than $3.4 trillion, all told.

But the sharp drop in its stock price Thursday was the latest sign of a broader anxiety creeping through Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on their massive investments.
The significant selling came after the company reported its latest quarterly financials Wednesday, revealing that revenues fell short of Wall Street expectations.
It also reported lackluster advertising sales.
The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a Thursday morning note.
For Subscribers

A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was because of Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads.
The company is working on addressing this, senior vice president Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results”
Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app.
For Subscribers

But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multi-year spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems.

The company said during its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, which is double what it spent in 2025. The company in June also raised almost $80 billion in capital, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI buildout.

Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft, whose shares initially rose in after market trading Wednesday and overnight, before  reversing course to fall about 2% by 10:50 a.m. ET Thursday.
The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which was down 1.6% by mid-morning. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.6%.
Stock in the chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.6%.
The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9% early Thursday.
Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that the company’s revenues beat Wall Street expectations, but by less than many traders had hoped.

As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI buildout, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, like Caterpillar, have been punished with dramatic sell-offs.

title: Alaska governor orders investigation into Peltola camp after report they recruited second Dan Sullivan
summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it recruited a candidate with the same name as her Republican rival, Sen.
story: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it recruited a candidate with the same name as her Republican rival, Sen. Dan Sullivan, onto the ballot in an effort to dilute his votes.

The Department of Public Safety would seek to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted,” Dunleavy said in an overnight post to X. “The evidence will determine what happens next.”

Dunleavy, a Republican, referred to Wednesday’s revelations from a bombshell New York Times report as “disturbing new evidence” and said that “anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”

The Times published an explosive report detailing the campaign and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s alleged efforts to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent, citing interviews with 12 people who were involved with or were told about the plan, or were contacted as potential recruits. The report also cited dozens of text messages among participants.

The Times’ report included information from Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August. Rios later contacted the Times and “retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race,” the outlet reported.

The revelations have rocked the critical battleground race. Republicans have widely condemned Democrats for allegedly trying to manipulate the ballot, which they argue could confuse voters, and the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan loses.
NBC News has reached out to the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment on Dunleavy’s announcement.

Reached for comment Wednesday on the Times report, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also pointed to instances of Republicans allegedly propping up “spoiler” candidates.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
A spokesperson for the DSCC, the campaign arm of Senate Democrats, said in a statement that the group “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit challenger Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law.
Following the report, President Donald Trump called for Peltola and the challenger Sullivan to be “removed from the ballot and prosecuted.”
Asked by a reporter whether he agreed that Peltola should be prosecuted, Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that “we should certainly look into whether she committed election fraud.”

“She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he said later. “So whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her.”

title: Ernie Johnson set to hang up his NBA microphone after this season
summary: Longtime “Inside the NBA” host Ernie Johnson announced Wednesday that this season behind the desk will be his last, ending a career that made him one of the most prominent voices of pro basketball.
story: Longtime “Inside the NBA”  host Ernie Johnson announced Wednesday that this season behind the desk will be his last, ending a career that made him one of the most prominent voices of pro basketball.
Johnson thanked show staff and co-hosts Shaquille O’Neal, Kenny Smith and Charles Barkley, calling his “Inside the NBA” gig as the ultimate “get-to” position for the past 37 years.

“I’ve long described it as a ‘get-to job.’ I’m still amazed that I get to do this for a living,” Johnson said. “It’s been an honor to share so many nights, decades actually, at the desk with my brothers — Kenny, Charles and Shaq — and with our production crews who are so talented and devoted. And I so appreciate the leadership at TNT and ESPN for allowing the show to continue.”
At age 70, Johnson said the homework he needs to do for every show had become enough a burden to make 2027 the year to step away.

The host has been fighting heart disease for at least two years and underwent bypass surgery 14 months ago. He also was previously diagnosed with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, a cancer of the lymphatic system, in 2003, and prostate cancer in 2019.

“So why now?” Johnson said. “Total honesty here. I’ve always prided myself on my preparation. The hours I put in every day, getting ready for the next show. I’ve always loved that part of my job. But I’ve always vowed that if that ever became more of a challenge than it is a joy, then I’ll know it’s time to step away.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
He added: “I know after 37 seasons, it’s time.”
Johnson’s stint on “Inside the NBA” began in 1990 on TNT and TBS before the show moved to ESPN last year.
Smith joined the show full-time in 1998 before Barkley was added in  2000 and then O’Neal in 2011.

Johnson’s retirement also throws in question Barkley’s future as a broadcaster. Barkley has called the two of them “a package deal,” and the 63-year-old former Philadelphia 76er, Phoenix Sun and Houston Rocket appeared to fight back tears as he thanked Johnson for all his work.

“That was tough,”  Barkley said on ESPN’s “NBA Tip Off.” “We knew the day was coming, still tough. (I’ve) been here for 26, 27 years and it’s been an honor and privilege to work with you all this time.”
Barkley said when he meets fans off camera, they always want to know more about his co-workers.

“ ‘Where’s Shaq and where’s Kenny,’ like I keep them in my damn back pocket,” Barkley said. “But the question I’m probably asked the most is, ‘Is Ernie Johnson as good a person as he seems?’ And I say, ‘Man, he’s better than that.’ ”

story: HONG KONG — Hong Kong’s leader made a rare apology Thursday for a residential fire that killed 168 people last year, announcing that a top housing official would resign after an investigation blamed corruption and regulatory failures for the Chinese territory’s worst human-caused disaster in decades.

The Nov. 26, 2025, fire at Wang Fuk Court, a high-rise housing estate in the suburban district of Tai Po, swiftly engulfed seven of its eight towers, killing 110 women and 58 men ranging in age from 6 months to 98 years old.
